0.title: The Letter to the Ephesians
0.overview:
Paul wrote this letter from a Roman prison, around AD 60–62, awaiting trial before Caesar. He was chained to a guard. And from that cell he wrote what has often been called the most majestic letter Paul ever penned — a letter so vast in its theological vision, so soaring in its doxology, that it feels less like correspondence and more like a window thrown open onto eternity.

The letter may have been circular — several early manuscripts omit the words “in Ephesus” from 1:1, suggesting it was passed between the churches of Asia Minor. Tychicus carried it personally (6:21). Whether it reached one church or many, it was written for the whole church in every age — including yours.

Did Paul really write it? Many modern scholars think a follower wrote it in his name, pointing to its long sentences and unusual vocabulary, its close overlap with Colossians, and phrases such as his holy apostles and prophets (3:5) that they take to look back on an earlier generation. But the letter names Paul twice (1:1; 3:1), the early church received it as his without dissent, and the differences are well explained by its subject and setting: a letter of praise and teaching rather than controversy, written at the same time as Colossians and carried by the same man (6:21; Col 4:7). A letter claiming to be Paul’s that was not would be a forgery, and the church of that day rejected such letters. The more likely conclusion is that Paul wrote it.

The heartbeat phrase is in Christ, appearing over thirty times. Everything God has done, is doing, and will do for his people is located in the person of his Son. Chosen in him. Redeemed in him. Raised with him. Seated with him. Built together in him. The letter is not primarily about what Christians must do; it is about who Christians already are — and the doing flows from the being.

The grand theme is God’s eternal purpose to unite all things in Christ — things in heaven and things on earth (1:10). The church is not a human institution that God blesses; it is the centrepiece of his cosmic plan, the body through which the manifold wisdom of God is displayed to the watching principalities and powers (3:10). To be part of this church is to be enrolled in the most significant project in the universe.

The structure is clean and powerful. Chapters 1–3 are the great indicative: what God has done in Christ from before the foundation of the world to the present moment. Chapters 4–6 are the great imperative: how the people of God now walk, in every relationship and in every spiritual battle. The hinge is the word “therefore” in 4:1 — one of the most consequential words in Christian ethics. The imperative is always grounded in the indicative. We do not obey in order to be accepted; we obey because we already are.

Preach this letter and you will give your congregation the full panorama of God’s saving purpose, from the eternal counsel of the Trinity before creation to the armour for the battle they face this week. There is nothing higher in Paul. There may be nothing higher in Scripture.

1.title: Grace, Election, and Prayer
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, To the saints who are in Ephesus, and are faithful in Christ Jesus: <sup>2</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>3</sup>Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, <sup>4</sup>even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him. In love <sup>5</sup>he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will, <sup>6</sup>to the praise of his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us in the Beloved. <sup>7</sup>In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace, <sup>8</sup>which he lavished upon us, in all wisdom and insight <sup>9</sup>making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ <sup>10</sup>as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth in him. <sup>11</sup>In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, <sup>12</sup>so that we who were the first to hope in Christ might be to the praise of his glory. <sup>13</sup>In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, <sup>14</sup>who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it, to the praise of his glory. <sup>15</sup>For this reason, because I have heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, <sup>16</sup>I do not cease to give thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers, <sup>17</sup>that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him, <sup>18</sup>having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints, <sup>19</sup>and what is the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his great might <sup>20</sup>that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — Every Spiritual Blessing in Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul opens with one of the most breathtaking passages in all of Scripture — a single unbroken sentence in the Greek, 202 words long, a cascade of praise that pours out of him like a river that has broken its banks. Before a single command is given, before a single duty is laid upon the Ephesians, Paul gives them twelve magnificent verses of pure gift: what God has done, is doing, and will do for his people in Christ. The grammar of grace always works this way — indicative before imperative, blessing before obligation, the gift before the task. You cannot rightly obey what you have not first received.

The structure of the passage is trinitarian and it is deliberate. The Father chooses and adopts (vv.3–6); the Son redeems and reconciles (vv.7–12); the Spirit seals and guarantees (vv.13–14). Every Person of the Godhead is active in our salvation. Every blessing flows from the coordinated purpose of the triune God. And the scope is cosmic — from before the foundation of the world, when we were chosen in Christ before time began, to the fullness of time, when all things in heaven and on earth will be united in him. We are not an afterthought in God's plan. We are its centrepiece, its showcase, the display case for the riches of his grace in the ages to come.

Count the phrase "in Christ" or "in him." It appears eleven times in twelve verses. Every single blessing — election, adoption, redemption, forgiveness, inheritance, sealing — is located not in ourselves, not in our performance, not even in our faith as such, but in Christ. We have these things because we are in him. This is the most important prepositional phrase in the Christian life. To be in Christ is to have everything. To be outside of Christ is to have nothing, however religious, however moral, however sincere one might be. The entire letter of Ephesians is an unpacking of what it means to be in Christ — and it begins here, with a doxology so full and so free it can barely be contained in sentences.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, Grace, and the Glory of God

These twelve verses are the biblical locus classicus of the Reformed doctrine of election. "He chose us in him before the foundation of the world" (v.4) — the election is personal, particular, and prior to anything in us. It is not based on foreseen faith; it is the ground of faith. God chose us before we existed, before we believed, before we had done anything good or bad (Romans 9:11). The choice was made in eternity, rooted in the sovereign good pleasure of his will (v.5), and directed toward the praise of the glory of his grace (v.6).

The purpose of election is not merely the salvation of individuals; it is the display of grace. "So that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus" (2:7). We are saved so that the universe — angels, principalities, and powers — might see what grace looks like. The church is God's exhibit A: the living demonstration that mercy triumphs over judgment, that the undeserving can be made heirs, that the dead can be raised.

John Calvin wrote that the knowledge of election is not given to breed pride or speculation but to ground assurance. The believer who knows they were chosen before the foundation of the world — not because of what they would become but because of God's sovereign love — has a security that no circumstance can shake. This is the pastoral gold of Ephesians 1: your standing before God does not depend on your spiritual performance today. It was settled in eternity, sealed by the Spirit, and guaranteed by the inheritance that awaits.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian Christians lived in the shadow of the great temple of Artemis — one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, a monument to a goddess who offered fertility, protection, and blessing to her devotees. The mystery religions of Ephesus promised spiritual elevation through initiation rites, secret knowledge, and ritual participation. Against all of this, Paul announces something infinitely more magnificent: you already possess every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places — not through ritual, not through initiation, not through any human achievement, but through your union with Christ. You have been chosen, adopted, redeemed, forgiven, enlightened, and sealed. The goddess in the marble temple has nothing to offer you. You are already heirs of the universe.

Now: We live in an age of spiritual seeking. The bookshops are full of self-help and spirituality. People curate their own spiritual experiences, their own moral codes, their own pathways to meaning and blessing. Against all of this noise, Ephesians 1 speaks with clarifying force: every spiritual blessing is in Christ, and in Christ alone. The person who has Christ has everything. The person who lacks Christ lacks everything that ultimately matters, however enriched their life may appear. The church's task is not to offer a slightly better version of what the world already has, but to announce that in Christ, the one thing that actually satisfies every longing of the human heart is freely and fully given.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, to the saints who are in Ephesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul introduces himself as “an apostle” — apostolos, one sent with the full authority of the one who sent him — and addresses his readers as “saints”. Both words are about what God has done, not what they have achieved.

“By the will of God” is not a modest disclaimer; it is the only explanation for his being an apostle at all. His apostleship did not begin with a sense of calling or a period of discernment. It began on a road, with letters in his pocket authorising the arrest of Christians, while he was “breathing threats and murder” against the people he would spend his life serving (Acts 9:1–2). He was not recruited from among the interested; he was intercepted mid-crime. That is why he can open a letter of this size without hesitation. A man who talked himself into a ministry can be talked out of it. A man stopped in the road cannot.

“Saints” (hagioi, “holy ones”) is his ordinary name for every Christian in the city. Today the word means either an exceptionally good person or a figure in a stained-glass window — in both cases an achievement, reserved for a few. Paul means the opposite. Before this letter is finished he will have to tell some of these same people to stop stealing (4:28), stop lying (4:25), deal with their anger before sundown (4:26), and stop the bitterness and slander among them (4:31). These are the saints. The word is not his verdict on how they are doing; it is a statement of who owns them. A temple bowl was holy not because it was beautifully made or unusually clean, but because it had been set apart for God. Its holiness was given from outside, and it did not rise and fall with the state of the bowl.

So try saying, without flinching, “I am a saint.” Most of us reach for a softener — “well, not really, not like some people.” But that flinch is a claim about your record, and the word was never about your record. Refusing the title is not humility; it quietly insists that the label must be earned, which is exactly what Paul is not saying. If you are in Christ, this is how your letter is addressed.

Notice the two addresses in one line: “the saints who are in Ephesus.” Saints belongs to the heavenly places, where they are already seated with Christ (2:6). In Ephesus is a real city, built around the temple of Artemis and so steeped in magic that when the gospel came, the converts burned occult books worth fifty thousand pieces of silver (Acts 19:19). That is the tension every Christian lives in: a settled identity in heaven and a difficult address on earth. Put your own town in the second slot. The letter is addressed to you at both.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote from prison, probably in Rome around AD 60–62. The ESV notes that some early manuscripts omit “in Ephesus”; the letter may have been meant to circulate among several churches of the region.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s greeting is a blessing: God’s free favour (“grace”) and the wholeness it produces (“peace”), coming from the Father and the Son together. Putting “God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” side by side as the single source of both gifts places them on the same level — Trinitarian theology stated before the letter has begun.

The two words themselves make a point. A Greek letter normally opened with chairein, “greetings”; a Jew greeted with shalom. Paul bends the Greek word into its cousin charis, grace, and sets it next to the Hebrew one. A Greek word and a Jewish word stand together in the first line of a letter that will explain how Christ has made Jew and Gentile one and broken down the dividing wall (2:14–16). Paul is not just saying hello; he is already demonstrating his argument.

The order never changes in any of Paul’s letters: grace, then peace. One produces the other. Grace is what God does; peace is what results. Many people want the second without the first — the calm, the quiet conscience — and hope to reach it by managing their lives well enough to deserve it. It cannot be done in that direction. Peace is not a mood you generate; it is the state of a person against whom nothing is held any longer, and only grace produces that: “since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God” (Romans 5:1).

We have also shrunk the word peace to an atmosphere — a peaceful evening, a quiet room. Shalom is wholeness: everything in its right relation and working as it was designed. That is why a Christian can have it in a hospital bed and a man can lack it entirely on a beach. The question is not how much pressure is on you, but whether the central relationship of your life is in order — and that one, Paul says, is settled.

There is no verb in the Greek. Paul does not write “I hope you receive” or “may you have”, but simply “grace to you and peace” — closer to a pronouncement than a wish, the way Aaron was told to put the LORD’s name on Israel (Numbers 6:24–26). And he says “God our Father”, putting himself in with a congregation of former thieves and idolaters. Two words in, and the family has been named.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul begins with praise: God deserves to be blessed, because he has already blessed us with every spiritual blessing there is, in Christ. Verses 3–14 are a single sentence in Greek — the longest in the New Testament, from a man so caught up that he cannot find a place to stop. Verse 3 is the headline; verses 4–14 are the list.

Two kinds of blessing. To bless (eulogeo, literally “to speak well of”) means different things depending on who does it. When we bless God, we cannot add anything to him; our blessing is praise — speaking well of him because he deserves it. When God blesses us, his word is never mere breath: his blessing does not just wish us well, it makes us well. So it was on the first page of the Bible: “And God blessed them. And God said to them, ‘Be fruitful and multiply’” (Genesis 1:28) — the word carried the gift it spoke. We bless God with our lips because he has first blessed us with his hand. (This word for God being “blessed” is reserved in the New Testament for God alone; the “blessed” of the Beatitudes, makarios, is a different word, describing a person’s happy state.)

“Spiritual” does not mean thin. To us “spiritual” suggests something wispy and private — a vague inner glow. For Paul, pneumatikos means belonging to the Holy Spirit, given and carried to us by him. These are not flimsy blessings compared to solid ones; they are more substantial than anything you could put in a bank. Your salary is temporary and your health is on loan; your adoption is not.

That collides with what “blessed” usually means to us: a circumstance that went well — the promotion, the clean scan, the parking space. Run that definition through this letter and it falls apart. The man writing is under arrest and will die in custody; some of his readers are slaves, and some will be killed for Christ within a generation. If blessing meant good circumstances, Paul would be an unblessed man telling unblessed people how blessed they are. He is not being ironic. Look at the list that follows, and notice what is not on it: not one item is a circumstance. Chosen (v. 4), adopted (v. 5), graced (v. 6), redeemed and forgiven (v. 7), given wisdom (v. 8), let into God’s plan (v. 9), given an inheritance (v. 11), sealed with the Spirit as the guarantee of the rest (vv. 13–14). None of it can be lost in a redundancy, a diagnosis or a bad year.

The tense. Paul does not say God will bless us, or is willing to if we ask properly. He says he has blessed us — done, with nothing outstanding. So the prayer “Lord, bless me”, offered as though the cupboard were bare, misunderstands where we stand. The Christian is not a beggar at the door; he is an heir who has not yet read the inventory. Your problem this morning is almost certainly not that God has withheld something, but that you do not know what you already have.

“In the heavenly places”. This phrase appears five times in Ephesians (1:3, 20; 2:6; 3:10; 6:12) and nowhere else in Paul. It cannot simply mean heaven as the home of the redeemed, because the fifth use places “the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places” (6:12). It means the unseen realm itself — the spiritual dimension where God, Christ, angels and hostile powers all operate, not far above us but just behind what we can see. Read the five together and they make an argument: the blessings are there (1:3), Christ is enthroned there (1:20), you are seated with him there (2:6), the powers there are watching the church (3:10), and your real struggle is there (6:12). Blessings, throne, seat, audience, battlefield — all in a realm you have never seen. Paul does not explain why he uses the phrase only here, but the likeliest reason is the city: Ephesus was famous for magic, its spells known across the empire as “Ephesian letters”. These readers had spent their lives trying to manage unseen powers. Paul does not tell them the unseen realm is imaginary; he tells them who is enthroned there and that they are seated with him above it all.

One guard: this is no invitation to drift into dreaminess. Having taken his readers into the heavenly places five times, Paul ends the letter with telling the truth, honest work, not provoking your children, and how to treat your household. The most cosmic letter in the New Testament ends in the kitchen. Knowing where the throne is does not lift you out of your Tuesday; it tells you who is over it.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 3–14 are a single long sentence of praise in the Greek. “The heavenly places” is the unseen realm where Christ reigns.

verseByVerse.quote: Even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before creation, God chose his people in Christ, and chose them to be holy. The ground of the choice lies entirely in God — not in foreseen faith or merit, but in his own free love.

Chosen for something. “That we should be holy and blameless before him.” Holy (hagios) means set apart, as the temple vessels were reserved for God. Blameless (amōmos) is the word for a sacrifice without blemish. And the key phrase is “before him” — blameless in God’s sight. Does Paul mean sinless perfection? He means two things at once. Now, you are already holy and blameless in God’s sight — not on your record but in Christ’s (Colossians 1:22). One day, God will finish the work and present you “blameless before the presence of his glory” (Jude 24). The standing gives you your footing: “I am not disqualified.” The direction gives you your goal: “I am not finished.” So a believer who sinned badly this week does not come back to God with a diminished holiness, because it was never measured by this week. That is not a licence to sin (Romans 6:1–2); it is the mercy that makes repentance possible.

Is it fair? The question assumes we were owed a choosing. We were not. Left to justice, every one of us would be passed by, for all have sinned (Romans 3:23). The marvel is not that some are not chosen but that any are. No one perishes who wanted Christ and was refused; the lost are lost by their own will, the saved rescued by God’s.

What about my choice — and why evangelise? Scripture holds both truths without apology. The same letter that says you were chosen before creation pleads with you to walk worthy of your calling (4:1); the same Paul begged people to be reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20). You heard and believed, and your believing was truly yours (v. 13); God’s choice runs underneath your choice, not instead of it. Where the two meet is deeper than we can see: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God” (Deuteronomy 29:29). And far from killing mission, election is why mission cannot fail. To a discouraged Paul in Corinth the Lord said, “I have many in this city who are my people” (Acts 18:10). We preach to everyone because God has a people to gather, and not one will be missed.

Other views. Many Christians in the Arminian tradition hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe (citing Romans 8:29 and 1 Peter 1:2). Others hold that election is corporate: Christ is the chosen one, and God chose a people rather than particular persons. But Paul says God chose us, and chose us that we should be holy — holiness and faith are the result of the choosing, not its reason — and he chose “according to the purpose of his will” (v. 5). The more likely reading is that God chose particular people in Christ, freely, before the world began.

“Am I one of them?” This is the question asked at two in the morning. Left there, a doctrine of election can sound like a sealed list in a drawer in heaven. But Paul says God chose us “in him”. Christ is himself the Chosen One — “my chosen, in whom my soul delights” (Isaiah 42:1) — and election means being joined to him. So the question is not answered by peering into eternity, where you cannot see, but by asking whether you are in Christ and find yourself wanting him.

And notice when the love was set on you: “before the foundation of the world.” There was nothing about you to see — no faith, no obedience, not even existence. That is the most secure thing that could be said about it. A love that began before you were anything cannot be ended by your turning out disappointing. The basis was never you, so there is nothing you can fail at that will lose it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “in love” may go with verse 4: “holy and blameless before him in love.”

verseByVerse.quote: In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s choice was a Father’s choice: “in love he predestined us for adoption”. “In love” most likely belongs with this verse — it was in love that he predestined. Predestination is not a cold decree but the Father’s affectionate purpose to have children.

“Adoption” (huiothesia) was a legal term for giving full sonship to someone not born to it. In Roman law an adopted son received the full standing and inheritance of a natural heir; his old family no longer had a claim on him. And the ground of it lies entirely in God: “according to the purpose of his will.” That is not harsh; it is the guarantee that it will last, because it does not depend on us.

But no doctrine more quickly sends a tender conscience into fear: “How do I know I am one of them?” The common mistake is to try to climb into heaven and read God’s secret decree. You cannot read it, and you were never asked to. God has laid the evidence within reach, in his Son. So do not look up into the hidden counsel; look at Christ, and at your heart’s answer to him. Do you want him? Do you find yourself — however feebly — trusting him, loving his people, grieved when you sin against him? That desire did not begin with you. Dead men do not long for God; the wanting is the fingerprint of the Spirit who sealed you when you believed (v. 13). Faith is not the ticket you must show to prove you were chosen; it is the evidence that you were. “Whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37) — and the proof that you were chosen before the foundation of the world is the plainest thing in the world: you came.

Theologians call this “unconditional election” — not because God chose arbitrarily, but because the condition was not found in us. Paul puts the reason elsewhere: “according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of his glorious grace.”
verseByVerse.note: In Roman law an adopted son received the full rights and inheritance of a natural son.

verseByVerse.quote: To the praise of his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us in the Beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything God has done in salvation ends in his praise: “to the praise of his glorious grace.” This is the first of three such refrains (vv. 6, 12, 14), closing the work of the Father, the Son and the Spirit in turn. Salvation has a purpose beyond the saved.

Is that vanity? A modern reader feels the question even if he never asks it aloud. We do not admire people who arrange every conversation to end in applause for themselves. Why is it admirable in God? C. S. Lewis was troubled by exactly this. What broke it open for him was noticing what praise actually is. We naturally praise what we enjoy — music, a landscape, a friend’s cooking — not because we are asked to, but because delight overflows into speech, and the enjoyment is not complete until it is spoken. The finest walk is only half enjoyed until someone says “look at that.” Praise is not payment extracted from us; it is enjoyment reaching its full form. If God is infinitely good, then calling us to praise him is not vanity but honesty — telling us the truth about the most valuable thing there is — and kindness, because it points us to our deepest joy. A father who tells his son to come and look at the sunrise is not fishing for compliments on his taste; he wants the boy to see it.

“With which he has blessed us” is in Greek a single verb, echaritōsen — he has “graced” us. It appears only once elsewhere in the New Testament, when the angel Gabriel greets Mary: “Greetings, O favored one” — literally, you who have been graced (Luke 1:28). She had done nothing to earn it; she was simply the object of God’s free favour. Paul uses the same verb of ordinary believers in Ephesus — dockworkers, slaves, tradespeople.

“In the Beloved.” Paul chooses the title the Father spoke from heaven over his Son (Matthew 3:17). The love that falls on you is not a second-class affection God worked up for sinners. You are inside the Beloved, so the love that has always run between the Father and the Son runs over you as well — exactly what Jesus prayed on his last night, that the world may know that the Father “loved them even as you loved me” (John 17:23). Not somewhat as. Even as.
verseByVerse.note: “The Beloved” is Christ, echoing the Father’s voice at his baptism.

verseByVerse.quote: In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Christ’s death we are set free and forgiven. “Redemption” (apolutrōsis) is the language of the slave market and the exodus: paying a price to secure someone’s release. The price was “his blood” — not his teaching or his example, but his death. And the result is “the forgiveness of our trespasses”: the actual cancellation of actual sins, given “according to the riches of his grace” — not the minimum, but lavishly.

See both pictures. In the slave market a man stands on the block; he cannot buy himself, because he no longer owns himself. Someone else pays in full, and he walks out with nothing to repay, having contributed nothing but his chains. In Egypt on the last night, what stood between each household and the destroyer was not their character or their remorse but blood on a doorpost. In both scenes the freedom is real, total, and entirely someone else’s doing.

Why blood? To modern ears it sounds primitive, and the question underneath is fair: why can God not simply forgive? Because no one ever forgives without cost. If someone smashes something of yours, there are only two possibilities. He pays — and then nothing has been forgiven, only settled. Or you forgive him — and then you absorb the loss; the thing stays broken and you carry it. That is why forgiving a real injury hurts. When God forgives, he is not waving away a small sum. Real wrong has been done to a holy God, and a God who simply ignored it would not be gracious but indifferent, like a judge who dismissed every case. God did what every true forgiver does, on a scale beyond measuring: he absorbed the cost himself. The blood is the measure of what it cost him. And it is the pattern the letter will ask of you: “forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (4:32) — bearing the cost rather than passing it on.

Notice the tense: we have redemption — held now, on your worst day as securely as on your best. And notice what is forgiven: “our trespasses”, plural and particular. Not a vague amnesty for humanity, but an account with your name at the top and your own items listed below — including the one you have never told anyone, and the one you did again last week. Those. Paid for, and gone.
verseByVerse.note: Redemption was the word for buying a slave’s freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: Which he lavished upon us, in all wisdom and insight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God poured out his grace on us generously — “lavished” — and wisely: “in all wisdom and insight.” This is not reckless giving but intelligent abundance.

Whose wisdom is it? It can be read as God’s: he gave wisely. But there is strong reason to read it as part of what he gave us. The two words are not synonyms: sophia is wisdom in the deep sense — grasping how things really are, God and his purposes; phronēsis is its practical partner — discernment, knowing what to do on Monday morning. Three things suggest these are given to believers. In the twin letter, Paul prays that the Colossians be filled “with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding” (Colossians 1:9). A few verses on he prays for the same gift here (vv. 17–18). And the sentence runs straight on: “making known to us the mystery of his will” (v. 9). A mystery cannot be made known to someone who has not been given the ability to receive it. The wisdom is the equipment for the revelation arriving in the next breath.

Nothing is lost if you take it the other way, because both are true: God’s plan is supremely wise (3:10). But the point to carry home is this. The grace that saves you does not rescue you and leave you baffled about what has happened. God gives the gift, and then gives the eyes to see it. That is why this letter can spend three chapters on God’s eternal purposes and still expect dockworkers, slaves and tradesmen in Ephesus to follow every word.

verseByVerse.quote: making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has let us into his plan: to bring everything in heaven and on earth back together under Christ as its head. A “mystery” (mystērion) in Paul is not a puzzle but a purpose once hidden and now revealed (Romans 16:25–26).

The key verb, anakephalaiōsasthai, means to sum up or gather everything under one head. The fall shattered a unified world: God and humanity estranged, people at war with each other, creation “subjected to futility” (Romans 8:20), the powers in rebellion. God’s plan, made before creation, is to reunite it all under Jesus Christ. Notice “all things”, not just all people. Salvation is bigger than rescuing souls out of a ruined world; it is the restoration of everything to its right relation to its true head. Creation is renewed, not discarded (Revelation 21:1–5), and the hostile powers, already disarmed at the cross (Colossians 2:15), are brought into subjection.

Does this mean everyone, even the devil, will be saved? No. To unite all things under Christ means to bring everything under his rule, not to save every creature. This same letter warns that the immoral and covetous have “no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God” and that God’s wrath comes on “the sons of disobedience” (5:5–6). Every knee will bow (Philippians 2:10–11) — some in worship, some in defeat. The universe will be put right; it will not be emptied of judgment.

What would it look like? Measure the promise against what is broken now. A world under one head has no thorns in the ground and no tumours in the body; no funerals, because nothing is left to bury; no armies, because nothing is left to defend against; no families quietly divided by something said twenty years ago. You will no longer be divided against yourself — the person you want to be and the person you are will at last be the same. Heaven and earth will no longer be two addresses. Now we pray, “your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10), a prayer that admits a gap; then, “the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3). And nothing good is lost: “the glory and the honor of the nations” are brought in (Revelation 21:26). Everything you have ever loved is kept; everything that spoiled it is gone.

Now or later? Both. Already Christ is seated above every authority and given as head over all things to the church (1:20–22). The gathering has begun, and it has a visible address. When a Jew and a Gentile sat down at one table in Ephesus, that was the future arriving early — and every genuine reconciliation in a church is the same. Not yet: “At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him” (Hebrews 2:8–9). We are not asked to pretend the world is already put right. We see him; that is enough to go on with.

Why it matters to God. The fall was at root a dishonouring: creatures refusing to be governed in the world their Maker made. Sin is not only damage but a rival throne. Gathering all things under Christ ends every rival throne, until every tongue confesses “that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:11). That is why the refrain keeps returning: “to the praise of his glory” (vv. 12, 14; compare v. 6).

And this is the world you already long for. The ache under our best music and our worst politics is the same: we keep trying to build a world that holds together and keep failing, because every attempt unites it under something that cannot bear the weight — a leader, a nation, an idea, a self. That homesickness for a country you have never visited is not a defect. It is the memory of what the world was for, and Paul here tells you its name: not a system or a golden age, but a Person, under whom everything finally fits.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we who were the first to hope in Christ might be to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Christ we have been given an inheritance, and it cannot fail, because God “works all things according to the counsel of his will.” Everything in this passage hangs on the words “in him”: chosen in him (v. 4), adopted (v. 5), redeemed (v. 7), and now given an inheritance in him. Your standing before God is not in your own name or record but in Christ, accepted because he is accepted.

What the inheritance is. The verb (eklērōthēmen) means to be given a portion, as the land was divided by lot among Israel’s tribes (Joshua 14:1–2). It has two sides.

First, God himself. When the land was divided, the other tribes walked away with a map — this valley, that ridge, the olive terraces. Levi was given no land at all, and God explained why: “I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel” (Numbers 18:20). The other tribes were given things God had made; Levi was given God. Test it on yourself: if you were given everything you ever wanted — health, every broken relationship mended, the people you have buried given back — but God himself were not there, would it be heaven? Every honest Christian knows the answer is no. “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you” (Psalm 73:25). And if you had him and nothing else, you would still be rich. That is why this portion cannot be lost. Everything else can be taken by a diagnosis, a market or time. A portion that is God cannot be repossessed.

Second, the glory to come, which Scripture describes concretely. A body raised imperishable, like Christ’s glorious body (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; Philippians 3:21). A renewed world, which “the meek… shall inherit” (Matthew 5:5; Revelation 21:1–5). A face: “they will see his face” (Revelation 22:4) — the one thing Moses asked for and was refused. A likeness: “we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2). And meaningful work with real responsibility (Luke 19:17). The measure of it all: we are “fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17). Not a small plot at the edge of the estate — whatever belongs to the Son is settled on you. The two sides are one thing: the coming glory is having God with nothing left in the way, together with everything he has made new.

If God works all things, what about our free will — and our sin? God’s purpose works through human choices, not around them. Joseph’s brothers chose freely and sinned, and “God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). The men who crucified Jesus were guilty, yet they did “whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:28). Many Christians hold that real freedom requires the power to choose otherwise, so God’s plan must make room for undetermined choices. The Reformed answer, which fits these texts better, is that God ordains all that happens, yet is not the author of sin, which comes from the creature, and every person is responsible for what he chooses (James 1:13). The cross is the proof that both are true at once.

Who are “we who were the first to hope in Christ”? Most likely the Jewish believers, Paul among them, who hoped for the Messiah before the Gentiles heard of him. That is why verse 13 turns to “you also”, the Gentile readers, and chapter 2 brings the two together into one people.

Note the tense: we “have obtained” an inheritance. The deed is signed in the blood of the Son; only delivery is outstanding. The poorest believer reading this is already an heir of God, and the estate is not in doubt, because the One who works all things is the executor of the will.

verseByVerse.quote: In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it, to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Paul turns to the Gentile readers: “you also.” The moment they heard the gospel and believed, they were sealed with the Holy Spirit, who is God’s guarantee that they will receive the full inheritance.

The seal. Picture the docks at Ephesus. A merchant’s cargo is bound, and he presses his signet ring into hot wax across the bindings. Everyone on the quay knew what it said: “This is mine” (ownership); “this is genuine” (not swapped along the way); and “this is protected” — to break the seal was to answer to the man whose ring made the mark. God’s seal on you is not wax or a certificate but a Person: “sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.” God’s answer to whether you will arrive is to put himself on you.

When it happens. Paul ties it to one moment: you heard, you believed, you were sealed. It is not a later upgrade for advanced Christians or a second blessing some receive and others wait for. Some dear brothers and sisters read it that way, out of a real hunger for more of God, which is nothing to sneer at; but the grammar here runs the other way. If you have believed, you are sealed already. You can recognise it not by hunting for a feeling but by the marks the Spirit leaves: you call God Father and mean it (Romans 8:15–16), sin now grieves you where it once did not, and Christ has become precious to you, not merely true.

The guarantee. The arrabōn was a legal down payment — in modern Greek the same word means an engagement ring. It is the first instalment that commits the giver to pay the rest, and it is part of the same thing, not a sample of something else. So what you have of the Spirit now is not a lesser commodity than heaven; it is heaven’s first payment in heaven’s own currency. The peace that came when nothing in your circumstances justified it, the joy that has caught you sideways in a hymn, the love you find for people you would never have chosen — that is not preparation for the inheritance. It is the inheritance, in instalments.

Can a sealed believer fall away? Some Christians hold that a true believer can turn away and be lost, pointing to the warnings in Hebrews (6:4–6; 10:26–29) and Galatians 5:4. Those warnings are real and must be heard. But the seal is God’s, not ours, and Jesus says of his sheep, “they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). Those who finally fall away show they were never truly his (1 John 2:19). The warnings are among the means God uses to keep the people he has sealed.

This also explains why the Christian life feels the way it does. You hold the deposit, not the estate, so the ache is not a sign that something is wrong with your faith; the deposit was designed to make you homesick. A man with an engagement ring is not less eager for the wedding than a man without one, but far more eager and far more certain. And notice who would lose if the day never came: the one who paid the deposit. God has put down a deposit he does not intend to forfeit.

So the praise closes for the third time: “to the praise of his glory” — after the Father choosing, the Son redeeming and the Spirit sealing. One salvation, three hands, one refrain.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and security. The “guarantee” was a first instalment, pledging full payment later.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul prays. The man who has just outlined the most concentrated doctrinal statement in the New Testament now falls on his knees for the people he loves. And his prayer is not for comfort, not for prosperity, not even for their safety — it is for illumination. He prays that they would know. Not know more information about God — they have just received an overwhelming cascade of theological truth. But know it experientially, vitally, in the way that transforms the soul rather than merely informing the mind. There is a vast difference between possessing a treasure and being fully aware of what you possess. Paul prays to close that gap.

Three things he asks for illumination about, each one more staggering than the last. First: the hope of their calling — the glorious future that God has promised and secured for those who are in Christ. Second: the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints — the almost incomprehensible truth that God himself regards his people as his inheritance, his treasure, his glory. Third: the immeasurable greatness of his power toward those who believe. And to give the Ephesians a sense of how great that power is, Paul reaches for the most powerful event in history as his measure: the resurrection of Jesus from the dead and his exaltation to the right hand of the Father, far above every name and authority and power in the universe. That power — the power that raised the dead and shattered the dominion of death — is at work in you.

The prayer closes with a vision of Christ as head over all things to the church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all. The church is not a voluntary association of like-minded believers. It is the body of the cosmic Lord, the community through which the exalted Christ exercises his reign in the world. To be part of the church is to be part of the most significant institution in the universe — the community of the risen King.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit of Wisdom and Revelation

Paul prays for "the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him" (v.17). This single phrase encapsulates the Reformed understanding of how divine truth moves from the page to the heart. The Spirit who inspired the Scripture is also required to illuminate the reader of Scripture. Without the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit, the words of God remain external — true, but not transforming; known about, but not known. Calvin devoted a famous section of the Institutes to this: the Scripture needs no external proof of its authority, because the Spirit who produced it also produces the certainty of it in the heart of the believer.

The practical implication is that Bible reading and prayer are inseparable disciplines. To open the Scripture without asking the Spirit to open our eyes to it is to work without our most essential tool. The Puritans understood this, and habitually prayed for illumination before they opened the book. The eyes of the heart do not open themselves. This prayer of Paul's is therefore not only a prayer about the Ephesians — it is a prayer for every reader of Scripture in every age who wants not merely to know about God but to know God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul writes this prayer from prison. He cannot visit the Ephesians; he cannot lay hands on them; he cannot preach to them in person. What he can do is pray — and his prayer from chains is not for his own release but for their illumination. This is one of the most searching things in the letter: the imprisoned apostle, whose situation would seem to give him every right to focus on his own needs, pours his intercession entirely outward, toward the people he loves. His joy is in their knowledge of Christ, not in his own circumstances. This is the mind of Christ (Philippians 2:5) applied to prayer.

Now: We live in an age of unprecedented access to biblical content. More sermons, commentaries, podcasts, and Bible apps exist today than at any point in history. And yet spiritual blindness remains our greatest problem. We have more information about God than any previous generation, and arguably less experiential knowledge of him. Paul's prayer cuts through all of this: what we need is not more content but opened eyes — the Spirit of wisdom and revelation, granting us not information but encounter. The Ephesians had Paul's letter. We have the whole Bible. Both of us need the same thing: the Spirit who makes the word alive.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason, because I have heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, I do not cease to give thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of everything God has done (“for this reason”), Paul prays — and he begins with thanks for their faith in Jesus and their love for all God’s people. Theology turns into intercession: a mind full of God falls to its knees.

See where he is as he writes: in Rome under guard, most likely chained to a soldier (Acts 28:16, 20). He cannot travel, send money or step in to sort anything out in Ephesus, and he may never see these people again. So he does the only thing left to him, which turns out to be the greatest thing one person can do for another: he carries them to God, and “I do not cease” doing it. Prison did not reduce his ministry to prayer; it revealed that prayer had always been the larger half of it.

And notice how he knows anything at all: “I have heard of your faith.” Someone talked — a traveller, a merchant, a courier — and news of a church where people trusted Jesus and cared for one another reached a cell in Rome. Your faith is being reported somewhere too, usually to people you will never meet. You are rarely the best judge of what your quiet obedience is doing at a distance.

He thanks God for two things that always go together: “faith in the Lord Jesus” and “love toward all the saints”. Faith looks up to Christ; love reaches out to his people — “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). And do not slide past “all”. Ephesus held Jews and Gentiles in one church — people raised to regard each other as unclean, who now had to share the same cup — and Paul is about to spend a chapter on how that wall came down (2:14–16). This is not warmth toward the agreeable but love toward the whole awkward company, including the ones you would cross the street to avoid. That is the only kind of love that proves anything.

And he starts with thanksgiving. There is plenty he will correct later, but the first thing he says about this church is gratitude to God for what is already there. Copy that the next time you think about a person or a congregation with a long way still to go.

verseByVerse.quote: That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul asks God to give the Ephesians “the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him” — not more information, but a real, personal knowledge of God himself.

He first addresses God as “the Father of glory”. The Hebrew word for glory, kābôd, means weight — what is solid enough to matter. That reverses how we rank things. What feels solid to us is what we can bank and put on a CV: salary, house, reputation. Scripture calls those the lightweight things, “like chaff that the wind drives away” (Psalm 1:4). God is the heavy thing, the most real object there is, and everything else has weight only as far as it reflects him.

The Ephesians already have the Spirit (v. 13), so Paul is not asking for a second giving of him. He asks that the Spirit would work as the one who opens eyes — taking what is already true of God and making it personally known. Wisdom is seeing reality as God sees it: reading your suffering within his purpose, seeing the cross, an apparent defeat, as the turning point of history. Revelation here is not new Scripture but the curtain drawn back on what is already given, so that words you have read for years suddenly land as if for the first time. The goal is “the knowledge of him” — epignōsis, knowing God, not merely knowing about him (John 17:3).

Notice what Paul does. He has just written twelve of the greatest verses in the New Testament, and he does not assume that will be enough. He prays, because he can put truth in front of their minds and still not get it into their hearts. Every preacher and parent learns this the hard way: you can explain something perfectly and watch it not land, and you have no lever for the last six inches. Only God can open eyes.

So ask yourself honestly: is God someone you know a great deal about, or someone you know? You can know a man’s birthday, job, hometown and the name of his dog, and never have met him. If the honest answer is the first, this verse tells you what to do, because it is a prayer and not an instruction: ask, in these words, for yourself, this week. Paul could have prayed for their circumstances to ease or their numbers to grow. He asked that they would know God, because someone who truly knows him is ready for anything that comes, and someone who does not is ready for nothing, however well life is going.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding

verseByVerse.quote: Having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that God would open “the eyes of your hearts” to see three things. This verse gives the first two: the hope God has called them to, and how precious they are to him.

In Scripture the heart is not mainly the seat of feeling but the centre of the whole person, and it has its own eyes. You can understand every word of a sentence and still miss what it means. Most Christians know the moment when a verse they have read a hundred times suddenly opens, and they sit very still over words that did nothing to them last year. Nothing changed in the text; the lights came on in the room. That is what Paul asks God for. He can improve the teaching; he cannot flip the switch.

The hope. “The hope to which he has called you” is not a wish but a certainty not yet seen: the resurrection of the body, the renewal of all things, the end of every grief, seeing God face to face — all guaranteed because Jesus rose. Scripture pictures it as an anchor (Hebrews 6:19). An anchor is not dropped behind a ship to hold it where it has been; it is thrown ahead, grips ground the crew cannot see, and steadies them in today’s weather. Christian hope is neither nostalgia nor optimism. Whether you have truly seen it shows up in very ordinary places: what happens inside you when money goes, what happens at a graveside, and whether the thought of your own death is a horror or a door. A real Christian can still live as if this life were all there is; the heart that has seen this hope holds the present loosely and can lose things without being destroyed.

God’s inheritance. “The riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints” — and the wording stops you. This is God’s inheritance in his people. God has an inheritance, and it is us — as he said of Israel, “you shall be my treasured possession” (Exodus 19:5). He owns the galaxies; they are his handiwork. What did the God who owns everything count as treasure and go out and buy at cost? Not the stars. You. Jesus told of a man who found treasure in a field and “sells all that he has and buys that field” (Matthew 13:44). We usually read ourselves as the buyer. Turn it round: he is the man who sold everything. And a treasure is priced by what the buyer paid: “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). So when you are tempted, as most believers are by about Tuesday, to think of yourself as someone God barely tolerates, this verse stands in the way. You are not what he tolerates; you are what he is inheriting.

The third thing Paul wants them to see answers the obvious objection — that people like us are too weak to make it to the end. That is the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: And what is the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his great might that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third thing Paul prays they will see is the size of God’s power at work for believers — and he measures it by the resurrection. It is the same power God used “when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places.”

Paul piles up words for power — dynamis (capacity), energeia (power at work), kratos (mastery), ischus (strength) — like a man describing something beyond description, and then anchors them to one event. Notice that he does not say God’s power is like resurrection power, or a smaller household version of it. It is “according to the working of his great might that he worked in Christ” — the same power, now aimed at you.

Look at what it had to do the first time. This was no resuscitation of a man whose heart had stopped a few minutes earlier. Jesus had been executed in public by professionals who did not make mistakes about it. He had been taken down, wrapped, carried and sealed in. The stone was in place, the guard was posted, and his friends had gone home to make arrangements for grief, not for Sunday. Death had won completely, with witnesses. Then God acted, and the one power that has never lost an argument simply gave way.

Now set your own situation beside that: the habit you have failed to break for twenty years, the person you cannot forgive, the fear you have never beaten, the prayer you have carried so long you no longer expect an answer. Ask the question the verse is built to make you ask: is any of it harder than a corpse?

What the power is for. Mostly not for spectacle. It is power to believe and keep believing (Philippians 2:13); power over sin, since the strength that broke death can break an old habit (Romans 6:4–6); power to endure — the long marriage, the chronic illness — “strengthened with all power… for all endurance and patience with joy” (Colossians 1:11); power to love difficult people (3:16–17); and power “made perfect in weakness” when your own strength runs out (2 Corinthians 12:9). And what it is not for: not removing all hardship — the man writing this is in prison, his thorn unremoved — and not a reward for impressive faith. It is “toward us who believe”, not us who believe flawlessly. “I believe; help my unbelief!” cried a desperate father, and Jesus acted (Mark 9:24). The power does not scale with your faith but with God, and any faith fixed on him lays hold of it.

Notice the word “toward”: the power is not locked in a vault awaiting the right paperwork; it is already in motion toward you. That is why it comes third in the prayer: the hope tells you where you are going, the inheritance tells you what you are worth to God, and then, just as you think people like you will never arrive, comes the power, measured by an empty tomb.

“And seated him at his right hand.” The right hand is the place of royal authority: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool” (Psalm 110:1). Christ sits because his atoning work is finished, and he reigns now (v. 22). And Paul will soon add that the same power has already been used on you: God “made us alive together with Christ… and raised us up with him and seated us with him” (2:5–6). The question of whether this power is equal to your situation has been settled in your own case. It did the hardest thing it will ever do for you while you were dead.

parallels.desc: sit at my right hand

verseByVerse.quote: Far above all rule and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Christ reigns “far above” every power there is, in this age and the next. There is no authority, earthly or spiritual, that he does not rule.

To us this may sound abstract. To the Ephesians it was liberation. Their city was full of spiritual power — the temple of Artemis and a whole industry of magic; when Paul preached, converts burned scrolls worth fifty thousand pieces of silver (Acts 19:19). They lived in dread of named spirits and rulers that had to be appeased. Into that fear Paul announces: Christ is above every one of them.

“Far above” (hyperanō) is a claim about kind, not just rank. Christ is not the highest name on the chart of powers; he drew the chart. The four words Paul lists — rule, authority, power, dominion — sound like the ranks and titles of a hierarchy, and he puts the whole structure under one pair of feet. These are not only human offices: in this letter such powers are spiritual before they are political (3:10; 6:12). The visible authorities that trouble us have invisible backing. And Paul is drawing on all of Scripture: the King at God’s right hand (Psalm 110:1), the Son of Man given everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:13–14), the name above every name (Philippians 2:9–11). At the cross, which looked like defeat, “he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame” (Colossians 2:15). They still oppose (6:12), but as defeated enemies, not sovereign lords.

“Above every name that is named.” In Ephesus that was an attack on an industry. In ancient magic, power lived in names: knowing a spirit’s name and saying it correctly gave you leverage over it. That is why Luke’s story from the same city lands so hard: the seven sons of Sceva tried to use “Jesus whom Paul proclaims” as one more name in the toolkit, and were beaten by the man they were trying to help (Acts 19:13–16). The name of Jesus is not a lever to be operated; he is a Lord to belong to. When you have the Person, you no longer need the formulas — which is why the converts burned their scrolls.

You have your own names. You can usually find them by asking what you find yourself appeasing: the market, the algorithm, the scan result, the mortgage, the opinion of people whose approval you have never actually enjoyed. We do not burn incense to them; we organise our lives around them and lie awake for them, which is the same thing done more discreetly. Every one of them is under his feet.

“Not only in this age but also in the one to come.” Every power that has ever terrified anyone has had an expiry date. Empires that once looked permanent enough to build a life around are now chapters schoolchildren find boring. Whatever is pressing on you this week has a shelf life; he does not. His authority is not up for renewal at the end of history. The end of history is simply when everyone finds out.

verseByVerse.quote: And he put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has put everything under Christ’s feet, and given this all-ruling Christ “as head over all things to the church.” He rules everything on behalf of his people.

“He put all things under his feet” quotes Psalm 8:6, which was about humanity: God crowned us with glory and set us to rule the earth. That was Adam’s commission, and it was lost. Hebrews quotes the same psalm and adds the ache: “At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him… Jesus, crowned with glory” (Hebrews 2:8–9). What Adam failed to hold, the last Adam has won. The feet once nailed to a cross are now the feet beneath which every power is placed. The subjection is not yet fully visible, but it is already real: “he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:25–26).

“To the church.” These are the strangest words in the verse. Not to the angels, or the impressive nations, but to a scattered collection of ordinary people, many of them slaves and tradesmen, meeting in borrowed rooms in a city that would not have noticed if they vanished. The universe has been placed under one head, and that head has been given as a gift to them. We instinctively imagine two separate stories: the big one out there — empires, markets, the news — and the small one in here, our own life and church. This verse says there is one story, run with reference to the second. That is why “all things work together for good” for those who love God (Romans 8:28): not that every event is pleasant, but that nothing is happening on a separate track, indifferent to you.

A head, not just a ruler. Paul chooses the picture of a head over a body, which carries two things: authority, and supply — the head is the source from which the body is nourished and held together (Colossians 2:19). So Christ’s rule over everything is not only the guarantee that nothing can crush you; it is the arrangement by which you are fed. And a body goes where its head goes. If the head has been raised and seated above every power, the body cannot be left on the floor (2:6).

The church’s great need in every age is to see Christ as large as he really is. We shrink him to the size of our problems and then wonder why we feel overwhelmed. When the world seems out of control, the question is never whether someone is in charge. The question is whose side he is on, and this verse answers before you can ask: he was given to you.

parallels.desc: you have put all things under his feet

verseByVerse.quote: which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church is Christ’s body, “the fullness of him who fills all in all” — the place where the Christ who fills the whole universe is present and seen in a particular way.

Why say Christ fills all things rather than simply rules them? A king can rule a land he has never visited. To fill something is to be present throughout it. The language comes from the Old Testament: “Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD” (Jeremiah 23:24). When Solomon dedicated the temple, the cloud of God’s glory “filled the house of the LORD, so that the priests could not stand to minister” (1 Kings 8:10–11). Paul applies that to the risen Jesus: the one who filled the temple now fills all things — and calls the church, his new temple of living stones, the expression of that fullness on earth.

Does the church “fill” Christ, or is it “filled by” him? The grammar allows both, and interpreters divide. The main sense is almost certainly the second: Christ pours himself into his people until they are “filled with all the fullness of God”, as Paul will pray (3:19). That guards something important: Christ lacks nothing; he did not acquire a missing part at Pentecost. Yet Paul has chosen an image that leans the other way. A head without a body is not a lesser head; it is a horror. He could have said king and kingdom and kept himself separate. Instead he chose the one relationship in which the greater looks unfinished without the lesser. He does not need us as we need him — but he has bound himself to us so closely that he is willing to be spoken of as incomplete until we are gathered in. That is not a deficiency in Christ; it is how far love has committed itself.

This puts weight on ordinary church life. A body is how a person acts in the world: your hands are how you are present to what you pick up, your voice to the people you speak to. Christ has chosen a body through which to act visibly in this world, and it is not a building or an institution. It is the people who were in the room with you last Sunday, including the ones you find difficult. When they carry a meal to a widow, that is not just kindness organised by volunteers; it is the fullness of the one who fills all in all, becoming visible on a particular street.

And there is nowhere you can go this week that lies outside him — the ward, the school run, the office where nobody prays, the flat you come home to when it is empty. You do not carry him into those places like a package. He already fills them, and he has given you a body to belong to, so that you go in as part of him.

2.title: Dead in Sin, Alive in Christ
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And you were dead in the trespasses and sins <sup>2</sup>in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience — <sup>3</sup>among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind. <sup>4</sup>But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, <sup>5</sup>even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved — <sup>6</sup>and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, <sup>7</sup>so that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. <sup>8</sup>For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, <sup>9</sup>not a result of works, so that no one may boast. <sup>10</sup>For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them. <sup>11</sup>Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands — <sup>12</sup>remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. <sup>13</sup>But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. <sup>14</sup>For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility <sup>15</sup>by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace, <sup>16</sup>and might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility. <sup>17</sup>And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. <sup>18</sup>For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father. <sup>19</sup>So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, <sup>20</sup>built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, <sup>21</sup>in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. <sup>22</sup>In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This is the gospel in its most concentrated and most searching form, and it opens with a diagnosis so radical it takes the breath away. We were dead. Not sick, not wounded, not spiritually impaired — dead. The Greek word is nekros, the same word used for a corpse. Paul is not being poetic; he is being precise. Before God's intervention, the human being in their natural state is spiritually lifeless — incapable of generating their own salvation, incapable of seeking God, incapable even of responding to God without God's prior action. The standard is not low; it is absolute. Dead people do not cooperate with their resurrection. They receive it.

And then — with two words that are among the most glorious in all of Scripture — the diagnosis is shattered by a declaration: But God. Rich in mercy. Because of his great love with which he loved us. Even when we were dead in our trespasses. God acted. He made us alive together with Christ. He raised us up with him. He seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus. Three movements of sovereign grace, each one more astonishing than the last — and the purpose of all of it: "so that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus." We are not saved merely for our own benefit. We are saved to be the eternal showcase of grace — the exhibit that the universe will study for ages to come, marvelling at the kindness of a God who raised the spiritually dead and made them heirs of glory.

The passage closes with one of the clearest articulations of the gospel anywhere in the Bible: "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (vv.8–9). And then the stunning turn of v.10: we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works which God prepared beforehand. Salvation is not by works — but it is absolutely for works. Grace is not the enemy of effort; it is the only soil in which genuine, God-honouring effort can grow.
verseByVerse.theology:
Total Depravity, Sovereign Grace, and the New Creation

"Dead in trespasses and sins" is the Reformed doctrine of total depravity in its most direct biblical expression. Total depravity does not mean that fallen human beings are as evil as they could possibly be — common grace restrains the full expression of human sin. It means that every faculty of the human person — mind, will, affections, conscience — has been corrupted by the fall, so that no part of us naturally seeks God or is capable of saving itself. The will is not neutral, waiting to choose God if only given sufficient reason; it is enslaved, "following the prince of the power of the air" (v.2), "carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind" (v.3).

Against this backdrop, the "but God" of v.4 is the hinge of history. God does not respond to a seeking sinner; he acts on a dead one. This is irresistible grace — not grace that overrides the will by force, but grace that transforms the will, making the dead alive, making the unwilling willing, making the seeking possible. If we seek the cause of our salvation, we find it not in ourselves but in God alone. The new birth is entirely God's work, and the faith through which we receive it is itself his gift (v.8).

The closing verse — "we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works" — is the Reformed answer to the charge that grace produces passivity. It does not. Grace produces the very thing that law could only demand. The person who knows they are entirely saved by grace, not by works, is freed from self-justifying performance and freed for genuine, joyful, Spirit-empowered good works — the works that God prepared beforehand for them to walk in.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The recipients of Paul's letter knew exactly what he meant by "dead in trespasses and sins" — it was their autobiography. Many had been worshippers of Artemis, practitioners of occult arts (Acts 19:19 tells us that converted Ephesians burned their magic books, worth fifty thousand pieces of silver). The darkness, the slavery to spiritual powers, the restless seeking for blessing through ritual and charm — they had lived it. The "but God" of v.4 was the turning point of their actual lives. The grace Paul describes was not theological theory to them; it was the story of what had happened to them, written in their own experience. This is why the passage carries such heat — Paul is describing something he and his readers have lived through, not merely thought about.

Now: "Dead in trespasses and sins" describes every human being outside of Christ, however educated, however moral, however spiritually sincere. The kind CEO, the generous philanthropist, the sincere seeker of truth — apart from Christ, all share the same condition: spiritual death, living under the dominion of the one who still holds sway over "the sons of disobedience" (v.2). This is not a comfortable diagnosis, but it is a necessary one — because a person who thinks they are merely ill will never seek the cure appropriate to death. The church must have the courage to declare both the diagnosis and the remedy with equal clarity: dead — but God.

verseByVerse.quote: You were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s diagnosis of life without Christ is one word: dead (nekrous). Not sick or weakened, but dead toward God — unable to perceive him, unwilling to submit to him, and powerless to change. And while dead, they were not lying still: they “walked”, following the world and the devil.

What “dead” means. A spiritually dead person may be cultured, generous and admirable; death in Paul’s sense does not touch that. It means no life toward God: no power to understand him (“The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God… and he is not able to understand them,” 1 Corinthians 2:14), no willingness to obey him (the mind set on the flesh “does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot,” Romans 8:7), and no ability to fix it. A weak man can try harder; a sick man can take medicine; a dead man can do neither. Lazarus did not help Jesus raise him; he heard a voice speak into death and came out (John 11:43–44). And Paul says dead in trespasses and sins: the sins are not just the cause of death but its form. That is why the cure cannot be moral improvement. You do not improve a corpse; you raise it.

What carried them. “The course of this world” is literally “the age of this world” — not the planet, which God made and loves, but human life organised as though God were not there. It is a current, and the dead do not feel it, because nothing feels less like being swept along than swimming with the tide; you discover the current only when you turn and try to swim against it. The second power is personal: “the prince of the power of the air” is Satan, a real person ruling a real dominion (6:12). “The air” suggests something near and all around, the pressure you breathe without noticing. With “the flesh” in verse 3, all three enemies appear together: the world around, the devil above, the flesh within. And notice what the dead man is doing: not fighting them, but following them.

But I know unbelievers kinder than many Christians. Think of cut flowers. A florist’s arrangement can be lovelier than anything in the garden, and nobody would call it dead; yet it has been cut from its root, and everything you admire in it is running on borrowed time. Paul is not saying unbelievers behave worse than believers — that would be false and would insult people we love. He is speaking of connection, not comparison. The kindness is real; the root is what is missing.

Other views. Many Christians in the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions hold that God gives every person enabling grace, so that though fallen they are able to respond to the gospel; they read “dead” as separated from God rather than unable, citing Jesus’ promise to “draw all people to myself” (John 12:32). But Paul says the mind of the flesh “cannot” submit (Romans 8:7), and Jesus says, “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). The more likely reading is that the inability is real, and that God makes the dead alive (v. 5) so that they believe.
