This diagnosis is not cruelty. A doctor who softens a fatal diagnosis is not kind but negligent, and Paul’s diagnosis exists to make verse 5 blaze: “even when we were dead… [God] made us alive.” And it gives you a test that does not depend on how you feel today. Corpses do not develop appetites. If you find in yourself any hunger for God at all — if his word sometimes lands with weight, if sin now grieves you where once it barely registered — then something has already happened to you that you did not do. A voice has spoken into a grave, and you heard it.
verseByVerse.note: “The prince of the power of the air” is Satan. The air was thought to be the realm of spiritual powers.

verseByVerse.quote: among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul includes himself: “we all once lived” this way, Jew and Gentile alike, ruled by our fallen nature and “by nature children of wrath”. No one is exempt, and the problem goes to the root.

“The flesh” (sarx) does not mean the body, which God made good and the Son took on. It means fallen human nature — the whole person curved in on itself. So its passions are not only sexual; Galatians 5:19–21 lists idolatry, jealousy, rivalry and fits of anger alongside immorality. The flesh produces boardroom sin as readily as bedroom sin; the respectable man who lives for status and control is living in the flesh as fully as anyone. And Paul adds “the desires of the body and the mind”, closing the moralist’s last escape: discipline your appetites and you may simply move the problem upstairs, to intellectual pride or the craving to be admired (Matthew 5:28).

“By nature children of wrath.” “By nature” is original sin in a phrase: fallenness is not an add-on to an otherwise neutral self. We are not sinners because we sin; we sin because we are sinners. And God’s wrath is not a loss of temper but his settled, holy opposition to evil. A judge who feels nothing when the guilty walk free is not merciful but corrupt (Romans 1:18).

How can I be blamed for a nature I never chose? Simply observe: no one has ever had to teach a child to lie, grab, or say “mine”. We teach the opposite, constantly, with mixed results. Every parent is an unwilling witness to original sin. And the doctrine is not that you are punished as an outsider for someone else’s crime, but that you were born into a family and have signed its charter with your own hand every day since. You would recognise it in yourself if you were honest for ten minutes.

What of infants who die? All are born in Adam (Psalm 51:5; Romans 5:12–19). But Scripture gives good ground for hope for those who die before they can understand: David expected to go to his dead son (2 Samuel 12:23), and Jesus took little children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16). “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25). Grieving parents may rest their child in his mercy.

Why say it at all? Because it is the only ground for real gratitude: “he who is forgiven little, loves little” (Luke 7:47). The shallowness of our worship usually matches the smallness of our sense of what we were saved from. And notice the tense: we were children of wrath. Every dreadful word in these verses — dead, walked, followed, lived, were — is past, held there until the two words of verse 4 break over them: “But God.” If you are in Christ, this passage is not your diagnosis; it is your medical history. Read it the way a healthy man reads the chart from the worst year of his life — and marvel that he is sitting up and reading at all.

verseByVerse.quote: But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But God.” Into that death God acted, out of rich mercy and great love, and made us alive with Christ while we were still dead. Martyn Lloyd-Jones called these perhaps the two most important words in the Bible: you were dead — but God; a child of wrath — but God. Every Christian testimony comes down to this hinge.

Rich in mercy. “Rich” (plousios) is the language of wealth: not barely adequate mercy, but mercy that does not run low or grow harder to obtain the more you have needed it. Mercy and grace are close but distinct: grace gives what we do not deserve; mercy withholds what we do. Mercy looks at misery and moves toward it; it sees the corpse and is not repelled. It had to be rich, because the debt was total — Jesus’ parable makes the point: the one forgiven much loves much (Luke 7:41–43). And beneath it all is love: “the great love with which he loved us.” God did not act from duty. He loved people as they actually were — dead, under wrath — and moved toward them anyway (Romans 5:8).

The verb. “He made us alive.” Not helped, not improved, not offered a second chance. Paul has spent three verses establishing that we were corpses so that this word would have nothing to compete with, because there is only one thing you can do for a dead man: raise him. And the word is synezōopoiēsen, “made alive together with”. The prefix “with” is repeated twice in the next verse — raised with him, seated with him. Your new life is not a separate resurrection resembling his, but a share in his. When Jesus came out of that tomb, you came out with him.

The timing. “Even when we were dead.” Not once we began to stir, or after some moral effort had shown promise, but when there was nothing to work with and nothing to reward. That settles the question anxious believers keep returning to — whether God might change his mind about them. You contributed nothing to your first resurrection; your standing has never rested on your contribution, and it is not about to start now. Read the sentence once more and let its shape do the work: the subject is God, the verb is “made alive”, and the object, entirely passive from beginning to end, is you.

verseByVerse.quote: And raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joined to Christ, believers share not only his resurrection but his enthronement: God has “raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places”. Three verbs built on “with” (vv. 5–6) describe one reality: what happened to Christ at his resurrection and ascension happened to his people through union with him. Where the head goes, the body goes.

The seating is stated as done, not hoped for. How can someone still walking on earth be seated in “the heavenly places” — the unseen realm where Christ reigns above every power (1:20)? Because God raised and seated his Son as the head of a body. So you are, at this moment, both living in a weak mortal body and seated with Christ in God’s sight. The first is what you feel; the second is what God sees; both are real (Colossians 3:1–3). This is already true, though not yet fully experienced.

Why “seated”? It is the posture of finished work and settled authority. Old Testament priests never sat in the temple, because their work was never done. Christ “sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high” (Hebrews 1:3) because his sacrifice was final — and you are seated with him, sharing his rest and security, not by anything you earned but because you are in him.

Not escapism. The heavenly places are also where the war is (6:12). Paul is not offering a quiet room above the noise but your position within the conflict: above it, with the one no power can move. It is the difference between a soldier pinned down in a trench, who cannot see the field and does not know who is winning, and a man standing beside the commander with the battle laid out before him. Both are in the war; only one knows how it ends.

So when anxiety says everything is out of control, do not deny the chaos — remember where you sit. When the accuser says you are disqualified, do not produce your record; point to your location. And notice that nothing here is graded. The believer converted last Thursday, who still cannot find Habakkuk and is fighting something he has not told anyone about, is seated exactly where the apostle is seated, because neither is there on his own account.

verseByVerse.quote: So that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why did God do all this? Not only to rescue us, but so that “in the coming ages” he might display “the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus”. Saved people are God’s eternal exhibit of his grace.

“The coming ages” is plural: not a single moment but an unfolding eternity. Paul does not over-describe it, but the direction is clear. What we have tasted here — forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, God’s nearness in prayer — is the down payment; the coming ages are the feast. And three words strain to say it: the grace is “immeasurable”, its supply is “riches”, and it comes “in kindness” — chrēstotēs, a warm, personal word, the kindness of someone leaning toward you rather than a benefactor signing a cheque at a distance. Think of your most profound moment of grace, when forgiveness felt most real. That came through a fallen mind, weak faith and a tired body, in a world still under the curse. What will it be when every barrier is gone? C. S. Lewis caught it at the end of The Last Battle: every room opens into a greater one, “further up and further in”.

You are the exhibit. God already has galaxies and landscapes to display, and they cost him nothing. What will be on show for ever is what he did with people. That turns something painful inside out. Most of us carry a chapter we would rather leave out — the wasted years, the thing we still cannot say aloud. We assume heaven will be discreetly silent about it. But what is displayed is not your record; it is “the immeasurable riches of his grace”, and grace can only be measured against what it had to overcome. A restorer’s skill is never shown by a painting that was never damaged. The chapter you would erase is the part of you that will testify most loudly to what God is like. In the coming ages no one will be embarrassed by your past; they will look at it and worship.

Even now the angelic powers are watching what God does with sinners (3:10). Eternity is not God finally paying a reward you were owed. It is God, for ever, delighting to be kind to people who had nothing coming.

verseByVerse.quote: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Salvation is entirely God’s gift: by grace, received through faith, “not your own doing… not a result of works, so that no one may boast.” Faith is not a contribution that earns grace; it is the empty hand that receives it.

Is faith itself the gift? A study Bible will point out that “this” (touto) is neuter in Greek, while “faith” is feminine, so “this” probably refers back to the whole of salvation by grace through faith. Grant the grammar entirely; it strengthens the point. If “this” covers everything Paul has just said, then grace, salvation and the faith that receives it are all gathered into the word “gift”. You cannot rescue a place for human contribution by narrowing the pronoun. And elsewhere faith is plainly called a gift: “it has been granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him but also suffer” (Philippians 1:29); Apollos helped “those who through grace had believed” (Acts 18:27). Wherever you draw the line, nothing is left that a saved sinner could boast in.

“So that no one may boast.” The ancient world ran on honour, and the only question was what you boasted in. Paul had a record to stand on — circumcised the eighth day, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, blameless under the law (Philippians 3:4–6) — and he counted it rubbish next to knowing Christ. If salvation held any human contribution, the saved could say, “I am in and you are out, and the difference, at some level, is me.” Grace rules that out. Today the boasting is subtler: the quiet sense that I believed because I was wiser or more open than others; the seasoned member eyeing the new convert with a touch of seniority; the testimony that casts the speaker as the hero who finally worked it out. The properly told story does the opposite: the more undeserving the sinner, the more brilliant the grace. John Newton knew which way the glory flowed — “that saved a wretch like me.”

The tense. “You have been saved” is a perfect passive in Greek: a completed action, done by someone else, whose effect still stands. That is why assurance is not arrogance. The man who says he is saved is no more boasting about his performance than a rescued swimmer boasts about the lifeboat.

“Is my faith the right sort? It feels so thin.” Paul never praises the faith itself; he calls it the channel — saved “through faith” — and its whole value lies in what it holds. Weak faith in a sound bridge will carry you over the river; strong faith in a rotten one will drop you in it. The father who cried, “I believe; help my unbelief!” went home with a healed son (Mark 9:24). So the question is never whether your faith is big enough — the honest answer to that will always be no — but what you are trusting. Put a trembling hand on Christ and you have all that he is.
verseByVerse.note: “This” most naturally refers to the whole of salvation by grace through faith.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having said that salvation is not by works, Paul brings works back in their proper place: we are saved for good works, not by them. They are the fruit of salvation, not its root — and God has prepared them in advance for us to walk in.

“His workmanship.” The word is poiēma (from which “poem” comes): a work made by an artist. It appears only twice in the New Testament — here, and in Romans 1:20 for the created universe, “the things that have been made”. The word Paul uses for the galaxies he uses for you. And the second work cost God far more: the first he spoke into being; the second required a death.

What good works are. Paul gives no checklist. They are the whole range of faithful, loving life that flows from a renewed heart: mercy to the poor and the stranger (James 1:27), integrity in ordinary things — honest work, a faithful marriage, patience with hard people (the very things listed in 4:25–32), and witness to Christ (1 Peter 3:15). The plumber who works well and charges fairly, the employee who works “as to the Lord” (6:7), the parent who disciplines with warmth (6:4) — these are good works. So are listening to the lonely, going back to apologise, and doing a hidden job thoroughly.

“Prepared beforehand.” God laid them out before you existed. You are not a robot running a script, but you also do not have to invent a life of good works from scratch or sustain it by willpower. God not only prepares us for good works; he prepares good works for us. So the question is not “what should I invent?” but “what has God put in front of me?” — the neighbour in need, the unexpected chance to serve.

“That we should walk in them.” The same verb as verse 2, where the dead “walked” following the world. Same verb, opposite road. Not admire, intend, or feel warmly about good works — walk: steps, one at a time, in a direction, usually with nobody watching. Conversion did not stop you walking; it changed the road. None of this is the basis of your acceptance — verses 8–9 have shut that door. A child does not obey to earn a place in the family; he obeys because he belongs. But neither is it optional: a faith that bears no fruit is dead (James 2:17).

And if you read “masterpiece” and thought, “not me”: you are standing inside the work while it is still being made, the one vantage point from which no work of art has ever looked finished. A house halfway through renovation looks worse than before anyone touched it — walls open, floors lifted, dust everywhere — and that is evidence the builder has begun, not that he has failed. The worth of a work is set by the artist, not by the marble’s opinion of itself. “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If vv.1–10 describe the miracle of individual salvation, vv.11–22 describe its corporate consequence — and the consequence is nothing less than the creation of a new humanity. The most profound social division of the ancient world was the division between Jew and Gentile. It was not merely ethnic; it was religious, covenantal, cultic, and moral. The Jew had the oracles of God, the covenants of promise, the temple, the law, the Messiah. The Gentile was "separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world" (v.12). The wall between them was literal — the Jerusalem temple had a stone barrier (the soreg) beyond which Gentiles could not pass on pain of death. And spiritually, the distance was infinite.

Christ has abolished it. Not by lowering the standard, not by relativising the covenant, not by pretending the distinction never mattered — but by fulfilling what the distinction pointed to and then, in his own body on the cross, "killing the hostility" (v.16). He made peace. Not peace by negotiation, not peace by compromise, but peace by blood — His own blood, shed for both Jew and Gentile, making one new man in place of two. The dividing wall of hostility has been broken down in Christ. The sign above the gate that once said "Keep Out" has been torn down and replaced with a welcome: "You who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ" (v.13).

The result is a building — a temple. Not the old temple in Jerusalem, with its courts of separation and its stone barrier. A new temple, built on the foundation of apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone, in whom the whole structure is joined together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord. The church is God's dwelling place by the Spirit. What the Jerusalem temple was in shadow, the church now is in reality: the place where God lives, the community through which he makes himself known to the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Atonement and the New Community

This passage reveals the ecclesiological dimensions of the atonement — a dimension often underemphasised in evangelical theology. We tend to think of Christ's death in purely individual terms: He died for me, my sins are forgiven, I am reconciled to God. All of this is gloriously true. But Paul insists that the cross accomplished something more: it created a new community. Christ died not only to reconcile individuals to God (vertical reconciliation) but to reconcile estranged human beings to one another (horizontal reconciliation). He "reconciled us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility" (v.16).

This means that the unity of the church is not merely a practical or organisational goal; it is a theological reality purchased by Christ's blood. To live in division, to maintain the walls that Christ has torn down, to prefer the company of people like us over the diverse community Christ has created — this is a denial of the atonement. Every genuinely reconciled, cross-cultural Christian community is a proclamation of the gospel: not with words but with existence. Its very existence says: the cross is real, the wall is down, God has made one new man.

The metaphor of the temple (vv.19–22) carries the further implication that the church's holiness matters. The old temple was the place where God dwelt, and its holiness was fiercely guarded. The new temple — the church — is also the dwelling place of God by his Spirit. The community of believers is not merely a gathering of like-minded people; it is the sacred space where the Holy God has chosen to make his home on earth. This gives both dignity and responsibility to every local church: you are the temple of God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The stone wall of the Jerusalem temple — the soreg — was not a metaphor. Inscriptions warning Gentiles that entry beyond it meant death have been found by archaeologists. The barrier was physical, legal, and deadly. When Paul says Christ has broken down "the dividing wall of hostility," his Jewish and Gentile readers understood exactly what wall he meant. They may have stood on opposite sides of it. Now they sat side by side at the Lord's table, eating and drinking together, addressed as fellow citizens and members of the same household. The sociological miracle was visible and daily, and it pointed to a theological reality: the cross had accomplished what no social programme could.

Now: The church in our age still struggles with the walls that Christ has torn down. Racial segregation in churches persists in many places. Class divisions shape congregational culture in ways we rarely examine. Political tribalism has entered sanctuaries and split families of faith. Against all of this, Ephesians 2 speaks with prophetic force: the wall is down. Christ killed the hostility. The new humanity he created is more fundamental than any human division that preceded it. The church that reflects this — that is visibly, sacrificially, joyfully diverse across the lines that divide the surrounding world — is not merely being socially progressive. It is being theologically faithful. It is showing the world what the cross actually accomplished.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands —
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul commands the Gentile believers to remember where they once stood: outside the covenant people, labelled “the uncircumcision” by their Jewish neighbours. The wider the gap looks, the more astonishing the bridge that follows (vv. 13–22).

“The uncircumcision” was not a neutral word but a stigma — compare David’s contempt for “this uncircumcised Philistine” (1 Samuel 17:26). It defined a whole people by an absence, the mark they did not carry. Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham (Genesis 17), and Paul does not despise it; it had real value as a sign (Romans 3:1–2). But he adds a pointed phrase: “made in the flesh by hands.” A physical mark made by human hands is no longer the boundary of God’s people. The new-covenant reality is circumcision of the heart, by the Spirit (Romans 2:28–29; Colossians 2:11).

Why remembering must be commanded. Forgetting is what we do naturally, and Christians forget this faster than most. The believer of thirty years, or the one raised in a Christian home, drifts toward feeling like the sort of person God would naturally have wanted — as though grace had found something worth finding. The cure is not a mood but a deliberate act of recalling what you were. God trained Israel in this. The law repeatedly says “remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt”, and nearly always attaches it to how they treat others: release your servant generously (Deuteronomy 15:15); “You shall not oppress a sojourner. You know the heart of a sojourner” (Exodus 23:9). Memory of your own rescue was meant to shape how you treat outsiders.

That is exactly Paul’s purpose. He is about to tell a mixed and uneasy church to live as one body, so he reminds the Gentile half how far outside they once stood. Every community has words like “the uncircumcision” that reduce a person to what they lack. Someone who genuinely remembers being on the outside cannot easily keep another person there.

verseByVerse.quote: remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul lists five things Gentiles lacked before Christ, each deeper than the last — the fullest picture of human lostness in the New Testament. Not to shame his readers, but so that the rescue in verse 13 lands with full weight.

Separated from Christ: Israel lived in the hope of the coming Messiah; the Gentile world had no framework in which his coming could even be expected. Alienated from the commonwealth of Israel: shut out from the people through whom God was visibly at work. Strangers to the covenants of promise: aliens with no claim on what God had bound himself to give — the offspring who would bless the nations (Genesis 12:3), the everlasting throne (2 Samuel 7:12–13), the new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–34). Having no hope: not a gloomy mood but no ground for hope. The ancient world was full of temples; what it lacked was any certain promise that death was not the end. A common Roman epitaph ran, “I was not; I was; I am not; I care not.” Without God: atheoi. Not that they denied all gods — they worshipped constantly — but they lacked the one true God who had revealed himself and kept his promises. Surrounded by gods, they were in the most precise sense without God.

Notice that Paul has gathered the exact vocabulary of exclusion: alienated, strangers, no hope. If you have ever stood at the edge of a group and known, without anyone saying it, that you did not belong — the family you married into, the workplace where everyone shares a history you do not, even a church where everyone seems to have known each other for years — you know the flavour of every word in this sentence. Paul says that was once your standing before God, in the only place where belonging finally counts.

And verse 13 answers each item. The outsiders were not given advice, a procedure or a probation period. They were “brought near”, by someone else’s blood, in one movement. All five are reversed: in Christ, citizens, heirs of the covenants, holding a living hope, indwelt by God’s Spirit. The answer to the whole catalogue of exclusion is not a policy but a Person.

verseByVerse.quote: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But now” — the second great turning point of the chapter (after “But God”, v. 4). Those who were “far off” have been “brought near”, and the means is specific: “the blood of Christ”. Not dialogue, not mutual understanding, not the passage of time — blood.

Far and near. “Far off” was almost a technical term: Jewish writers used it for the Gentile world, and “brought near” was the language used of a convert admitted to the covenant people. Isaiah had promised “Peace, peace, to the far and to the near” (Isaiah 57:19), and Peter preached that the promise is “for all who are far off” (Acts 2:39). But how near is near? Within nine verses these same people are fellow citizens, then family members, and finally stones in the temple where God lives. They began outside a barrier that threatened death to any Gentile who crossed it (v. 14), and they end up being the building.

Why blood. The distance was never really geographical or cultural; it was moral. Dialogue does not remove guilt, time does not erase it, and shared values do not answer for what has been done. Under the law, blood dealt with sin, because “the life of the flesh is in the blood” and God had given it “to make atonement” (Leviticus 17:11) — a life given in place of a forfeited life. And this was never only a Gentile problem. The Jew inside the barrier could not walk into God’s presence either; he watched the high priest go in once a year, “and not without taking blood” (Hebrews 9:7). The wall kept Gentiles out of the court; sin kept everyone out of the holiest place. So blood is not an entry fee charged to latecomers. It was always the only door, and at the cross the final sacrifice was offered once, and both groups walked through together.

Hold on to this when your own heart accuses you. This nearness was not produced by your feeling close to God, and it is not undone by your feeling far from him. It was established by an event outside you, at a cost you did not pay. You may feel a long way off on a Tuesday afternoon and still be, in the only sense this verse means, near.

parallels.desc: peace, peace, to the far and to the near

verseByVerse.quote: For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ himself is our peace. He has made Jew and Gentile one and broken down the wall that divided them, and he did it “in his flesh” on the cross.

“He himself is our peace.” The Greek puts “he himself” first: not his teaching or example, but his person. Christ does not broker a settlement and step back; he is the peace. And biblical peace is not just the absence of conflict but wholeness — peace with God, peace between peoples, a life rightly ordered. “Not as the world gives do I give to you” (John 14:27): the world manages conflict; Christ gives himself.

“Made us both one.” Jew and Gentile were separated by the most entrenched boundary of the ancient world. Christ did not just bring them closer; he made them one. Two people joined to Christ are thereby joined to each other, whatever their cultures say. The ground at the foot of the cross is level (Galatians 3:28).

“The dividing wall of hostility.” Almost certainly Paul has in mind the stone barrier in the Jerusalem temple that kept Gentiles out of the inner courts. Archaeologists have found its inscription, warning in Greek that any Gentile who went further would be responsible for his own death. That wall said, in stone: “God’s presence is not for you; stay outside.” Christ did not lower it or make it easier to climb; he broke it down. The temple curtain torn “from top to bottom” at his death made the same point (Matthew 27:51).

Was Christ undoing God’s own work? The separation of Israel was God’s doing — the law, the covenant signs, the holy distinctions. But the Son was finishing that work, not undoing it. The separation was like a cast on a broken limb: it preserved a people through whom the Messiah would come and taught the world that God is holy and not casually approached. Paul says “the law was our guardian until Christ came” (Galatians 3:24). When the bone has knit, the cast comes off — not because it was a mistake, but because it has done its work.

It was costly. For a Jewish believer, unity meant eating at a Gentile’s table — setting aside food laws his ancestors had died rather than break. For a Gentile, it meant accepting that salvation came through a nation he had been raised to think strange. Acts shows how hard it was: a sheet let down from heaven three times before Peter would believe it (Acts 10), a council because the argument would not settle (Acts 15), and Peter later withdrawing from Gentile tables until Paul opposed him to his face (Galatians 2:11–14). Paul announces a finished fact and spends the rest of the letter urging the church to live inside it.

The temple wall is rubble; the instinct that built it is not. Every congregation has its own unwritten inscriptions: the professional and the unemployed, the settled family and the single man, the politically confident and the politically suspect, the respectable and the one whose past everyone knows. Two questions will usually locate your own wall: who do you sit near on Sunday without ever deciding to? And whose home have you actually been inside? A church that rebuilds these walls is reassembling the very thing Christ died to destroy.
verseByVerse.note: The temple courts had a stone barrier with inscriptions forbidding Gentiles, on pain of death, to go further.

parallels.desc: he shall be their peace

verseByVerse.quote: by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ removed the barrier by “abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances”, in order to “create in himself one new man in place of the two” — a single new humanity, with peace at its heart.

Which law? The phrase is misread in two opposite directions. Paul means the ceremonial and boundary-marking laws that defined Jewish identity and kept the two peoples apart: circumcision, food laws, purity rules, festivals, the temple system. God gave them for a season, to keep his people distinct and to foreshadow Christ: “These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:17). He does not mean that God’s moral law is abolished. Jesus said, “I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17). Reformed theology has long distinguished the moral law, which reflects God’s character and stands; the civil law, given to Israel as a nation; and the ceremonial law, which pointed to Christ. It is the boundary-marking function Paul has in view. What ended was not God’s standard but the wall.

“Create … one new man.” The verb is creation language, the same word Paul used of believers in verse 10. Not Gentiles absorbed into Judaism, nor Jewish identity diluted, but a third thing: one new humanity defined wholly by union with Christ. That means the church is not at bottom an institution. Committees found institutions every week; no one can found a creature. The church’s unity is something God made, and the most we can do is refuse to damage it.

Not a melting pot. “One new man” does not mean a Jew stops being a Jew or a Gentile a Gentile. Paul tells converts to remain as they were called (1 Corinthians 7:18–20), and the last picture of the redeemed is “a great multitude… from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages” (Revelation 7:9). The differences remain in glory; they simply stop deciding anything. Your background is still yours; it is no longer your standing.

Does the church replace Israel? Christians answer in three ways. Dispensational Christians hold that Israel and the church are two peoples with separate promises, and that national Israel still has a future of its own. Some have taught that the church has simply replaced Israel, and that the Jewish people have no further place in God’s purposes. The more likely reading is the one this passage gives: one people of God, into which believing Gentiles have been brought, sharing the promises once given to Israel (v. 12). Gentiles are grafted into Israel’s olive tree, not planted beside it (Romans 11:17), and Paul still expects many Jews to be grafted back in by faith (Romans 11:23–26).

“So making peace.” Peace is not a mood that eventually settled, or what happens when two sides grow tired of arguing. It was made, as anything is made — with materials, labour and cost: his flesh, a crucifixion, everything he had. So peace in a church is never just the absence of friction or good manners in the porch afterwards. It is the keeping of something expensive that someone else paid for. That is why Paul later says, “eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (4:3) — not create it, but maintain it.

verseByVerse.quote: And might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cross does two things in order: it reconciles both Jew and Gentile to God, and in doing so it kills the hostility between them. The vertical comes first and makes the horizontal possible.

Reconcile. The word assumes real enmity. You do not reconcile people who simply never met. “While we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10). The hostility ran both ways — our rebellion against God, and his settled opposition to our evil — which is why the remedy had to be a death and not an explanation. And because the root problem is alienation from God, purely social efforts at reconciliation cannot produce lasting unity on their own; the cross deals with the root.

In one body. God did not reconcile us to himself and then, as a separate matter, suggest we try to get along. The same act that brings you to God sets you down among people you did not choose. You are not saved privately and then invited to consider joining a church at your convenience. Remember that on the Sunday when the congregation seems more trouble than it is worth: you did not choose these people, and they did not choose you. He reconciled you both, in one body, and the arrangement is not open to renegotiation.

“Killing the hostility.” Not soothed, managed or talked through in meetings — put to death, because hostility is a living thing that grows when it is fed and often outlives the people who started it. And notice where it died. They killed Christ, and in being killed he killed the thing that was killing everyone. The cross is the one place where hostility did its absolute worst and was destroyed by the very thing it did.

This gives a plain path for anyone at odds with a fellow believer. Go vertical first: stand at the cross and look honestly at the size of what was forgiven you. It is very hard to keep a grievance at full strength there — which is the point of the servant forgiven ten thousand talents who went straight out to demand a hundred denarii (Matthew 18:23–35). Two people each forgiven an unpayable debt by the same Person will not, in the end, have much left to hold against each other.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ “preached peace” to Gentiles far off and Jews near, and through him both now have the same access, in one Spirit, to the Father. The promise of Isaiah — “Peace, peace, to the far and to the near” (Isaiah 57:19) — has been carried out.

When did Jesus preach to the Ephesians? In his earthly ministry he went almost only to Jews, and once told the Twelve, “Go nowhere among the Gentiles” (Matthew 10:5). He never preached in Ephesus. The answer is that the risen Christ came to them through his messengers. “How are they to hear without someone preaching?” Paul asks, and quotes Isaiah: “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!” (Romans 10:14–15). The feet belong to the messenger; the voice belongs to Christ. When the gospel is faithfully preached — from a pulpit or across a kitchen table, even nervously and badly — Christ himself is preaching. The Ephesians never saw him, but they heard him.

Peace to the near. The Jews had the Scriptures, the temple and the promises — and they needed the same message. Nearness was not the same as peace. Every congregation has people who have never been outsiders in any social sense: raised in church, at home with the songs and the vocabulary. Peace had to be preached to them too, on exactly the same terms. Being near the building was never the same as peace with God.

Access. Prosagōgē is the word for the right of approach to a king — being ushered into the royal presence by someone with standing to bring you in. Now Jew and Gentile come “through him… in one Spirit to the Father”. Why mention the Spirit? Because he makes the access real now. Christ secured it at the cross, two thousand years ago; the Spirit living in us makes it present today: “God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Galatians 4:6). The very cry of “Father” in your prayers is the Spirit at work. And there is “one Spirit” — not one for Jewish believers and another for Gentiles. All come on the same ground with the same standing.

So whenever a believer prays, however haltingly, something Trinitarian is happening: the Father is approached, through the Son who opened the way, by the Spirit who carries the prayer from within. Prayer is never a lonely cry to a distant deity. The way is open, and it is held open not by our effort but by the Spirit who lives in us (Hebrews 10:19–22).

verseByVerse.quote: So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“So then” gathers everything up into a new identity. The Gentiles are no longer strangers and aliens; they are fellow citizens, members of God’s household, and part of a building founded on the apostles and prophets with Christ as the cornerstone. Each image reverses an exclusion from verse 12.

Fellow citizens. In Ephesus this was no mild word. Roman citizenship was the most prized status in the empire. Paul once stopped a flogging just by asking whether it was lawful to scourge an uncondemned Roman; the shaken commander said he had bought his citizenship “for a large sum”, and Paul replied, “But I am a citizen by birth” (Acts 22:25–28). Now Gentiles have been made citizens of a commonwealth beside which Rome is a temporary local arrangement — and they did not buy it; they were born into it. “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

Members of the household. Warmer than citizenship: not a tolerated guest but family, with a Father who provides and brothers and sisters in every nation (Galatians 6:10).

The foundation. The church rests “on the foundation of the apostles and prophets” — not their personal holiness, but their testimony, the authoritative word they were commissioned to deliver, now given us in Scripture. Calvin put it plainly: the foundation is the doctrine they preached; move away from it and the building falls. That is why Scripture alone is not a preference but a structural necessity. Are there apostles and prophets today? A foundation is laid once. Continuationists hold that these offices, or at least prophets, continue. But if the apostles and prophets are the foundation, they cannot also be the walls. The more likely reading is that those offices belonged to the church’s founding generation and have ceased. What continues is their word.

The cornerstone. Christ is the stone on which everything depends and by which everything is aligned. Isaiah spoke of “a precious cornerstone” laid in Zion (Isaiah 28:16), and the psalm said, “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 118:22) — words Jesus claimed and Peter preached (Acts 4:11). The cornerstone was laid first, cut and squared with great care, and every other stone took its line from it. The mason did not measure each stone against the one below; he measured against the corner. So an error there is never small: a wall built off a crooked corner is wrong all the way up and becomes more obviously wrong the higher it rises. That is how churches drift — rarely by one dramatic decision, but by quietly taking their line from something other than Christ: the founder’s personality, denominational habit, the surrounding culture, the preferences of the biggest givers. Every stone laid after that looks fine on its own, and is out of true.

And you are not a visitor admiring the architecture; you are a stone in the wall — “living stones… being built up as a spiritual house” (1 Peter 2:5). A stone in a wall fits the stones beside it, carries weight and has weight carried on it, and cannot be removed without leaving a visible hole. A stone lying alone in a field, however fine, is not yet part of anything.
verseByVerse.note: A cornerstone was the first, carefully placed stone that set the line of the whole building.

parallels.desc: a precious cornerstone

verseByVerse.quote: in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul ends with a building that grows: in Christ “the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord.” Buildings do not grow; bodies do. Paul mixes the pictures on purpose, because neither alone says what he means.

The temple picture tells us what the church is: the place where God now dwells on earth, solid and lasting. The growth picture tells us it is alive, still becoming what it is meant to be (he develops this in 4:15–16). A church goes wrong by losing either. Lose the growing and you have a building and nothing more: beautifully maintained, the order of service unchanged in thirty years, the accounts impeccable, and the whole thing starting to resemble a place kept open by a heritage trust so visitors can admire the windows. Lose the building and you get the opposite: energy without shape, a movement that generates warmth for five years and then finds it has no foundation and nothing solid to give anyone. Paul will have neither: rooted and growing, fixed and alive.

“Being joined together” (sunarmologoumenē, found only in Ephesians, again in 4:16) means precisely fitted, each stone set where it belongs and bearing on its neighbours. There are no spare stones. And the verb is present and passive: it is happening now, and it is being done to the stones, not by them. No stone ever moved itself into place or chose its neighbours — worth remembering when the people beside you are not the people you would have picked. They did not pick you either. Neither of you is the mason.

Ask yourself two questions this week. Is anyone in your congregation actually bearing weight on you — someone for whom your absence would be a practical problem, not just an empty seat? And whose weight are you carrying? If the honest answer to both is no one, you are not yet joined into the wall; you are a stone resting against it. The difference is invisible from the road and total in a storm.

And the building is unfinished; it “grows into” a holy temple. So when your church disappoints you — and a growing thing is always partly unformed — you are not looking at a ruin but standing on a building site. The dust and noise and half-built walls are not evidence that the project has failed, but that it is still going on, and that the Builder has not left.

verseByVerse.quote: In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with God’s great purpose for his people: they are “being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.” Not a place where people come to find God, but where God himself lives.

The thread through Scripture. Why would the God who fills all things (1:23) want a home? Because he has always wanted to live among his people. He walked with Adam in the garden (Genesis 3:8). After sin broke that, he told Israel to build the tabernacle “that I may dwell in their midst” (Exodus 25:8), and his glory filled it, and later Solomon’s temple, so completely that the priests could not stand to minister (Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11). Then came the catastrophe: because of Israel’s idolatry, Ezekiel watched the glory leave the temple (Ezekiel 10–11). The deepest wound was not the Babylonian army but the presence departing before it came. Yet Ezekiel was promised that the glory would return, and the city’s new name would be “The LORD Is There” (Ezekiel 48:35). It returned in a form no one expected: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” — literally pitched his tent — “and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). Then at Pentecost the Spirit came not on a building but on people (Acts 2:3): “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

The staggering choice. God wanted a home, and he chose not a cathedral or a holy mountain but forgiven, still-unfinished people. The ordinary congregation on a Sunday morning, with all its rough edges, is the dwelling place of the living God — not when it becomes worthy enough, but now. And notice the tense again: “being built” — present, continuous, passive; it is happening to you, not by you.

Where to look for God. Almost everyone who has wanted God has gone looking for his presence somewhere: a place, a view, a piece of music, a conference, a certain silence early in the morning. That hunger is not silly; it is the oldest ache there is, going back to the afternoon two people hid from God in the garden. But Paul gives a different address: not a mountain or an atmosphere, but a people. That makes an ordinary Sunday more serious than it looks. The people around you — the awkward ones, the one who talks too long afterwards, the family whose children never sit still — are not the setting in which you might meet God; together, they are where he has chosen to live. If you have been looking for his presence and finding it thin, ask when you last looked for it among the people he actually indwells, rather than only in the half-hour of music beforehand.

And see how far the chapter has come. It opened with corpses following the world and the prince of the power of the air. It ends with those same people as the house God lives in. That is the distance grace covers, in twenty-two verses.

3.title: The Mystery of Christ and the Fullness of God
3.text: <sup>1</sup>For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles — <sup>2</sup>assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you, <sup>3</sup>how the mystery was made known to me by revelation, as I have written briefly. <sup>4</sup>When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ, <sup>5</sup>which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit. <sup>6</sup>This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel. <sup>7</sup>Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given me by the working of his power. <sup>8</sup>To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, <sup>9</sup>and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things, <sup>10</sup>so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. <sup>11</sup>This was according to the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord, <sup>12</sup>in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him. <sup>13</sup>So I ask you not to lose heart over what I am suffering for you, which is your glory. <sup>14</sup>For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, <sup>15</sup>from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, <sup>16</sup>that according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being, <sup>17</sup>so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith — that you, being rooted and grounded in love, <sup>18</sup>may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, <sup>19</sup>and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. <sup>20</sup>Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us, <sup>21</sup>to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul begins to pray and then stops himself. "For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles—" and then the sentence breaks off, swallowed by a parenthesis that doesn't resolve until v.14. He cannot proceed to the prayer without first explaining the stewardship that has brought him to prison — because the mystery he has been entrusted to proclaim is itself the reason for the prayer, and the prayer only makes sense in light of the mystery. Paul is constitutionally unable to speak of anything without grounding it in the gospel.

The mystery he describes is one of the most world-altering disclosures in all of Scripture. "The Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel" (v.6). In the Old Testament, the Gentiles were at the periphery of God's purposes — they could be blessed through Israel, they could join themselves to Israel, but they were not Israel. Now the secret is out: the wall was always meant to come down. The distinction was always meant to be temporary, a pedagogy pointing toward its own dissolution. In Christ, there are no second-class citizens of the Kingdom, no Gentiles-in-the-anteroom. Fellow heirs. Fellow members. Fellow partakers. The same body. The same promise.

And the disclosure of this mystery has dimensions that exceed the merely human. "Through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places" (v.10). The angels are watching the church. The principalities and powers — the spiritual intelligences that inhabit the heavenly realm — are learning the wisdom of God by observing the community of the redeemed. The church is God's cosmic classroom. When a Jew and a Gentile, a slave and a free person, a man and a woman sit together at the Lord's table — the universe sees something it could not have deduced by any other means: the manifold, many-coloured, inexhaustible wisdom of a God who makes all things new.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mystery Hidden and Revealed

The concept of "mystery" (mysterion) in Pauline theology is not something puzzling or obscure. It is a technical term for a secret previously hidden in God that has now been disclosed in the gospel. The mystery of Christ — the inclusion of the Gentiles as co-heirs — was not absent from the Old Testament, but it was not fully clear. It was there in the Abrahamic promise ("in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed," Genesis 12:3), in the prophets (Isaiah 49:6; 60:3), in the Psalms (Psalm 87; 96:3). But the full disclosure awaited the coming of Christ and the apostolic proclamation of the gospel.

This "already hidden, now revealed" pattern is the structure of all biblical revelation. The Old Testament is full of types, shadows, and partial disclosures that only become fully visible in the light of Christ. This is why the Reformers insisted on the unity of the two Testaments — they are one revelation progressively unfolding, not two contradictory religions. And it is why reading the Old Testament through the lens of Christ is not an imposition on the text but the fulfilment of its own internal logic. The mystery of the Gentiles was always there; the church is now living in the age of its full disclosure.

Paul's description of himself as "the very least of all the saints" (v.8) has been the theme of Reformed meditation on gospel humility. The man who had been the church's most zealous persecutor, who had dragged men and women to prison and consented to their deaths, now counts himself the least worthy recipient of the grace he proclaims. This is not false modesty; it is the grammar of genuine encounter with grace. The closer you are to Christ, the more clearly you see how far you fall short — and the more marvellous it becomes that grace extends even to you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul describes his ministry as the proclamation of "the unsearchable riches of Christ" (v.8). The Greek word for "unsearchable" (anexichniastos) means literally "untraceable" — riches so vast that you cannot find their boundary, cannot trace their perimeter, cannot reach their end. To the Ephesian church, surrounded by the very traceable riches of Artemis and the mystery cults — gods who could be appeased, blessing that could be earned, secrets that could be unlocked for a price — Paul announces something of a different order entirely. The riches of Christ are boundless. They cannot be exhausted. The more you receive, the more remains to be given. No mystery religion could offer this.

Now: Paul is in prison when he writes this, and he explicitly tells the Ephesians not to lose heart because of his sufferings (v.13). The apostle who has been entrusted with the most glorious news in the universe is sitting in a Roman cell when he writes it. This is the pattern of the gospel: its glory travels in the most unlikely vessels. The imprisoned apostle, the persecuted church, the minority community that the world dismisses — these are the means through which the manifold wisdom of God is made known. When the church is most visibly weak, it is often doing its most significant cosmic work. The angels are watching — and what they see is the wisdom of God displayed in jars of clay.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul starts to pray (“for this reason” looks back to the reconciliation of chapter 2), but first he names himself: “a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles.” He then breaks off into an explanation of his calling that runs to verse 13, before resuming the prayer in verse 14.

Whose prisoner? The Roman chain is real, and so is the soldier at the other end of it. But Paul does not write “a prisoner of Nero” or “of Rome”. He writes that he belongs to Christ. Rome thinks it is holding him; Paul knows who actually put him there, and why. His imprisonment is not defeat but the cost of his calling.

“On behalf of you Gentiles” is more literal than it looks. Paul was seized by a mob in the Jerusalem temple, shouting that he had brought Greeks past the barrier and defiled the holy place. Luke explains why: they had seen him in the city with “Trophimus the Ephesian” (Acts 21:27–29) and assumed Paul had taken him in. He had not. But in a deeper sense the charge was true, because Paul had spent his life insisting that the wall was down. So the man who has just told the Ephesians that Christ demolished the dividing wall (2:14) is writing from prison because he was accused of taking an Ephesian through it. The doctrine of chapter 2 cost him his freedom.

That speaks to anyone in circumstances they did not choose and cannot change — the job that has become a cage, the illness that closed the door on the life you planned. Paul does not call the chains good. He simply says whose they are. Listen to how you describe your own situation this week. Most of us say, “I am stuck here because of…” and then name the employer, the diagnosis, the decision, the person. Paul had every right to that sentence and never used it. He looked at a Roman chain and named a different owner.
verseByVerse.note: Paul was imprisoned because of his mission to the Gentiles; he breaks off here and resumes in verse 14.

verseByVerse.quote: assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God's grace that was given to me for you, how the mystery was made known to me by revelation,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul explains his calling as a “stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you”: a trust from God, given to him for others. And the content of it, “the mystery”, was not something he worked out but something God revealed to him.

A steward. In that world a steward was usually a trusted slave who ran the whole estate. He owned nothing and controlled almost everything: the keys, the accounts, the stores, the distribution of food to the household. So two things were true of him at once. Nothing in his hands was his, and everything in his hands was there to be given out. A steward who hoarded the master’s grain was not being careful but unfaithful. That is how Paul sees his apostleship: the grace was given to him “for you”. It arrived addressed to someone else.

That is the pattern for everything God gives. Take an honest inventory of what you have — money, skills, a house with a spare room, a good marriage, years of experience, the gospel itself — and ask the steward’s question of each item. Not “am I using this wisely?” — a careful man can answer that comfortably without ever opening the storehouse — but “who was this given to me for?” Only the second question gets the grain to the household.

“Made known to me by revelation.” Notice the passive: he did not deduce it. Paul had the best theological training of his generation, “at the feet of Gamaliel” (Acts 22:3), and none of it produced this. It was disclosed to him on a road, by the One he was travelling to persecute (Galatians 1:12). That is a great mercy for the rest of us. If the mystery had to be deduced, only the clever would have it. Because it is revealed, it belongs to anyone willing to receive it.

“Assuming that you have heard” — why say that after three years in Ephesus? The phrase expresses no doubt; it means “since, as I take it, you have heard”. It also fits a letter meant for several churches in the province, some of whom had never met Paul, which agrees with the early manuscripts that lack “in Ephesus” in 1:1. And “as I have written briefly” (v. 3) points back to what he has already said in this letter (1:9–10; 2:11–22), not to a lost letter.
verseByVerse.note: A stewardship is a trust given to a household manager.

verseByVerse.quote: as I have written briefly. When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s “mystery” is not something obscure kept in the dark; it is God’s plan, hidden in earlier ages and now openly revealed. In the Greek world a mystērion was the secret rite of a cult, reserved for initiates and sworn from outsiders. Paul takes the word and turns it inside out: his mystery is not kept secret but proclaimed, not for a few but for all nations, not hidden in ritual but written down and read aloud. It is a truth “hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints” (Colossians 1:26). The hiddenness was God’s timing, not the truth’s unimportance.

And the hiddenness was real. The prophets spoke of blessing for the nations and of a servant who would be “a light for the nations” (Isaiah 49:6). But the precise shape — that Jew and Gentile would become one body of equal standing, with the dividing wall gone — was not yet visible: present in seed, promised, but veiled. Calling it a mystery honours both the continuity with the Old Testament and the genuine newness of what is now made plain.

verseByVerse.quote: The mystery of Christ, which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul names the secret: “the mystery of Christ” — the plan that centres on Christ and could only be revealed through him. It was not known in earlier generations as it has now been revealed to the apostles and prophets by the Spirit.

What the mystery is. In Ephesians it has two sides: the cosmic — God’s purpose to unite all things under Christ (1:9–10); and the church — that Gentiles are fellow heirs and members of one body (v. 6). Not Gentiles brought under the Jewish covenant, nor two peoples on improved terms, but one body with equal standing. And it is finally the mystery of a person. Paul puts it most personally in Colossians 1:27: “Christ in you, the hope of glory.” The risen Christ actually lives in his people, Gentiles included without qualification.

Not known in other generations. It was not absent from the Old Testament, but not yet fully visible there. The prophets “searched and inquired carefully, inquiring what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating when he predicted the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories” (1 Peter 1:10–11). Picture it: Isaiah writes of a man “pierced for our transgressions”, then goes back over his own sentence trying to see whose face he has described. Daniel is told to “shut up the words and seal the book” (Daniel 12:4). They handled what they could not open. And Peter adds: “It was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but you” (1 Peter 1:12).

Which apostles and prophets? Not the Old Testament prophets, to whom Paul says this was not made known as it is now, but the New Testament prophets who, with the apostles, received the revelation on which the church is built (2:20). That revelation was foundational, and it has been written down for us. Continuationists believe prophets still receive revelation today; but the more likely reading is that revelation of this kind closed with the founding generation.

Where you stand. Most of us assume the great age of faith was back then, and that we are latecomers reading the record. Jesus said the opposite: “Blessed are your eyes, for they see… many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it” (Matthew 13:16–17). On an ordinary Tuesday, with a cup of tea and an open Bible, you know what Isaiah went back over his own page trying to see. That is no reason for smugness — it was revealed, not earned. It is a reason to stop handling your Bible as a duty and start handling it as what it is: the answer to someone else’s lifelong question, put into your hands.

verseByVerse.quote: This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the mystery in one sentence: “the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.” Equal standing, the same inheritance, the same body, the same promise — and it comes through the gospel, not through circumcision or the law.

Three “fellow” words. Paul welds three words together with the prefix sun-, “with”: co-heirs, co-bodied, co-sharers. The middle one, sussōma, is not found in any Greek writing before this letter; Paul seems to have coined it. He reaches for a word that does not exist because what he is describing had never existed either. The Gentile is not attached to the body or admitted alongside it, but is body with you.

What promise, and how do Gentiles share it? The promise is the one to Abraham, that in his offspring all nations would be blessed (Genesis 12:3), and the offspring is Christ, in whom Gentiles become Abraham’s heirs (Galatians 3:16, 29). Here covenant theology and dispensationalism read Paul differently. Covenant theologians (Calvin, Hodge, Vos) see Gentile believers sharing fully in the one covenant of grace made with Abraham and fulfilled in Christ — grafted into the one olive tree (Romans 11:17); the “mystery” is that this full inclusion was not clearly seen before. Dispensationalists (Ryrie, Walvoord, MacArthur) keep a careful distinction between Israel and the church: the church shares the spiritual blessings flowing from those promises, while specific promises to ethnic Israel await a future fulfilment, and the “mystery” is the church age itself. Both affirm what Paul states plainly: Gentile believers have full, equal standing before God now. The first reading fits this letter better: the Gentiles are fellow heirs of the one promise, members of one body (2:12–19; Galatians 3:29).

In real church life. No one writes second-class membership into a church constitution. It grows quietly in who is treated as family and who as a guest: the convert with a visible past whom people are glad to see and slow to trust; the newcomer gently corrected when he uses the vocabulary wrongly; the person who cannot give or host, or arrives with noisy children; the one from the “wrong” background, whichever direction that runs in your church. None of them is told they are lesser. They are simply never quite folded in.

So here is the test. “Fellow heir” means they will inherit exactly what you inherit — not a smaller portion, not later, not on conditions. On Sunday, find the person you would least naturally have chosen, and ask whether you really believe that in the age to come the two of you will stand on identical ground, with the identical inheritance from the identical Father. If that is true then, it is true now, and how you treat him this week is either a rehearsal for it or a contradiction of it. Paul had to invent a word to say this. The least we can do is not quietly unsay it.

verseByVerse.quote: Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given me by the working of his power. To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul was made a servant of this gospel purely by God’s grace — and he, “the very least of all the saints”, was given the task of preaching “the unsearchable riches of Christ” to the Gentiles.

“The very least.” Paul invents a word here, a comparative of “least” — “leaster than the least” — pushing below what grammar allows. It is not false modesty. Luke tells us what he had been: “Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison” (Acts 8:3). House after house: a door opening at the wrong hour, a mother taken out in front of her children. At Stephen’s execution, the witnesses laid their coats at his feet (Acts 7:58). And notice the tense: decades later, an apostle with churches across the empire, he writes, not “I was”, but “I am the very least”. The memory never left him. And it never disqualified him either. Both halves stand in one sentence: “to me, though I am the very least… this grace was given.”

That is exactly where many readers are stuck. There is something in your past that you assume has quietly ruled you out — perhaps not out of heaven, but out of usefulness. You would not put yourself forward for anything or offer to teach anyone, and when someone says God uses ordinary people, you privately add, “but not people who have done what I did.” Paul’s sentence meets you there. He is not the exception; he is the pattern. The unsearchable riches of Christ were given, for preaching, to a man who had dragged women out of their houses for believing in him. Put the thing you are thinking of beside that, and ask honestly whether it is worse.

“The unsearchable riches of Christ.” “Riches” is one of Paul’s favourite words in this letter — riches of grace (1:7; 2:7), of glory (1:18), and now of Christ himself. And the riches are not something Christ hands out at a distance; they are him: forgiveness, adoption, reconciliation, the Spirit, the inheritance, and above all “the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8). “Unsearchable” (anexichniastos) means untraceable, like a path through a forest where the footprints simply stop — the same word Paul uses of God’s ways in Romans 11:33. No theology exhausts them, no lifetime of preaching uses them up, no eternity reaches the bottom. That is what Paul was sent to preach: not a moral code but the inexhaustible wealth of a person who gives himself to those with nothing to offer in return.

verseByVerse.quote: and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s second task is “to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things” — to make visible what God has been doing all along.

The plan. The word is oikonomia, the running of a household by a purposeful manager: nothing random, nothing wasted, everything moving toward an intended end. The one new humanity in the church is not a contingency plan but what God was working toward from the beginning. It was “hidden for ages in God” — held within his own counsel, out of reach of any creature until he chose to reveal it. “None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). It came by disclosure, not discovery. And Paul adds that this is the God “who created all things”: the Maker of the world is the one who hid the plan in it, and the God who made all things is working to unite all things in Christ (1:10). Creation and redemption have one Author and one horizon.

“Nothing wasted”? That is easy to write and hard to believe on a Thursday afternoon. Most of us can point to stretches that look like waste from the inside: years in a job that led nowhere, training never used, a decade lost to illness or a failed marriage. Paul does not answer by denying the experience; he names who is managing the household. And you can test it tonight, on paper. Trace how you came to hear the gospel at all — not the theology, the mechanics. Who told you? How did you come to be in that room, that school, that friendship? Follow it back four or five links and you will find a chain of things that looked accidental at the time, mostly arranged by people who had no idea what they were doing. Someone moved house; someone fell ill; someone invited the wrong person by mistake. That is oikonomia. If God managed all that without consulting you, the years you have written off are far more likely to be rooms in the same house than evidence against it.

“To bring to light.” Light does not create what it shows. Switch on a lamp in a dark room and nothing new appears — the furniture was there all along, and you had been barking your shins on it. God’s plan did not begin when it was published; it stood complete before the world was made, and at Christ’s coming the light went on. A Christian is not someone who has thought up a better explanation of things, but someone who has been shown the room he was already standing in.

verseByVerse.quote: so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s purpose is that “through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places.” The church is not only the beneficiary of God’s plan but his display of it to the spiritual powers.

“Manifold.” The word, polupoikilos, was used of richly embroidered, many-coloured cloth. God’s wisdom is not a single colour but a spectrum, and the canvas that shows it is the church: the place where the impossible has happened, where former enemies — Jew and Gentile — share one table and one Lord. No diplomacy ever dissolved that division; the only explanation is what God did in Christ. His wisdom shows in the method too: he “chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27) — a crucified Messiah, a persecutor as chief missionary, forgiven sinners as the display of his glory.

The audience. “The rulers and authorities in the heavenly places” appear four times in this letter (1:21; 2:2; 3:10; 6:12), perhaps because Ephesus was gripped by fear of named spiritual powers. The display is not for their benefit but a declaration, like a conquering king parading his triumph. Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame” (Colossians 2:15), and the church is the ongoing proclamation of that victory. Every time former strangers call the same God Father, God is saying to every power: you could not predict this, could not prevent it, and cannot undo it.

The back of the cloth. Anyone who has watched embroidery being made knows it has two sides. From the back it is a mess: knots, loose ends, threads running off at angles, colours stopping dead. Turn it over, and every thread was going somewhere. That is the honest position of anyone in a real congregation. From where you sit, the church does not look like the display of God’s wisdom. It looks like a rota that keeps failing, two families not speaking, a treasurer worried about the roof, a sermon that ran long, and a man in the third row you gave up on some time ago. You are looking at the back of the cloth. Paul does not say the knots are imaginary, only that you are not the one standing in front of it.

And notice what the powers are studying: not the building or the music, but what happens between people who would never otherwise be in the same room — two members reconciling after eighteen months of coldness, a widow driven to hospital by someone who does not much like her, six people at a prayer meeting on a wet Tuesday, a former enemy passing the bread to a former enemy. That is the embroidery. Remember it the next time you decide some relationship in the church is not worth the effort. That relationship is not a distraction from the exhibit. It is the exhibit.

verseByVerse.quote: This was according to the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this follows God’s “eternal purpose”, now carried out in Christ — and because of it every believer has “boldness and access with confidence” to God through faith in Christ. Paul said it in 2:18; he says it again, more strongly, because it needs saying twice.

Two words. His readers came from a world of spiritual dread: pagan gods were capricious and managed by ritual, and even Israel’s holy God was approached through a priest, a sacrifice and purification, the high priest entering once a year. Against all that, Paul says every believer may now approach the Father directly. Boldness (parrēsia) was the free citizen’s right to speak openly before a ruler — plainly, in his own words, without first obtaining permission. Access (prosagōgē) is the right of entry into a king’s presence, granted by someone with standing to bring you in. Your introducer is Christ, whose welcome is permanent, and being in him you share it; it does not rise and fall with your performance. Paul presses the point from prison: what I suffer does not change what you have.

How we actually pray. Listen to the prayer of someone who does not believe he has this freedom. It is hedged. There is much throat-clearing before anything real is said. “If it be thy will” arrives early — not as submission but as insurance, so that nothing has quite been asked and nothing can be refused. The requests stay small, because small requests are safer. The voice changes into a register used at no other hour. And after a bad week the praying stops altogether, on the grounds that it would be decent to stay away until things improve. Every one of those instincts belongs to a servant on probation, and Paul says that is not what you are. Grief may come out as grief, confusion as confusion — not because God needs informing, but because a son does not brief his father the way a petitioner briefs an official: “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16).

One guard: free speech before a King is not familiarity with an equal. We draw near with confidence, and what we draw near to is a throne. The confidence was never in ourselves, but in the one who brings us in.

“Faith in him.” Some translators read this as “his faithfulness”, meaning Christ’s own faithfulness gives us access. The ESV’s reading fits best here, since boldness and access are what we receive by trusting him (compare Galatians 2:16; Philippians 3:9). Either way, the ground of our access is Christ, not ourselves. And note the tense: we have it — now, held by a man in chains and shared with everyone reading over his shoulder.

verseByVerse.quote: So I ask you not to lose heart over what I am suffering for you, which is your glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
