Paul asks his readers not to lose heart over his sufferings, because they are “your glory”: his imprisonment is the price of the gospel reaching them.

The comfort is travelling the wrong way round. The man in the cell is worried about the morale of the people who are free. He does not ask for sympathy; he says, “I ask you not to lose heart.” The danger he heads off is real, and it still empties churches. The word means to grow weary, lose your nerve, give up. What makes people give up is often not their own suffering but someone else’s: a respected pastor diagnosed at fifty-two, a couple who prayed for years for a child burying one, a missionary family coming home broken. No one announces a change of belief; it happens quietly, in the gap between what was preached and what was watched, and people conclude that the thing does not seem to work. Paul knows the Ephesians are doing this arithmetic about him, and he interrupts it.

“Which is your glory.” Picture a father who works night shifts to put his children through university. The nights are hard, but one day they graduate, and you could say those nights were their glory: his cost became their inheritance. Paul is in chains because he actually delivered the gospel to the Gentiles; the Ephesians are believers because he did. So when they look at his chains, they are not seeing a man abandoned by God, but the cost of the gospel reaching them, written into a human life. Suffering inside God’s plan is not a sign that the plan has failed. It follows the logic of the cross, where the death that looked like the end was the turning point (Philippians 1:12–14; 2 Corinthians 4:17).

Notice what Paul does not do: he does not explain why God allowed the arrest, when release might come, or what it is achieving in Rome. He gives one sentence about what the suffering is for and leaves the rest alone. That restraint is instructive, because most of our attempts to comfort each other fail by supplying reasons we do not actually have. And it gives a test. When someone faithful suffers, what is your first instinct? For most of us it is to look for the flaw — the hidden sin, the wrong decision, the weak faith — because a flaw would make the arithmetic work again. Paul offers no flaw. He offers a purpose: what this is costing me is for you. Try meeting the next hard providence, in your life or someone else’s, with that as the first question rather than the last.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul falls to his knees. He began the sentence in v.1 and was swept away by the parenthesis of his own apostolic calling. Now, in v.14, he takes it up again on his knees — and what follows is the most doxologically charged prayer in the New Testament. Four requests of escalating grandeur, each one building on the last, until the whole structure reaches a summit it cannot contain and erupts into one of the greatest doxologies ever written. The prayer is a mountain, and at its peak the clouds part.

He prays first for inner strengthening by the Spirit in the inner person — the deep, hidden, interior part of the human being where the real life is lived. He prays then for Christ to dwell in the heart by faith — not merely to visit, but to take up permanent residence, to be at home there. He prays third for the comprehension of something incomprehensible: the breadth and length and height and depth of the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge. Four dimensions — suggesting something that cannot be measured in any direction, a love that exceeds every capacity to contain or categorise it. And then, the goal that gathers all of this up: "that you may be filled with all the fullness of God." The finite vessel of the human soul invited to receive the infinite fullness of the divine life.

The doxology that follows (vv.20–21) is the most expansive statement of God's power to answer prayer in all of Scripture: He is able to do "far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us." "Far more abundantly" is a single word Paul builds up prefix upon prefix (huperekperissou) — language stacking on language, because language cannot contain what Paul wants to say about the inexhaustible capacity of God to exceed every prayer and every imagination. We always pray too small. God always answers beyond the asking. The prayer ends where the letter began: to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Indwelling Christ and the Fullness of God

The prayer of Ephesians 3:14–21 reveals the goal of the Christian life with startling clarity: not moral improvement, not doctrinal accuracy, not even evangelistic fruitfulness — but the fullness of God. "Filled with all the fullness of God" (v.19) is a goal so vast it cannot be reached in a lifetime, which is precisely the point. The Christian life is not a project with a completion date; it is a journey into an infinity that perpetually exceeds the traveller. Paul set no limit to his desires for the Ephesians — he asked for the infinite, because the infinite is what God offers.

The means of this fullness is the indwelling of Christ. "That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith" (v.17) — the verb "dwell" (katoikein) means to settle, to take up permanent residence, as opposed to merely passing through. This is not the occasional visitation of religious experience; it is the abiding presence of the living Christ in the interior life of the believer. The Reformers consistently emphasized that union with Christ — not merely forgiveness, not merely a changed record before God, but genuine, living union with the risen Lord — is the foundation of the entire Christian life. It is from this union that everything else flows: assurance, holiness, prayer, service, suffering, joy.

The doxology of vv.20–21 is also a theology of prayer. It teaches us that God is not limited by the smallness of our asking. The greatness of our petitions cannot exhaust his capacity to answer; the boldness of our faith cannot outrun his willingness to give. The God to whom we pray is the God who can do more than we can imagine asking — and the power by which he does it is "at work within us." It is the same resurrection power of Ephesians 1:19–20. Our prayers are small; his answers are not required to match them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The mystery religions of Ephesus promised spiritual fullness — union with the divine, access to hidden power — through initiation, through ritual, through the gradual ascent of the initiated. The costs were significant: financial, social, sometimes physical. And the fullness promised was always partial, always provisional, always requiring the next level of initiation. Paul prays for his readers to receive a fullness that no mystery religion could offer and no initiation could achieve: the fullness of God himself, freely given, received through faith, sustained by the Spirit. The contrast with what Ephesus was selling could not have been more pointed.

Now: "Far more abundantly than all that we ask or think" — this phrase has stood as one of the great encouragements of Christian prayer across the centuries. When we pray small, God answers large. When we cannot find words, the Spirit intercedes. When the situation seems beyond recovery, we serve the God who raises the dead. The doxology of Ephesians 3 is not merely a liturgical flourish; it is a declaration of the character of the God to whom we pray. He exceeds our prayers not because he is indifferent to them but because he is inexhaustibly generous. Every time this doxology is spoken in corporate worship, the church is reminding itself — and the watching powers — of who their God is.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now returns to his prayer and kneels “before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named.” Before asking, he shows us who he is asking.

He kneels. Jews usually prayed standing; kneeling was for moments of special intensity — Solomon at the temple’s dedication (1 Kings 8:54), Daniel at his open window (Daniel 6:10), Jesus in Gethsemane (Luke 22:41). And this man is in custody. A prisoner going down on a stone floor, probably watched, to pray at length for a church hundreds of miles away that he may never see again, is not performing for anyone. There is no one there to impress.

The Father. There is a wordplay English loses: patēr (Father) and patria (family) share a root. The very idea of family — belonging, being named, a household you are bound to — exists because there is an original Father. Human fatherhood did not invent the idea and project it onto God; God is Father first, eternally, and human fathers are partial reflections. And “every family in heaven and on earth” reaches beyond human households to every ordered community of creatures. Does that make God the Father of everyone? He is the Creator from whom all fatherhood takes its name. But the fatherhood that saves is adoption, given to those in Christ (1:5; John 1:12; Romans 8:15). Every person is God’s creature; only believers can call him Abba.

The face you imagine. For anyone whose earthly father was absent, harsh or cruel: your experience is not the standard by which God is measured. He is the standard, and what you knew was a distortion of something undistorted. Next time you pray, notice what face you are imagining; nearly everyone imagines one. For some it is disappointed but too polite to say so; for others distracted, giving you whatever time it can spare; for others already scanning for the fault before you finish. That face usually belonged to someone — a parent, a teacher, someone whose approval you never secured — and it has been on loan to God ever since. You will not shift it by trying to feel differently. You shift it by looking at Jesus, “the exact imprint of his nature” (Hebrews 1:3), who said, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). Watch him with the people no one wanted: the leper he touched (Mark 1:41), the woman at the well (John 4), the thief given paradise with hours to live (Luke 23:43). That is not Jesus being kinder than the Father. That is the Father showing you his face.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “family” renders patria, a word closely related to “father” (pater) in verse 14.

verseByVerse.quote: That according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s first request is for strength — not over circumstances, but in “your inner being”, by the Spirit, “according to the riches of his glory”: not out of an account that might run low, but on the scale of God’s own wealth.

The inner being is the self no one else sees: your will, your faith, your ability to trust God when nothing visible supports it. Two people can face the same illness or grief and look alike from outside; one is quietly falling apart, the other genuinely anchored — not unaffected, but held somewhere the storm cannot reach. The difference is not temperament but the condition of the inner person. Paul had written years earlier, “Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16), and it is true in this prison: the outer man in chains, the inner man being renewed.

What this strength does. It keeps the will fixed on God when feelings give out and prayer seems to hit the ceiling. It gives endurance in long suffering: “strengthened with all power… for all endurance and patience with joy” (Colossians 1:11). It produces love that costs something when natural love has run out. And it gives a peace that does not depend on circumstances (Philippians 4:7). Notice what Paul prays instead of: not that their circumstances improve, but that their inner life be strengthened. A person strong inside can face any circumstance; a person weak inside cannot be rescued even by the best conditions.

Two tests. First, write down honestly what you asked God for this week, for yourself and others. For most of us the list is almost entirely external: a diagnosis, a job, an exam, safe travel, a house sale, a wayward child’s circumstances. Nothing on it is wrong — Scripture invites us to bring these things. But Paul’s request rarely appears on church prayer lists at all. We pray almost only about the outside of people’s lives, then wonder why they are not stronger inside. Second, the inner being is what is left when the supports are taken away. What are you like in the hour when nothing is required of you and no one is watching? What happens to your faith in a week with no encouragement, no visible fruit and no sense of God’s nearness? That week is not an interruption of the Christian life; it is the examination of the inner person.

And the strength comes “through his Spirit” — from a Person, not a technique. So if you read this and find yourself weak, the answer is not a self-improvement programme. It is to ask. The whole sentence is a prayer; Paul is showing you how to get what he describes.

verseByVerse.quote: So that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, that you, being rooted and grounded in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that Christ would truly be at home in their hearts through faith, and that they would be “rooted and grounded in love” — their whole life resting on God’s love for them.

“Dwell.” The word, katoikeō, means to settle in permanently, to move in and unpack, as opposed to lodging for a night. Paul prays not that Christ would visit in a crisis and then go quiet, but that he would be at home at the centre of you — on an ordinary Monday, at work, in the argument with your spouse, in the moment of temptation. It is possible to be a real Christian and still give him the guest room rather than the master bedroom. “Through faith” is the channel: not a one-time decision but a daily turning of the heart to him — “Abide in me, and I in you” (John 15:4).

Two pictures. A tree is only as strong as its hidden roots. To be rooted in love is to send your roots down into the certainty that God loves you — not because you earned it, but because that is who he is. When the storm comes — loss, failure, accusation — the deeply rooted believer bends but does not fall, because he knows the one thing the wind cannot change. The one whose sense of God’s love rises and falls with his performance has nothing to hold him, because the thing he leaned on is what the storm attacks. And a house is only as safe as its foundation (Matthew 7:24–27). A faith built on moral achievement cracks when you fail badly enough; a faith built on fear either crushes you or bolts when the pressure lifts. Love is not the decoration on top of the Christian life; it is the ground beneath it.

Both words are passive and perfect in Greek: you have been rooted; you have been founded. Trees do not plant themselves, and no building lays its own foundation. Sending your roots deeper is real work, but it responds to a planting that already happened and was never your idea.

The test. You never discover what you are rooted in on a good day. The most revealing storm is not bereavement or illness but your own sin. So ask honestly: after you have failed badly — the thing you would not say aloud — what happens to your sense of being loved by God? If it collapses and stays collapsed until you have made up the ground with better behaviour, then whatever you believe about grace, you are actually rooted in your own performance. That explains the whole pattern: the shame, the distance, the not praying, the waiting until you feel presentable. But if, under genuine grief over the sin, something does not move — a floor you have not fallen through, the knowledge that you are loved by a God who knew about this before you did it — then you have found the foundation. It was there before the storm, it was laid by someone else, and it is the one thing your worst week cannot get underneath.

verseByVerse.quote: may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that, together with all believers, they would have strength to grasp “the breadth and length and height and depth” of Christ’s love (v. 19) — a love without limits in any direction.

“With all the saints.” The comprehension is shared. The love of Christ is greater than any one believer or culture can take in; the whole church is needed even to begin. That is why theological isolation — reading only one tradition, knowing only one kind of Christian — quietly shrinks the soul.

Four dimensions. Preachers often map these onto the cross, which preaches well, but Paul does not make that link. Four directions were the ancient way of describing all of space. Paul means the love of Christ fills every direction as far as you can go: no edge, no ceiling, no floor. Its breadth is wide enough to include you — your history, failures and doubts — and the person beside you whose life looks nothing like yours, and people from every nation. Its length runs from before the foundation of the world (1:4) to beyond the last age; it did not begin when you became lovable, and nothing “will be able to separate us” from it (Romans 8:38–39). Its height seats you in the heavenly places (2:6) and brings you before the Father with boldness (3:12). Its depth reaches you where you really are, not where you pretend to be — shame, addiction, grief, the thing you have never told anyone — for “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20).

Why “strength” to comprehend? Understanding usually needs intelligence or time, not strength. But this answers the question left open in verse 16: what is the Spirit’s power in the inner being for? Not chiefly for miracles or great achievements, but so that you can take in how much you are loved. That sounds strange until you watch someone try. It takes little strength to accept a compliment. It takes a great deal to accept a gift you can never repay, from someone who knows exactly what you are. Everything in us resists being loved on those terms; we would rather be admired, or at least useful. To stand still and be loved with nothing to contribute undoes a person, and it takes God’s power not to flinch and start earning again. So if you have ever read a passage like this, felt something rise, and then changed the subject or remembered a job that needed doing — that is exactly what Paul is praying about. He is asking not that they be taught the dimensions, but that they be given strength to stand in front of them.

parallels.desc: higher than heaven, deeper than Sheol

verseByVerse.quote: and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that they would know the love of Christ “that surpasses knowledge” and so be “filled with all the fullness of God” — the highest thing he could ask.

Knowing what surpasses knowledge is not a contradiction. You can know facts about the ocean without ever standing on the shore. Paul wants you on the beach, feeling the spray, understanding in your bones that this ocean has no other shore.

Filled with God’s fullness does not mean becoming God or losing yourself in him; the creature remains a creature. It means being filled with what God gives of himself — his life, love, holiness, joy and peace — as much as a finite person can hold. Picture a jug held under a waterfall. The waterfall is beyond comparison larger, yet the jug can be completely full. Paul prays that nothing in you would be left to fear, self-sufficiency or the old life. In practice it looks like loving more deeply, growing in a patience and holiness not native to your temperament, and a joy that does not evaporate when things are hard. And “be filled” is passive: the jug does not fill itself; it holds itself under the water. Your part is to stay open to the source — prayer, the word, worship, confession, the company of God’s people (5:18). This prayer is answered more and more as you grow, and completely when you see Christ face to face (1 John 3:2).

The space. You do not pray for someone to be filled unless there is a space in them. Everyone knows the restlessness that survives getting what you wanted. The promotion is pleasant for a fortnight; the house is bought, the qualification finished, the relationship secured, and within a season the same low hum returns. We usually assume we chose the wrong thing and pick another. But Paul is describing a capacity no created thing was ever the right size for. The hollow is not a design fault; it is the shape of a container built for the fullness of God.

Plural “you”. Every “you” in this prayer is plural. Paul is asking that a congregation — this mixed Jew-and-Gentile assembly — would together be filled, just as he called the church Christ’s fullness in 1:23. So this is not something you accomplish alone in a quiet room. Some of it arrives only through the people you have been joined to, including those you would never have chosen; hold yourself apart from them and there are dimensions of this you will never be filled with.

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul ends the prayer with praise: God “is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think”, by the same power already at work in us. “Far more abundantly” (huperekperissou) piles prefixes together — beyond, out of, overflowing — because no single word goes far enough.

When the answer was no. This promise can wound. Someone reads it with a specific prayer in mind that met a plain no: the healing that did not come, the marriage that ended anyway, years of asking that returned only silence. To them it can sound like mockery: “I asked and got less, not more.” The answer is in two small words: “or think”. God does more than we ask, and also more than we know to ask. Our prayers are often not only too small but wrong in content, asking for the lesser thing because we cannot yet see the greater. A loving father does not give a child everything the child names, and the withholding is his love at work. Paul himself asked three times for his thorn to be removed; the answer was no, and the “more” turned out to be grace sufficient and power made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). And where no better thing is yet visible, the “more” is not cancelled but kept — much of it for “the coming ages” (2:7), for the day God wipes away every tear (Revelation 21:4). The account does not close at the grave.

“The power at work within us.” The verb is present: this power is operating in you now — the same power that raised Jesus from the dead (1:19–20). Then why does it so often not feel like it? Because it works whether felt or not, like a seed breaking through concrete — “our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). Because it is aimed first at the inner person: you may be waiting for it to change your situation while God is using the situation to change you. And because it is most visible in weakness: “my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Where your strength ends, his is found.

The hinge of the letter. This doxology is not a decorative ending. Everything from 1:3 to here has been about what God has done — chosen, redeemed, sealed, raised, seated, reconciled. Apart from a call to remember (2:11), there has not been a single command in three chapters. The moment the praise ends, the tone changes: “I therefore… urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling” (4:1), and the rest of the letter is instruction — how to speak, work, handle anger, be married, fight. Between the doctrine and the duty Paul places not a summary but praise. That order does not reverse. Anyone who takes up chapters 4–6 without first being undone by chapters 1–3 will find the commands crushing, because he will be trying to produce by effort a life that was only ever meant to overflow from astonishment. The obedience of this letter runs downhill from a doxology. If it is running uphill in your life, you may have started in the wrong chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer ends with God: “to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.”

What does it mean to give God glory? Behind the word is the Hebrew kābôd, weight — the overwhelming reality of who God is (see 1:17). Giving him glory does not add anything to him; the sun does not brighten because someone looks at it. It means recognising and declaring what is already true of him, and living consistently with it. That takes ordinary forms. Honest praise: kneeling by your bed on a Tuesday night with no audience and saying, “You are good and I am not; you saved me when I had nothing to offer.” Gratitude is glory in its simplest form (Psalm 50:23). A life that points to him: when you are patient with a difficult colleague and they wonder what you have that they do not, and the answer is Christ — “whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). And trusting him when it is hard — “I do not understand this, but I trust you” — perhaps the deepest form: “Though he slay me, I will hope in him” (Job 13:15).

Two places. “In the church and in Christ Jesus” — side by side as the venues of God’s eternal glory. One is the risen Son, seated above every power. The other is a congregation with rota problems, awkward silences and a roof that needs money no one has. Paul neither apologises for the pairing nor explains it away, because he has told us why it holds (1:23): the church is Christ’s body, and the glory of the head shows in the body he fills. You are not a spectator of something happening elsewhere; you are one of the places where God’s glory is meant to be seen. And “throughout all generations”: your Tuesday-night prayer does not vanish by morning; it joins the chorus of every generation of believers.

Amen. The last word is not Paul’s but yours. Amen is a Hebrew word of agreement — “so be it; count me in.” Paul has written the sentence; the Amen is where the reader signs it. Do you actually want this: God’s glory in the church, through all generations? Saying it commits you to being one of the places where that glory becomes visible, in the particular congregation you will sit in this Sunday.

4.title: Unity, Gifts, and the New Self
4.text: <sup>1</sup>I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called, <sup>2</sup>with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, <sup>3</sup>eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. <sup>4</sup>There is one body and one Spirit — just as you were called to the one hope that belongs to your call — <sup>5</sup>one Lord, one faith, one baptism, <sup>6</sup>one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all. <sup>7</sup>But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift. <sup>8</sup>Therefore it says, “When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men.” <sup>9</sup>(In saying, “He ascended,” verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Walk Worthy: The Unity of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Therefore. The great hinge of the letter. Three chapters of indicative — what God has done in Christ, what we have been given, who we are — and now three chapters of imperative: walk worthy. The imperative is entirely grounded in the indicative, and this sequencing is not accidental. Paul never tells us to become something we are not; he tells us to become in practice what we already are in Christ. The Christian life is not the achievement of a new status; it is the outworking in daily experience of a status already secured in the heavenly places. You are already chosen, adopted, redeemed, sealed. Now walk like it.

The first and most foundational imperative is the preservation of unity — and the way Paul frames it is telling. He does not say “create unity” or “achieve unity.” He says “maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (v.3). The unity already exists; the Spirit has already made one body. The question is not whether it is real but whether it is visible, whether our daily behaviour reflects the theological truth of our oneness in Christ. And the means of maintaining it are not structural or organisational but dispositional: all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love.

The sevenfold “one” that follows (vv.4–6) is the theological bedrock of this unity — and it moves from the experiential to the ultimate. One body, one Spirit, one hope: the dimensions of our shared life. One Lord, one faith, one baptism: the shared confession and initiation. One God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all: the ultimate ground, the Father in whom all the “ones” find their source and their destination. The unity of the church is rooted in the unity of the triune God. We are one because he is one — and because he has made us one in his one Son by his one Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Unity of the Church as Theological Reality

The passage reveals that the unity of the church is not an aspiration or a programme — it is an ontological reality that precedes and grounds every effort to express it. The Spirit has already created one body. The question is not whether unity exists but whether our behaviour honours the unity that does. This distinction between the given reality and the required response is characteristic of Paul's ethical method throughout the letter: indicative first, imperative second. Be what you are. Express what is already true.

The four virtues through which unity is maintained — humility, gentleness, patience, forbearance — are a portrait of Christlike character applied to community life. They are not soft virtues; they are demanding ones. Humility means thinking of others' interests above your own (Philippians 2:3). Gentleness (prautēs) belongs to the word Jesus used of himself (“I am gentle and lowly in heart,” Matthew 11:29) — strength in service of love. Patience is the willingness to absorb rather than retaliate. Forbearance is the daily choice to keep choosing the person in front of you rather than withdrawing when they disappoint. Together these virtues create the environment in which the given unity of the Spirit can be made visible.

The Reformers consistently emphasised that doctrinal unity and relational unity are inseparable. The sevenfold “one” of vv.4–6 grounds the relational unity of vv.2–3 in doctrinal reality. We are not called to unity by ignoring our differences or pretending that doctrine doesn't matter. We are called to unity because there is genuinely one Lord, one faith, one baptism — and the body that confesses these things is, by that very confession, one. Preserving this unity is not sentimentality; it is theological faithfulness.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church was the most socially diverse community in the city. Former Artemis worshippers, Jewish converts, Greek philosophers, slaves and freedmen, wealthy merchants and harbour workers — all brought together by the preaching of the gospel. The centrifugal forces were enormous. Every human instinct would have been to fracture along existing social fault lines. Paul's “therefore” connects the unity he calls for directly to the cosmic reality of chapter 2: the wall has already come down. The body is already one. Now: walk like it. Bear with one another. Choose the humility that makes room for people unlike you. This was not a small ask in first-century Ephesus.

Now: The church in our age is under intense pressure to fragment — along political lines, cultural lines, worship-style lines, theological nuance lines. The market logic of contemporary Christianity encourages us to shop for churches that suit our preferences, reinforcing the very homogeneity that Paul's vision challenges. Against this, Ephesians 4:1–6 calls the church to a costly unity rooted not in shared preference but in shared confession: one Lord, one faith, one baptism. The local church that perseveres through its internal differences — that chooses patient, humble, forbearing love over the easier path of fragmentation — is doing something more theologically significant than it knows. It is bearing witness to the one God who is over all and through all and in all.

verseByVerse.quote: I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Paul turns from what God has done to how his people should live: “walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called.” This is the banner over chapters 4–6. The calling was described in chapters 1–3; the walk is that calling lived out.

The turn. For three chapters Paul has issued almost no commands — one call to remember (2:11), nothing else. He has only described: chosen, redeemed, sealed, made alive, raised, seated, reconciled. Then a doxology. And when the first real instruction finally arrives, after all that grandeur, it is: walk. It is the most ordinary verb available, and Paul uses it to organise everything that follows (2:2, 10; 4:17; 5:2, 8, 15). Walking is what you do all day without thinking about it. It is not an event; nobody schedules or photographs it. That tells you where the Christian life is lived: not in the peaks, but in the ordinary going-along of an ordinary week.

“Worthy” is easily misheard as earning, and the man who wrote 2:8–9 is not reopening that account. Axios is a merchant’s word, the picture of a balance: goods in one pan, answered by weights in the other. You cannot add anything to the calling side; God filled it before the world was made. You are simply asked to bring your side into line with it. A son who bears the family name worthily is not earning the name; he already has it. He is being asked to live like someone who has it.

And notice who is asking: “a prisoner for the Lord.” The man urging you to walk has had his own walking reduced to the length of a cell. He is asking others to do freely what has been taken from him — which may be why he does not command but “urge”.
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 1–3 set out what God has done; chapters 4–6 show the life that follows.

verseByVerse.quote: With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul names four qualities by which the church’s unity is kept: humility, gentleness, patience, and bearing with one another in love. His sentence runs straight on into verse 3: these are the ligaments that hold the peace together.

Humility was not a virtue in the Greek and Roman world; the word described the cringing posture of a slave. Paul makes it the foundation of Christian character, as Jesus showed in washing feet (John 13:1–17) and on the cross. Gentleness (prautēs) was used of a horse broken to the bridle: it has lost none of its strength, but the strength now answers to another hand. So it is not the same as being mild-mannered; a naturally timid person is not gentle in this sense, because he has nothing needing restraint. Gentleness is strength under command. Patience is long-suffering toward people, not only circumstances. And love keeps the others healthy: without it humility becomes self-contempt, gentleness passivity, and patience resentment.

“Bearing with one another” does the real work. The word means to put up with, to carry the weight of — and the weight is other Christians. Make it concrete: the man who tells you the same story every time you meet; the woman who is late to everything and always has a reason; the one whose theology is slightly off and wants to discuss it after the service, at length; the person who takes twenty minutes to say what needed three. None of them is sinning. They are simply heavy, as people are, and the instruction is to pick up the weight and keep walking.

Everyone reading this casts himself as the one doing the bearing. Turn it round: who in your church is bearing with you? Someone is. There is a person who finds your manner difficult, your opinions tiring, your particular blind spot wearing, and who has decided, quietly and without telling you, to put up with it and love you anyway. You are someone’s Wednesday morning. When that lands, humility stops being a doctrine and becomes possible.

verseByVerse.quote: Eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers must be “eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” The key word is maintain: not create or achieve, but guard and keep. The unity already exists (vv. 4–6); the task is not to break it.

You could not build this unity if you tried; it is made by the Spirit. It is like the difference between founding a family and not wrecking one. No one creates his own family; he finds himself in it, and what remains is how he behaves toward people he did not choose. But keeping it takes effort. “Eager” (spoudazontes) means make it your business, hurry to it. And maintenance is unglamorous. A house is maintained by someone clearing the gutters in November; a marriage by two people apologising rather more often than they would like.

What actually damages it. We imagine the threat is doctrinal, and it seldom is. Churches rarely divide over the person of Christ. They divide over a message never returned, a decision taken without consulting someone who expected to be consulted, a remark repeated to the wrong person, a slight at the door that was probably not even intended. Theology is usually recruited afterwards, to give the wound a respectable name.

Unity with every church? The unity Paul describes rests on “one Lord, one faith” (v. 5), so it cannot include those who deny the gospel itself. Paul pronounces a curse on another gospel (Galatians 1:8–9), John forbids welcoming those who deny Christ’s teaching (2 John 10), and Romans 16:17 tells believers to avoid those who teach against the doctrine they learned. But among those who share the gospel, Christians should not divide over secondary matters such as church government, the details of the last things, or styles of worship. They may worship in different churches, but they should treat one another as brothers. Separation is right only where the gospel itself is at stake.

The bond of peace never breaks in the abstract; it breaks between two particular people. So: is there anyone in your congregation with whom you are not at peace — someone you avoid at coffee, or whose name produces a small tightening? That is where this verse is addressed, and no amount of general goodwill toward the church covers it. Paul is not asking you to feel unified. He is asking you to go and repair one specific ligament.

verseByVerse.quote: There is one body and one Spirit — just as you were called to the one hope that belongs to your call — one Lord, one faith, one baptism,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church’s unity rests on seven things believers already share: “one body and one Spirit… one hope… one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father” (vv. 4–6). The list is Trinitarian — one Spirit, one Lord, one Father — so Christian unity is not merely organisational or emotional; it reflects the oneness of God himself.

Count them: seven times in three verses Paul strikes the same note. He is not writing elegantly; he is hammering, fixing in the mind how much is already held in common before any difference is allowed to come up. One body: a single organism, not a collection of individuals. One Spirit: the same Spirit who sealed every believer. One hope: the same final destiny. One Lord, one faith, one baptism: marks of belonging to the one Lord who claimed his people.

What is the “one baptism”? Some take it as the Spirit’s baptism into Christ (1 Corinthians 12:13); others as the water baptism by which every believer publicly enters the church. The more likely reading is water baptism, the one rite of entry shared by all Christians, which signifies union with Christ (Romans 6:3–4). Churches still disagree about who should be baptised and how; these notes hold that baptism belongs to those who have come to faith. But because baptism is one, it is never repeated, and all who are truly baptised into Christ belong to one body.

A one-minute test. Think of the last serious disagreement you saw in a church — the one that cooled a friendship, emptied a few seats, or is still carefully not mentioned. Run it against Paul’s seven. Was it about the one body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism or Father? For most church disagreements the honest answer is that the subject is not on the list at all: the music, the timing, the building, how a decision was communicated, a preferred translation, a political instinct. Some of those matter a good deal, but not one of them is load-bearing, and Paul has just named seven things that are.

And take “one hope” personally. The same finish line means the same finishing group. The people you find hardest in your church are not a temporary arrangement you will be relieved of at the end; they are the people you will be with, in unclouded friendship, for ever. Learning to love them now is an early start on what you will be doing for eternity anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list climbs to its summit: “one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.” Three prepositions describe how God relates to his people: over all (he rules; nothing outranks him), through all (he works in and through every circumstance, including the ones you would never have chosen), and in all (he lives within his people). This is not pantheism, but the living God who stands above, sustains and indwells his people at once. Over you, at work through your week, living inside you — which leaves no position from which anything could reach you without passing him first.

Does “Father of all” mean everyone is God’s child? The phrase is often used to prove that all roads lead home, and the context will not allow it. Paul is in the middle of a passage about the church — one body, one Spirit, one faith, one baptism. The “all” he keeps repeating is the all of the previous chapters: Jew and Gentile together, the wall down. Scripture does call God the Father of all in the sense that he made and sustains every person — “In him we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28) — but it reserves sonship in the saving sense for those who receive Christ: “to all who did receive him… he gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12). Both are true; only the second is in view here. And because the church’s unity rests on the one Father, a church that splits into factions contradicts the very nature of the God it worships.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having called the church to unity, Paul introduces the glorious diversity that serves it — and its source is the most unexpected one imaginable: the triumphant, ascended, gift-giving Christ. Paul quotes Psalm 68, a victory psalm describing God ascending Mount Zion after defeating his enemies, distributing plunder to his people. He applies it to Christ: the One who descended to the lowest depths of the earth — to death itself, to the far country of human ruin — and then ascended far above all the heavens, has taken the spoils of his victory and distributed them as gifts to his beloved people. And the gifts are not impersonal endowments. They are people. Christ gives gifted persons to his church — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers — as the ongoing fruit of his conquest.

And the ascended Christ who gives these gifts is himself the one who “fills all things” (v. 10). This is the great fullness theme that pulses through the whole letter: the church is his fullness (1:23), the goal of every believer is to be filled with all the fullness of God (3:19), the target of every ministry is the fullness of Christ (4:13). The mission of the exalted Lord is to fill all of creation with his presence, his glory, his life. The church is the first instalment of that filling. To serve in this body is to participate in the most significant project in the universe.

The four gifted offices — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers — are not interchangeable. The apostles and prophets belong to the foundational era: they laid the once-for-all deposit of Scripture and revelation on which the whole church stands. The evangelists press outward to where the gospel has not yet reached. The pastor-teachers build up what remains, week by week, year by year, through patient feeding of the word. Each equips the saints in their own way: through the apostolic Scriptures, through the whole counsel of God applied to conscience and life, through training every member to be a witness, through the slow, faithful formation of souls.

And the purpose of this equipping subverts every instinct toward a passive, receiver-only congregation. The saints do the ministry; the gifted leaders equip the saints to do it. The congregation is not the audience; it is the army. The pastor is not the performer; he is the trainer. Diakonia — service — belongs to every member: serving the poor, encouraging the struggling, teaching and discipling one another, praying, giving, witnessing.

The goal is breathtaking: unity of the faith, full knowledge of the Son of God, mature manhood, nothing less than the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ (v. 13). Not a few exceptional souls reaching great heights, but the whole body — every member — growing together toward the complete image of Christ. This growth is mature, not merely numerical. It is deep, not merely wide. It means speaking the truth in love (v. 15).

The result, when every part is working properly, is a body that builds itself up in love (v. 16): growing more mature, more loving, and more attractive to a watching world. Most of this growth is invisible — the unseen ligament, the quiet conversation, the faithful prayer. But it is real, and it is aimed at the most glorious end imaginable: a church that together reflects the full stature of Jesus Christ, the one who fills all things, until God is all in all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ascended Christ and the Equipping Ministry

The passage grounds all ministry in the ascension of Christ — a movement of Pauline theology that is often underemphasised. It is the ascended Christ who gives gifts to his church. The one who has “ascended far above all the heavens” (v.10) is also the one who “fills all things” — present everywhere, sovereign over all, distributing gifts according to his wisdom and his grace. Ministry is not primarily a human enterprise; it is a dimension of the ongoing, active reign of the risen and ascended King.

The list of gifted persons — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers — has generated significant debate about which offices are permanent and which ceased with the apostolic age. The Reformed tradition has consistently held that the foundational offices (apostles and prophets, Ephesians 2:20) were unique to the founding of the church, while the equipping offices (evangelists, pastor-teachers) continue throughout the church's history. What remains constant in every age is the purpose: equipping the saints for ministry until the whole body reaches the fullness of Christ.

The metaphor of the body in vv.15–16 is Paul's most developed statement of mutual ministry. The body grows “when each part is working properly” — not when a few parts are exceptionally active while the rest remain passive, but when every member is fulfilling their function. This is the vision of a church in which every person is a minister — not because every person preaches, but because every person contributes the grace-gift they have received to the building up of the whole. The body that achieves this grows toward Christ in every way. The body that fails at this — where a few do everything and the many receive — stunts its own growth.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church had known extraordinary leadership — Paul himself had spent three years there, and the elders he had appointed knew the weight of shepherding a flock in a hostile city (Acts 20:28–31). Now Paul is gone, and his letter is itself an act of equipping: preparing the church to continue faithfully without his physical presence. The gifted leaders he describes in vv.11–12 are, in the first instance, the elders and teachers of the Ephesian church — men charged with the immense responsibility of preparing every member for a ministry that would build the body in Paul's absence. This was not a programme; it was a pastoral theology applied to a real community facing real challenges.

Now: The consumer church — where the congregation pays for spiritual services delivered by professional clergy — is the precise opposite of Paul's vision. It produces spiritual infants who cannot feed themselves, who are vulnerable to every wind of doctrine, who have no sense of their own giftedness or their own call to ministry. The equipping church — where gifted leaders deliberately, systematically invest in the ministry capacity of every member — produces a body that is robust, maturing, and growing in love. The question for every church leader is not “How well am I performing?” but “How well am I equipping?” And the question for every member is not “Am I being fed?” but “Am I contributing?”

verseByVerse.quote: But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Within the one body, every believer has been given grace for service: “grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.” No member is without a gift, and Christ decides the measure.

This is not saving grace (chapters 1–2) but grace for service: the same word, a different work. God’s grace does not stop at the door of salvation; it fills every room of the Christian life, including service. And it is Trinitarian: here Christ gives the gifts (vv. 7, 11), while 1 Corinthians 12 says the Spirit distributes them and the Father empowers them (vv. 4–6, 11).

“What is my gift?” Many believers do not feel gifted, and the right question is not “do I have a gift?” but “am I using what Christ has given me?” But that needs an answer, because many people accept it in principle and still have no idea what theirs is. The New Testament never suggests identifying your gift first and serving afterwards; it works the other way round, which is a relief, since the modern instinct is to take an inventory and wait for clarity. Begin with what is in front of you. What needs doing in your church that nobody is doing? What need are you uncomfortable walking past? What do people keep thanking you for, especially when you thought you had done nothing much? What do others keep asking you to do? Those four questions, answered honestly over a year of ordinary service, will tell you more than any questionnaire. Gifts are discovered in use, the way you discover a muscle by lifting something.

“The measure.” Christ apportions, the measures genuinely differ, and both usual reactions are ruled out. If your measure is smaller than someone else’s, you have not been short-changed; it was measured by the one who knows what he intends to do with you, and envy is finally a complaint about his arithmetic. If yours is larger, there is nothing to be proud of: a bigger delivery of something you did not earn is not an achievement. So ask yourself: whose gift in your church do you quietly envy, and whose do you quietly think does not matter much? Both answers show the same misunderstanding — treating gifts as possessions to rank rather than assignments to use. No one in a body admires the hand and dismisses the liver.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore it says, 'When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul quotes Psalm 68:18 — “When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men” — and applies it to Christ’s ascension. The cross was the decisive battle, the ascension the victory procession, and the gifts to the church are the spoils of that victory.

The picture. Every subject of Rome knew what a triumph looked like: the victorious general in a chariot with laurel on his head, the army behind him, the treasure of the defeated carried through the streets — and, walking in chains in full view, the conquered kings. At the end, the spoil was handed out. So here: Christ ascending, the powers in chains, the plunder distributed.

The captives are the powers that once enslaved us. Sin, whose penalty he bore (Romans 8:1–3). Death, which he walked into and out of — not yet abolished, but stripped of its sting (1 Corinthians 15:54–57). The devil and his powers, whom “he disarmed… and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them” (Colossians 2:15). And the law’s power to condemn, which he bore in our place (Galatians 3:13). Christ is not a victim who survived; he is the conquering general.

“Gave” or “received”? The Hebrew of Psalm 68 says the victor “received gifts among men”, but Paul writes “gave gifts to men”. This is not carelessness. In an ancient triumph, receiving tribute and handing it out to the soldiers were two stages of one event, and Paul stresses the giving because that is his point. (An ancient Jewish Aramaic paraphrase of the psalm also reads “gave”.) The Son ascended, received all authority, and poured out gifts, the Spirit above all (Acts 2:33).

Where you were in the parade. By chapter 2 you were on the losing side: dead in trespasses, following “the prince of the power of the air”. You were not a spectator who backed the winning general; you were in the camp that lost, and the campaign was fought for you, not by you. That is why no one in the New Testament boasts about a spiritual gift. Loot is not an achievement. A soldier carried off the field during the battle does not, on receiving his share, give a speech about his contribution. Everything in your church that actually works — the teaching, the hospitality, the administration nobody notices, the person unaccountably good with the dying — is plunder from a battle in which we were the ones rescued. So take the gift seriously and yourself lightly.
verseByVerse.note: The psalm pictures God ascending Mount Zion in victory, receiving tribute; Paul applies it to Christ, who in triumph gives gifts. A Jewish Aramaic paraphrase of the psalm also reads “gave gifts.”

parallels.desc: you ascended on high, leading a host of captives

verseByVerse.quote: (In saying, 'He ascended,' what does it mean but that he had also descended into the lower regions, the earth? He who descended is the one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul draws out the logic of “he ascended”: whoever went up must first have come down. The one who rose “far above all the heavens” is the one who first “descended into the lower regions, the earth” — and he did it “that he might fill all things.”

Does this teach a descent into hell? Many readers connect it with the Apostles’ Creed — “he descended into hell” — and with the idea of Christ visiting the underworld between his death and resurrection. That idea does not rest on this text. Paul’s “lower regions, the earth” most likely means the earth itself, so the descent is the incarnation; or, if it reaches to death, the grave — not a tour of the underworld. The “harrowing of hell” picture leans chiefly on one much-debated verse, “he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison” (1 Peter 3:19), over which careful Christians have long disagreed; it is not settled enough to build a doctrine on. And the creed’s line need not mean a mission through hell: Calvin and much of the Reformed tradition took it to mean the depth of Christ’s suffering — that on the cross he bore the anguish and God-forsakenness of hell in our place. You can say the words with full meaning and import no legend.

How far down. Count the descent rather than summarising it. From the throne to a womb. To a manger (Luke 2:7). To a village with a poor reputation (John 1:46) and years as a carpenter (Mark 6:3). To a homeless itinerant life (Luke 9:58). To his own family thinking him out of his mind (Mark 3:21). To a friend’s kiss in a garden at night and the rest running away (Mark 14:45, 50). To the friend who swore he would die with him denying he knew him (Mark 14:66–72). To a rigged trial, a flogging, a crown of thorns as a joke (Mark 15:15–17). To an execution reserved for slaves and rebels, between two criminals. To a cry of forsakenness (Mark 15:34). To a corpse, and a grave with a stone across it. Every step goes down.

Set your own depths beside that. Misunderstood by the people who should know you best; let down by friends at the moment it mattered; praying in anguish and hearing silence; shamed publicly and unjustly; physically broken; dying — he has stood in every one of those places, not as an observer.

“That he might fill all things.” Filling is a thread through this letter: the church is his fullness (1:23), believers are to be filled with God’s fullness (3:19) and with the Spirit (5:18). The ascended Christ fills the universe as Lord, the church as head, each believer by his Spirit. And he earned the right to fill all things by going underneath all things first. Name the one place you suspect he cannot reach — the part of your situation that feels beyond anyone’s sympathy, his included — and hold it against that list. There is no cellar in your life with a floor lower than the one he has already stood on.
verseByVerse.note: “The lower regions, the earth” may mean his coming down to earth in the incarnation.

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ascended Christ gives his church not just abilities but people: “the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers.”

Apostles and prophets come first because they are the foundation (2:20). The apostles were personally commissioned by the risen Christ, witnesses of his resurrection, with authority to speak and write his word (Paul among them, 1 Corinthians 15:8). The prophets here are New Testament prophets who received revelation before the New Testament was complete. A foundation is laid once. Continuationists, including those who speak of a “fivefold ministry” today, argue that all five gifts must continue “until we all attain to the unity of the faith” (v. 13), and that Paul’s instructions about prophecy (1 Corinthians 14:29) assume it would go on. But Paul has already called apostles and prophets the foundation, and a foundation is not relaid in every generation. What continues is their word, preserved in Scripture.

Evangelists and pastor-teachers continue. Evangelists carry the gospel where it has not been heard, like Philip (Acts 21:8) and Timothy (2 Timothy 4:5). “Shepherds and teachers” are almost certainly one office (the Greek groups them): the pastor who cares for the flock by feeding it the word (John 10:11–14; 1 Peter 5:1–4). Every faithful pastor and every gospel-carrying missionary is a gift from the ascended Christ.

He gave people. Not programmes, structures or a curriculum — people, with a name, a family, a limited temperament and a telephone that rings at inconvenient hours. That cuts both ways. The gift is better than any resource: a book cannot sit with you in a hospital corridor at two in the morning or notice that you have stopped coming. And the gift will disappoint you as a resource never would. Your pastor has a temperament, some of which will grate, and blind spots you will find, and he will preach a thin sermon in the very month you needed a good one. Congregations often conclude that the wrong man was given, when what has happened is that a man was given — which was the arrangement from the beginning.

So when did you last pray for your pastor by name, about the specific things you know he carries? And when did you last tell him something particular that helped? Most ministers live on general encouragement and precise criticism: the criticism comes with details, dates and examples; the encouragement comes as “nice sermon” at the door. Reverse those two for a year and you would hardly recognise the man at the end of it.
verseByVerse.note: “Shepherds” is the word often translated “pastors.”

verseByVerse.quote: to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ gives leaders “to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ.” The leaders equip; the members do the ministry.

Equip (katartizō) is the word for mending nets and setting broken bones — making something fit for its proper use. The result Paul pictures is a congregation of ministers, not a minister with a congregation. And the ministry (diakonia, service) is broad: caring for the sick, the widow and the stranger (James 1:27); encouragement that strengthens faith (Hebrews 3:13); teaching and discipling, older and younger, one to one (2 Timothy 2:2; Titus 2:3–5); witness to neighbours (1 Peter 3:15); prayer (6:18); generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:6–8). The woman who visits the lonely widow, the man who opens his home, the teenager who shares the gospel with a classmate — all are doing the work of ministry. The goal is “building up the body”: growth in numbers as people are converted (Acts 2:47), in maturity toward the fullness of Christ (v. 13), and in unity (v. 16).

The comma. A reader with an older Bible will notice that everything here turns on punctuation. The King James has three parallel tasks for the leaders: “for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ.” Read that way, the ministry is what the leaders do. Modern versions drop the second comma: leaders equip the saints for the work of ministry. That comma has been called the most consequential in church history, and a great deal about clergy and congregation follows from it. The modern reading has the better case: Paul changes his preposition. The first phrase uses one word (pros, “toward”), the next two another (eis, “resulting in”). Three parallel items would naturally take the same preposition; the change marks a sequence instead. Leaders equip the saints, which results in the work of ministry, which results in the body being built up.

That gives an uncomfortable measure of a church. We usually judge a congregation by its minister: was the sermon good, does he lead well, does he visit enough? This verse asks whether the members are functioning. If your pastor were removed for six months, how much of your church’s actual ministry would simply stop? If the answer is nearly all of it, that is no compliment to the pastor; it is exactly the condition this verse was written to prevent.

verseByVerse.quote: until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by human cunning, by craftiness in deceitful schemes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The goal of all this ministry is maturity: that the whole church reaches “the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” — so that we are no longer like children tossed about by every new teaching.

Four pictures of the goal. The unity of the faith: not the unity of tolerance that smooths over truth, but deep agreement in the apostolic gospel held together (Jude 3). The knowledge of the Son of God: epignōsis, full, personal knowing of Christ. We are never so advanced that we do not need to know him better, and the aim of ministry is not a better-informed congregation but one more captivated by Jesus. Mature manhood: the whole church together reaching adulthood — stability, a faith not easily capsized. The fullness of Christ: the standard is not the finest elder in your church but Christ himself. It will not be fully reached until the last day, but it is the real goal.

The alternative. Paul’s picture is a small boat with nothing to steady it: tossed by the waves (the swell of feeling and circumstance from underneath) and carried by every wind (whatever is blowing from outside this season) — no keel, no anchor, going wherever the water and air decided last. You can recognise it: the Christian whose convictions can be dated by whatever he last read or listened to; the one enthusiastic about a new teacher every eighteen months, each time the one who finally makes sense of everything; the one persuaded by whoever spoke most confidently in the room. None of this needs bad motives. “Children” is not an insult but a stage; the tragedy is only in staying there.

How error arrives. The word for “cunning” is the one Paul uses of the serpent deceiving Eve (2 Corinthians 11:3), and the serpent began not with a denial but with a question (Genesis 3:1). Error arrives warmly, from likeable and sincere people, wrapped in a great deal of truth. If it announced itself as error, no one would take it. What makes it dangerous is that nine-tenths of it is right, and the remaining tenth is load-bearing.

So ask honestly: over the last five years, has your view of something significant shifted more than once, and when you trace why, was it a passage of Scripture you finally understood, or a person you found compelling? Both can move you; only one anchors you. And the remedy is not to become suspicious of everything, which produces a hard and frightened Christian rather than a mature one. It is to know the Son of God so well that counterfeits show themselves by contrast — the way someone who handles real banknotes all day needs no course in forgery.

verseByVerse.quote: Rather, speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and held together by every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead of being blown about, the church grows up into Christ by “speaking the truth in love”, and the whole body, every part doing its work, “builds itself up in love.”

Truth in love. The Greek is literally “truthing in love”: not only speaking truth but living it, in love. Truth without love is cold; love without truth is hollow. The truth is the gospel truth of verses 13–14, and it must be spoken — in preaching, in correction, in daily life (Colossians 3:16). “In love” means more than a pleasant tone; it means love with a goal, the good of the other person. Love is what separates the surgeon’s scalpel from the bully’s fist: both may hurt, but only one aims at healing. “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Proverbs 27:6).

Two abuses. This may be the most quoted and most abused phrase in the chapter, used both to license what it forbids and to excuse saying nothing at all. The first failure: a man decides something must be said, says it plainly, and feels the satisfaction of having been faithful — and everyone who heard it knows the satisfaction was the point. The sentence was composed in advance and delivered with relish; it cost him nothing and left the other person no way forward. That is candour with a Bible verse pinned to it. The second failure is more respectable and does more damage: someone is drifting, a marriage is quietly failing, a man’s temper is frightening his children — and no one says a word. We call the silence love. It is almost never love; it is avoiding an unpleasant conversation. If you have belonged to a church for years and never once said a hard thing to anyone in it, that needs a better explanation than gentleness. Three questions tell you which you are doing: Have you prayed for this person more than you have rehearsed the sentence? Will it cost you something, or only them? Would you want someone to do this for you next month, about your own blind spot?

Growing into Christ. “In every way” allows no partial growth: not knowledge while love withers, or zeal while wisdom lags. And verse 16 is a picture of church growth from the head: the body “joined and held together by every joint… when each part is working properly” grows and “builds itself up in love”. It grows deeper (toward Christ’s fullness), warmer (maturity without growing love is only sophistication), and wider (such love is itself a witness: “By this all people will know that you are my disciples,” John 13:35). And it happens not through the heroics of a few but through the ordinary contribution of every part: the encourager who seeks out the one who is struggling, the small group that prays and holds people up, the older woman discipling a younger (Titus 2:3–5), the deacon who visits the sick, the intercessor who rises early. A ligament is never seen and a joint never applauded, but remove them and the body collapses.

Notice that learning to tell one another the truth in a way that heals is the first thing Paul names about growing up. A church that can do that will mature. A church that cannot will remain a nursery, however good the preaching.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Put Off the Old, Put On the New
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul turns from theology to the street. “No longer walk as the Gentiles walk.” Not a gentle suggestion — an apostolic command, issued in the Lord’s name. And the reason it must be commanded is itself the warning: becoming a Christian does not automatically remake your habits. The old gravity is still there. You must walk differently, deliberately, because the new life does not run on autopilot.

The diagnosis is sober: a mind cut loose from God loses its anchor. Not its intelligence — its direction. It thinks hard but goes nowhere. The understanding darkens. The heart hardens — not in a single dramatic moment but through the quiet accumulation of small refusals, each making the next a little easier, until the conscience is worn smooth and the soul no longer notices what it has lost. Sensuality, insatiable craving, the futile pursuit of things that cannot satisfy — this is where the road ends. Paul is not describing monsters. He is describing the trajectory of every unrenewed human heart, including the one that used to belong to these Ephesians.

But they have learned Christ — heard him, and been taught in him, for the truth is in Jesus (v. 21). Not truth posted to them from a distance, but truth with a face, lodged in a Person; and it stands directly against the deceitful desires that are rotting the old self in the very next verse. The contest is truth against a lie about where happiness is kept. And that changes everything. The old self — the whole person oriented away from God, rotting through deceitful desires — is to be stripped off like a stinking garment. The mind is to be renewed, daily and continuously, by the Spirit working at the deepest level. The new self — a new creation, bearing the restored image of God in genuine righteousness and holiness — is to be put on. This is not self-improvement. It is resurrection applied to daily life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Renewal of the Mind and the New Humanity

The “old self” and “new self” of this passage are not psychological categories — they are eschatological ones. The old self is the Adamic humanity: the self that has inherited Adam's corruption, lives under the dominion of sin, and is “corrupt through deceitful desires” (v.22). The new self is the new humanity created in Christ — what Paul elsewhere calls “the last Adam” (1 Corinthians 15:45). To be “in Christ” is to have been transferred from the old humanity to the new, from the domain of the first Adam to the domain of the Second.

The renewing of the mind (v.23) is the cognitive dimension of this transfer. Romans 12:2 makes the same point: “be transformed by the renewal of your mind.” The mind that has been shaped by the world — its values, its assumptions, its desires — must be reshaped by the word and Spirit of God. This is not achieved in a moment; it is the work of a lifetime. Every act of sustained Bible meditation, every time truth displaces a lie, every time a Spirit-given desire overcomes a flesh-driven one, the mind is being renewed. This is the slow and glorious work of sanctification.

The goal of the renewal is “the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness” (v.24). This is the restoration of the image of God that was defaced at the fall. God made humanity in his image; sin corrupted that image; Christ has come to restore it. The new self is not merely morally better than the old — it is ontologically different, created anew after the very likeness of God. This is why the Christian life is not ultimately about rule-keeping but about becoming who you already are in Christ: the image-bearer of God, restored and renewed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus was a city of extraordinary sensual abundance. The temple complex of Artemis, the bath-houses, the theatre, the commercial district — pleasure was available in every form and at every price. To be a Christian in Ephesus was to swim against a powerful and relentless current. Paul does not tell the Ephesian Christians to try harder or to exercise greater willpower. He gives them something more powerful: a new identity. You are not the old self anymore. The garment of the old life is to be put off — not held on to, not worn occasionally for old time's sake, but removed and discarded. And in its place: the new self, created after God's own likeness.

Now: The pornified, entertainment-saturated, hyper-stimulated culture of the 21st century is Ephesus with better technology. The mechanisms of desire-manipulation are more sophisticated; the availability of darkness is more immediate; the cultural current against a holy life runs faster. Paul's answer is unchanged and still the most powerful available: not more discipline applied to the old self, but the daily renewal of the mind in the truth of the gospel — who you are in Christ, what you have been given, who you are becoming. The Christian who meditates daily on Scripture, who submits their thinking to the word of God, who asks the Spirit to renew their mind — this person is not swimming against the current on their own. They are being transformed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this I say and testify in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul solemnly charges believers to live differently: “you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds.” “Testify” (martyromai, from the root that gives “martyr”) is a solemn, almost legal word: he is not giving friendly advice but staking his witness on it. That he must say it at all shows that conversion does not automatically end the old patterns. The new life has to be deliberately walked.

Futility. Mataiotēs means emptiness — the word the Greek Old Testament uses for idols, “worthlessness” (Jeremiah 2:5); and “mind” (nous) is the faculty by which a person weighs what is real and decides how to live. So the diagnosis is exact: a mind whose every judgment is bent because what sits at its centre is empty. Ephesus was built around the temple of Artemis: a life of praying to stone, buying charms, consulting magicians (Acts 19:19) — busy and even religious, but aimed at gods who were not there. A person can pour out his whole life on what is in truth nothing.

Underneath is a hunger. God made the heart for himself; as Augustine prayed, “our heart is restless until it rests in you.” We try to fill the ache with good things — family, work, a well-earned holiday — gifts of God, every one, but not built to carry that weight. That is the whole burden of Ecclesiastes: the Preacher tried pleasure, work, wealth and wisdom and called it all “vanity” — a vapour you cannot hold — and when the book was translated into Greek, that refrain was rendered with this very word. Only the idols have changed clothes: the bigger house, the endless scroll, the next achievement that was finally going to satisfy.

How to fight it. You are redeemed and still catch yourself reaching for the old empty wells. Not mainly by gritting your teeth to want less — a hungry heart is not talked out of eating. Thomas Chalmers named the real cure: “the expulsive power of a new affection.” A lesser love is driven out not by willpower but by a greater one. So when the itch comes — “if I just had that, I would be content” — name it: that is the hunger again, and that thing cannot fill it. Preach the truth back to yourself (“be transformed by the renewal of your mind,” Romans 12:2 — the same word, nous: what is empty here is what grace makes new). Feed the real hunger at its source: the word, prayer, the Lord’s table, God’s people. And receive the good gifts — your spouse, your work, your Saturday rest — not as gods that must satisfy, but as gifts from a Father who already has.

So do not hear “you must no longer walk” as nothing but duty. God is not calling you out of a good life into a grey one. He is calling you out of the empty life into the full one. The old way looked like freedom and proved a cage; this way looks like surrender and proves to be the open field.

verseByVerse.quote: They are darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart. They have become callous and have given themselves up to sensuality, greedy to practice every kind of impurity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul traces how a life away from God works, from the surface down to the root: a darkened understanding, cut off from God’s life, because of a willed ignorance, caused by a hardened heart — ending in a conscience that no longer feels and an appetite that cannot be satisfied. The heart hardens first, and everything else follows.

“Darkened in their understanding.” The verb is passive: they have been darkened. This is not stupidity — such people may be brilliant. It is the faculty by which a person decides what is worth living for, still pointing confidently, but the wrong way. Then it looked respectable: a man pouring his years into status and the favour of Artemis while his neighbours nodded. It looks just as respectable now: a decent, hard-working man pouring his one life into the career, the retirement fund, the renovated house, the evenings given to a screen — nothing scandalous, all reasonable, aimed at a horizon that ends at the grave, while Christ quietly seems optional. Paul has already prayed the cure: “having the eyes of your hearts enlightened” (1:18). The god of this age blinds (2 Corinthians 4:4); the God who said “Let light shine out of darkness” shines in the heart (2 Corinthians 4:6).
