Do not draw the wrong conclusion. Paul is not saying work and family are “worldly” and only church activity counts. God gave work before sin entered (Genesis 2:15) and called marriage good. The road was not the problem; the compass was. Take the same Monday and change the aim: work “as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23), love your family as a trust rather than a monument to yourself, and do it all “to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). To the neighbour nothing looks different; underneath, everything is.

“Alienated from the life of God.” There are two kinds of life: breath and heartbeat, which everyone has, and God’s own life flowing into a soul. Without the second, a person can be up and about, laughing and working, while cut off from the root. Christ came to reverse exactly this: “I came that they may have life and have it abundantly” (John 10:10).

Hardness of heart. Beneath that lies willed ignorance — not lack of information but a man shutting his eyes against the sun and complaining that it is night (Romans 1:21). And at the root, hardness: pōrōsis, a medical word for tissue calcifying where it should be supple. It is not one dramatic rebellion but an accumulation of small refusals, each making the next easier. Pharaoh is the case study: again and again he hardened his own heart, and again and again the LORD hardened it (Exodus 8:15; 9:12) — the man hardened himself until God confirmed him in the hardness he chose. That is the most frightening sentence a soul can receive: not lightning, but God ceasing to interrupt. Hence the plea: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:7–8).

The end of the road is a conscience worn smooth — “callous” — giving itself to “sensuality”, appetite with the brakes removed, and “greedy” for more. Indulgence does not satisfy; it inflames. And that insatiability shows what the soul was made for: a thirst this deep was meant for the One who said, “whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again” (John 4:14).

The reversal. A heart can harden itself, but it cannot soften itself. So God promises to do what the sinner cannot: “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). Because the hard heart drove the whole descent, when grace changes the root everything above it changes too. For the Christian this passage is a warning, read with recognition, not superiority. None of it begins with a dramatic fall; it begins quietly — a little hardness, a little less sensitivity, a little more drift. This was the road we were on. Grace interrupted it. Do not drift back.

verseByVerse.quote: But that is not the way you learned Christ!
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But that is not the way you learned Christ!” After the bleak picture of verses 18–19, Paul turns sharply: that is not what you were taught. And notice what he says: not that you learned about Christ or learned his teaching, but that you learned Christ — a Person, not a curriculum.

In the ancient world you learned a philosopher’s ideas; the philosopher was only the delivery mechanism. Paul says the content of Christian learning is Christ himself. Jesus framed discipleship the same way: “learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29) — not learn my system, but learn me. A disciple (mathētēs, a learner) did not master a syllabus but apprenticed himself to a Person until his life was reshaped. Its far end is Paul’s: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). This is the sharpest contrast with the drifting, futile mind of verse 17. The Christian mind has a fixed point: a Person who does not change and who makes himself known.

How do you learn a person? Not by reading a summary of him. It takes time, attention, presence, and watching him under pressure. So use the ordinary means that way. Read the Gospels not mainly for information but to watch him: how he handles interruptions, what makes him angry, whom he stops for, how he speaks to people who have failed badly. Pray as conversation rather than recitation. And obey — the part we usually leave out. Jesus said, “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me… and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21). Obedience is not the fee for knowing him; it is one of the ways the knowing happens, because you discover what a person is like chiefly by doing things alongside him.

A quick, revealing test: try to say in one sentence what Jesus is like — not what he did, taught or accomplished on the cross, but what he is like to deal with. Most of us can say a great deal under the first three headings and find the fourth unexpectedly hard. That gap is the difference between learning about him and learning him. And it matters, because a man handed a rulebook keeps the rules badly and resents them by Thursday, while a man who has come to love a Person finds his behaviour changed from somewhere deeper than his will. Paul is about to spend two chapters on how to live; he lays this down first, because nothing that follows would be possible on any other footing.

verseByVerse.quote: assuming that you have heard about him and were taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were “taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus.” Paul is not doubting their conversion (“assuming that you have heard”), but reminding them what they received.

Notice “taught in him”, not merely “by” him. It is the “in Christ” language of the whole letter: the teaching did not arrive as a parcel of facts handed over at arm’s length, but within their union with Christ. That is why the futile mind of verses 17–19 could never get here, and why what follows is not a rulebook posted from a distance but instruction from inside a relationship, able to produce a new self (v. 24).

“As the truth is in Jesus.” Paul uses the human name — not the title “Christ” but “Jesus”, the man who walked in Galilee, touched lepers, was crucified under Pilate, and rose. Truth is not an abstract system; it has a face, in a particular human life. And this sets the axis of the passage: truth is in Jesus (v. 21); the old self is corrupted “through deceitful desires” (v. 22). Truth against deceit — that is the real contest. The old life is not merely naughty; it is a lie told to a person about where his happiness lies.

So when you want to know what truth looks like in flesh and blood — how to forgive, how to suffer — you do not consult a definition; you look at Jesus. You could give someone the dictionary meaning of courage, accurate and bloodless, or point to the soldier who threw himself on a grenade for his friends. A piano teacher can explain the theory of a sonata, or sit down and play it: “There — that is how it should sound.” In Jesus the truth about God and about what a human life was made to be became a life you can watch. The world says truth is whatever feels right to you. Paul says it is not ours to shape, because it is found in a Person who cannot be revised: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Hebrews 13:8).

verseByVerse.quote: to put off your old self, which belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers were taught “to put off your old self”: to strip off the whole person they were before Christ, along with the way of life that belongs to it, because it is rotting “through deceitful desires”.

The old self. Literally the old man (as in Romans 6:6; Colossians 3:9): not the body or the personality but the whole self as it was in Adam, turned away from God. It “belongs to your former manner of life”, and the two come as a package: you cannot keep the old self and expect new behaviour. It is “corrupt” — not dishonest but rotting, decaying, something actively dying. You do not renovate what is rotting; you take it off.

How? Not by willpower wrestling a living master to the ground, but by faith counting on a death already died: “We know that our old self was crucified with him” (Romans 6:6). To “put off” is not to kill something thriving but to stop dressing a dead man every morning. And you were also raised with Christ (Colossians 3:1–3), which is why the next word is not another command to grit your teeth but a promise: be renewed (v. 23). “Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (Galatians 5:24).

Deceitful desires. They are called deceitful because they make promises they cannot keep, and it is worth writing their words down, because they are few and they hardly vary. Just this once. You have earned this — look at the week you have had. Nobody will ever know. You will feel better afterwards. You can stop whenever you like. Everyone does this; you are being ridiculous. That is nearly the whole script. It needs no sophistication, because it is delivered at the moment you are least inclined to examine it. Then notice what is actually delivered: ten minutes later, no real satisfaction, a slight flatness, the beginning of the wish that it had not happened. The thing that was going to make you feel better has made you feel worse, and left you a little further in. That is what Paul means by corrupting. The trouble with the desire is not that it is naughty but that it lies, and the lie costs you something every time you believe it.

So bring to mind the thing that most reliably pulls at you — you will not have to search — and ask not whether it was pleasant, but what its record is. Has it ever once, in all the years you have listened to it, delivered what it actually promised: the satisfaction, the relief, the sense that things would now be all right? The answer will be no, every time, because the promise is the deceit and the pleasure is only the bait. A voice with a hundred-per-cent record of lying to you has no claim on your trust. You are not being asked to give up something that works.
verseByVerse.note: The “old self” (literally “old man”) is the person we were in Adam, before union with Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Between putting off (v. 22) and putting on (v. 24) stands the hinge: “be renewed in the spirit of your minds.” It is ongoing, not a one-off experience; it is done to you (“be renewed”, not “renew yourself”), which rules out both passivity and mere willpower (Philippians 2:12–13); and it happens at the mind’s governing centre, which is why behaviour cannot simply be commanded from outside (“be transformed by the renewal of your mind,” Romans 12:2).

You cannot manufacture this renewal, but you can use the means through which God gives it: Scripture that retrains the mind, prayer, honest fellowship, regularly hearing the preached word. Neglecting these is not neutral; it starves the very faculty God is renewing.

A mind whose reflexes change. A renewed mind is not chiefly a mind with more information in it, but one whose reflexes have changed. Notice where your mind goes on its own. Someone criticises you in front of others: what happens in the first half-second, before you arrange your face? A colleague you think less able than you is promoted over you: what is the first movement of the heart, before the congratulations? Money is tight and you are awake at two in the morning: what does the mind reach for? You are alone with a phone and twenty empty minutes. In every case there is a default, installed long before you were converted. So do not measure renewal by your convictions; assent to doctrine is cheap. Measure it by the unguarded reaction — the thought you think before you have time to compose a better one. That shows what your mind actually assumes about God, yourself, and what you cannot do without.

Then be encouraged rather than crushed, because this is exactly the faculty God has promised to renew, slowly and from underneath. The first sign is rarely that the wrong reflex has gone; it is that you notice it. A year ago the resentment simply was the truth about the situation; now it arrives, and something in you recognises it as an intruder and refuses to agree with it. That is the renewal showing its first light. Think of John Newton, once the hard-hearted captain of a slave ship, renewed degree by degree over a lifetime until that same mind gave the church “Amazing Grace”. Near the end, his memory almost gone, he is reported to have said: “I remember two things: that I am a great sinner, and that Christ is a great Saviour.” “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6). Do not measure the work by a single day.

verseByVerse.quote: and to put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers are to “put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness.” Clothing is deliberate — no one gets dressed by accident — and Paul uses the same image elsewhere: “put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 13:14).

The new self is “created after the likeness of God” — an echo of Genesis 1:26. This is what humanity was made for: to reflect God’s character. The fall defaced that image; in Christ it is being restored, not as an improved old self but as a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). And it is more than Eden restored. Adam was innocent but not secure; he could fall. The pattern of the new self is the last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45): Christ, tested in every way, obedient to death, risen beyond all falling. The destination is a likeness to Christ that can never be lost (Romans 8:29). It shows in “true righteousness” (what we owe our neighbour: honesty, justice, love) and “holiness” (toward God: reverence, devotion) — “true”, the real thing, not a mask.

How do you do it? Paul’s silence is a clue: it is not complicated. Putting on the new self is simply acting from who you now are in Christ, not who you used to be. Picture a child taken off the street and adopted into a noble house. His birth has not changed, but his belonging has. The old instincts linger — he hoards food, flinches at kindness, waits to be thrown out — and learning to put on his new self is simply learning to live as what he now is: a son at his father’s table. He does not earn the sonship by behaving like a son; he behaves like a son because he is one (1:5). So in any moment — a conversation, a temptation — ask what the person you are in Christ would do, and do it by faith before the feeling follows. Paul gives the concrete shape in the next verses. And measure by direction, not perfection: the adopted son still flinches, and is a son all the same. The question is which way you are facing, and whether, having fallen, you get up and walk on in the clothes your Father gave you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Now Paul lands the rubber on the road. Theology becomes Tuesday morning. Five commands, each grounded in the gospel, each aimed at the one thing that makes the body of Christ function or fail: the daily choices of ordinary people in ordinary relationships.

Tell the truth — because we are members of one another and a body cannot survive on false signals. Deal with anger before the sun goes down — because unresolved grievance is a beachhead the devil will occupy and you will not evict him easily once he is inside. Work and give — because the hands that once took are now instruments of grace. Speak only what builds — because your words can carry grace or corruption to the soul of the person who hears them.

Forgive — as God in Christ forgave you. That last phrase is everything. The standard is not proportional. It is not “forgive reasonably.” It is: forgive the way the cross forgave you — absorbing the cost, releasing the debt, not because the other person has earned it but because you have been forgiven the unearnable.

Behind it all stands the Holy Spirit (v. 30) — not an impersonal force but a Person who can be grieved. He grieves at falsehood because he is the Spirit of truth. He grieves at unresolved bitterness because he is the Spirit whose unity the bond of peace keeps. He grieves at corrupting words because he is building a holy body.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Grieving of the Spirit and the Ethics of Grace

Verse 30 — “do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” — is one of the most searching statements in the New Testament about the nature of the Spirit. He can be grieved. The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal force that responds mechanically to human sin; he is a Person with genuine emotional sensibility who is affected by the moral life of the community he inhabits. The sins Paul has listed — falsehood, uncontrolled anger, stealing, corrupting speech, bitterness, wrath, malice — do not merely harm the community; they wound the indwelling Guest.

The phrase “by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” provides the context for the warning. The Spirit who can be grieved is the same Spirit who has sealed us for the final day — who is our guarantee of the inheritance (1:14), the deposit of our future glory. To grieve him is therefore not a trivial matter; it is to harm the very relationship that is the ground of our assurance and the means of our transformation. This is not a threat to the believer's salvation; Paul does not say “by whom you were sealed unless you grieve him.” The sealing is certain. But the quality of the Spirit's presence and work in the community is affected by how the community lives.

The climactic command — “forgive one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (v.32) — sets the standard for Christian forgiveness at the level of the cross: freely given, fully extended, without conditions. The Reformers consistently emphasised that forgiveness is not a feeling but a decision — the decision to release the debt, to no longer hold the offence against the offender, to treat them as God treats us in Christ: with kindness and grace. This is impossible from human resources. It is possible only for those who have received it from God and draw on the same source to extend it to others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church was extraordinarily diverse. With diversity comes friction. The command against falsehood (v.25) — “speak truth with your neighbour, for we are members of one another” — addresses the social lubricant of deception that holds many human communities together. In the body of Christ, truth-telling is not optional; it is structurally necessary. A body in which the members lie to one another cannot function. The command against corrupting speech (v.29) — only what builds up — addresses the tongue that tears down, the word that diminishes, the comment that cuts. In a diverse community under pressure, these are the sins most likely to do lasting damage.

Now: “Do not let the sun go down on your anger” is one of the most practically demanding commands in Scripture, and one of the most consistently violated in married life, family life, and church life. We carry grievances. We nurse wounds. We let distance harden into walls. The apostle's word cuts through all of it: move toward resolution before night falls.

This does not mean every conflict is resolved in an evening — some wounds take weeks of patient, humble work to heal. But the direction must always be toward each other, not away. The community that actually practices this — that refuses to let resentment calcify, that keeps short accounts, that forgives as God in Christ forgave — will be noticed. It will be extraordinary. It will be a sign of the Kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first piece of the new clothing is truthfulness: “having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbor, for we are members one of another.” Falsehood was put away in principle when you put off the old self; now your speech must match it.

What falsehood includes. More than outright lies: half-truths designed to mislead, flattery that says what people want to hear, silence when something honest needs saying, and careful management of how others see you. Falsehood is any communication meant to create a false impression. Paul is quoting Zechariah 8:16, so “neighbour” reaches to anyone you deal with, but his reason narrows the focus: “we are members one of another.” Lying to a fellow member is like one part of a body sending false signals to another.

A body that cannot feel. That picture describes a real disease. In leprosy, the damage that destroys hands and feet is done not directly by the illness but because the nerves stop reporting. The sufferer does not feel the stone in his shoe, so he walks on it all day; he does not feel the heat, so he leaves his hand where it is. Nothing hurts, and that is the catastrophe: an injury that cannot be felt cannot be treated. A congregation where people do not tell each other the truth is in exactly that condition. The quietly failing marriage, the man drifting toward a decision that will wreck him, the coldness between two families — each is a pain signal that never arrives, so nothing is done while it would still be simple. And the falsehood that does this is rarely a lie. It is one word, said thousands of times on a given Sunday: “Fine.” Not exactly untrue; just the careful management of an impression. So ask yourself: over the last month, did you tell anyone the truth about how you actually were? Is there one person in your church who knows the real state of things with you, rather than the summary? If not, you are a nerve that has stopped reporting.

Is it ever right to lie? Every thoughtful reader eventually asks: what about the woman with a Jewish family behind a false wall and soldiers at the door, or the man asked by an abusive husband where his wife has gone? Scripture itself puts the case. The Hebrew midwives disobeyed Pharaoh’s order to kill the boys and gave an evasive answer, and “God dealt well with the midwives… because the midwives feared God, he gave them families” (Exodus 1:20–21). Rahab hid the spies and sent the king’s men the wrong way, and is commended for her faith (Hebrews 11:31) and her works (James 2:25). The answer the Reformed tradition has generally given is that the commandment forbids false witness against your neighbour — speech that wrongs someone who has a right to what you know. A man bent on murder has forfeited that right; he is not a neighbour asking a question but an assailant demanding a weapon, and words are the weapon. In both biblical cases, too, the deception protected someone else’s life, not the speaker’s interests. Two guards. This is an extremely narrow door: it concerns an aggressor with no right to the answer and a life he intends to take. It does not stretch to the awkward conversation, the padded figure or the managed reputation; if you reach for Rahab to spare yourself embarrassment, you have left the category. And even here the honest position is not that lying became good, but that a fallen world sometimes leaves no innocent option, and the guilt lies with the man at the door. Some in the tradition say such a person does no wrong; others that she chooses the lesser evil under duress and needs grace like the rest of us. Both agree on what she should do.

And none of that touches Paul’s actual point. He is writing to a congregation about ordinary speech between members of one body, and there the standard is unqualified. Corrie ten Boom’s family, who sheltered Jews behind a false wall in Haarlem, disagreed among themselves about what could rightly be said at the door. None of them was in any doubt about what they owed each other inside the house.

parallels.desc: speak the truth to one another

verseByVerse.quote: Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger.” Paul, quoting Psalm 4:4, permits anger but limits it: anger itself is not sin; what you do with it can be.

Right anger. There are things you should be angry about. Jesus was angry at the money-changers in the temple (John 2:15–16) and at hearts that preferred a rule to a man’s healing (Mark 3:5). Anger at injustice and cruelty is right; never being angry at anything is not holiness but indifference. But say a colleague takes credit for your work. Your anger is legitimate. If you then tell the whole office, start quietly undermining him, or lie awake rehearsing and adding to it, the anger has crossed into sin. Hence the deadline: do not go to sleep still nursing it. Paul does not mean every conflict must be resolved by sunset — that is not always possible — but before the day ends, do something: go to the person if you can, or at least hand the anger to God in prayer rather than carrying it into tomorrow. Anger nursed through the night hardens: a legitimate grievance in the evening becomes resentment by morning and something darker by next week (Matthew 5:23–24).

Anger that goes underground. For many conscientious Christians the other danger needs naming. Some believers decide anger is unspiritual and permit themselves none. They never raise their voice, and ask them if they are angry and they sincerely say no. The anger has not gone; it has stopped announcing itself. It comes out as sarcasm that can always be defended as humour, a coolness that never quite becomes rudeness, sudden urgent work whenever a particular person needs something, an unreturned message, a decision taken without consulting someone — all deniable, none accidental. Buried anger is not put to death; it is put to work, and does more damage underground than it would in the open, because no one can address a grievance that has never been stated.

Telling them apart. Two questions do most of the sorting. First, what was injured? Righteous anger is stirred by harm to someone else or to God’s honour: the mistreated child, the twisted truth, the vulnerable person used. Sinful anger is almost always stirred by harm to me: my standing, my convenience, being overlooked, corrected or made to look foolish. A surprising amount of what feels like moral indignation turns out to be wounded pride in a better coat. Second, what does the anger want? Righteous anger wants the wrong put right and is satisfied when it is; it can even want the good of the offender. Sinful anger wants the person diminished, and repair does not satisfy it. You can detect it: when the offender apologises, you feel a faint disappointment, and the grievance is reluctant to be given up. Anger that does not want to be resolved has told you what it is.

parallels.desc: be angry, and do not sin

verseByVerse.quote: and give no opportunity to the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Letting anger run overnight “give[s]… opportunity to the devil.” The word (topos) means a place or position — a foothold, a beachhead inside your lines from which an enemy can operate.

How it happens. Two elders disagree sharply over a decision. Words are exchanged; neither goes to clear the air — it feels awkward, and the matter was technically settled. A week later they are polite on Sunday but something has cooled. Months later the congregation senses tension in the leadership without naming it; people notice which elder they are more comfortable around; within a year there are two quiet camps. No one planned it. A small, unresolved anger was given time to harden, and the devil, who is in no hurry, used it. He does not need to tempt you into great sin if he can get you to leave a small wound unattended — “so that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs” (2 Corinthians 2:11).

The sentences that open the door. A foothold is usually granted not by a decision but by something we say to ourselves: “It would be awkward.” “It’s not a big deal; I’d look petty raising it.” “He probably didn’t mean it that way.” “I’ll leave it and see whether it happens again.” “I’ve forgiven it, so there’s nothing to discuss.” Any of these can be true — and any can be the polite name for avoidance. The enemy is content either way, because the result is the same: the thing stays unsaid and gets a night’s growth.

So find your own beachhead tonight. Is there a conversation you have been not having — not a dramatic one, but the small one, with the person you have started sitting a little further from, or replying to a little more briefly? That is the ground in question. And the remedy is embarrassingly ordinary: a message tonight instead of tomorrow; a sentence at the door — “Can I check something with you? Did I take that the wrong way?” Most footholds are closed by one short, awkward exchange that turns out far less terrible than a fortnight of imagining it. The enemy’s strategy depends on delay, which is exactly why Paul sets the clock at sundown. He is not asking for heroism, only that you not sleep on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labour, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labor, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need.” Three steps — stop stealing, work honestly, give — and the third is the surprise.

Were there thieves in the church? Evidently; Paul is not writing hypothetically. These churches were full of day labourers, dock workers and household slaves living hand to mouth, and petty theft was part of survival: pilfering from a master’s stores, skimming at the harbour, “forgetting” to return what was borrowed. The culture barely blinked. Paul does: in the body of Christ the common thing is no longer the acceptable thing. And the gospel never merely empties a life; it refills it, pointed the other way. The hand that took becomes the hand that gives. Zacchaeus got there in an afternoon (Luke 19:8–9).

You may never have burgled a house, but theft has respectable forms: the padded expense claim, the hours billed but not worked, the cash job kept off the books, the borrowed tools that never come home. The command is the same.

“With his own hands.” In Paul’s world manual work was widely despised; a gentleman did not work with his hands, and the philosophers said so. Paul, trained at the highest level (Acts 22:3), made tents for a living and was not embarrassed by it (Acts 18:3; 1 Thessalonians 2:9). So he is dignifying work his culture looked down on, in a letter that has spent three chapters in the heavenly places. The person laying bricks, cleaning floors, driving a van or stacking a warehouse is doing something the New Testament honours.

“So that he may have something to share.” Paul does not say “so that he may support himself”, true and necessary as that is, but “so that he may have something to share.” That rearranges the purpose of a wage, and you can test it with a bank statement. Is anything in your finances there on purpose for giving — planned first, before the rest is allocated? Or does giving come out of whatever survives the month? Most of us find our generosity is funded by the remainder, and the remainder is a notoriously unreliable donor. “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35).

One guard, because this verse can wound where it was never aimed. Paul is addressing a thief who is able to work; he is not making employment the measure of a person’s worth. If you are ill, unemployed or past working, the verse is not weighing you and finding you light. It describes the direction a redeemed life travels whenever it has the means — from taking, through honest getting, to giving.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear.” “Corrupting” (sapros) means rotten, like decaying food: speech that tears down, gossips or belittles is as out of place in the church as rotting meat at a feast.

Words that give grace. The standard is high: build up, fit the moment, and “give grace” — charis, the same word as God’s undeserved gift. Your words can carry it: an honest encouragement to someone doubting, a gentle truth to someone drifting, a simple acknowledgement to someone who feels invisible. When Jesus spoke, people “marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth” (Luke 4:22) — literally, words of grace. And the reverse is true: a careless word can undo in a moment what months of encouragement built.

Swearing and crude talk? Yes. Paul says it plainly a few verses later: “Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking” (5:4), and tells the Colossians to put away “obscene talk” (Colossians 3:8). Profane, crude or blasphemous speech does not build up or give grace. Jesus said we will give account “for every careless word” (Matthew 12:36).

True is not enough. Most of us screen our speech with one question: is it true? Paul closes that loophole. Suppose two members hear that a third, James, has lost his job. “Did you hear about James? I always thought he wasn’t cut out for that role” — possibly true, no grace, and James is now worse off in the community. Or: “James has lost his job and he’s shaken — could we pray for him now, and someone reach out this week?” Same information; grace given; the body moves toward him. Gossip is very often true; that is what makes it feel allowed. So use Paul’s full filter before something leaves your mouth: Is it true? Does it build up rather than flatten? Does this moment call for it, or am I just unloading? Will the hearer be better off, or am I the one who gets the relief? Run an ordinary day’s talk through that and it is a sobering audit; a great deal passes the first gate and fails the other three.

And notice where the rot spreads: never back to the speaker. Gossip does its work in the hearer, and in his picture of a third person who is not there to answer — which is why it is so easy and feels almost harmless. You have confronted no one; you have simply made someone a little smaller in another’s eyes, in a room he was not in. Measure your speech by the empty chair: what did the absent person just lose, and would you have said it with him sitting there?

verseByVerse.quote: And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.” Paul pulls back the curtain and shows who is in the room while we speak and act: the Holy Spirit himself, who can be hurt.

“Grieve.” Paul does not say anger, provoke or defy the Spirit, but grieve him — to cause sorrow, the language of close relationships. He is not saying the Spirit withdraws or that you lose your salvation, but something more intimate: the Spirit is a Person, and he feels the pain of holiness spurned by those he lives in. And grief is not the reaction of an official whose rules have been broken. You cannot grieve a stranger; a traffic warden is not grieved when you park badly. Grief is reserved for those to whom you matter. So before this verse is a warning, it is a staggering statement of how the Spirit regards you. Your sin does not chiefly irritate him; it wounds him, because he loves you.

What grieves him is named in the surrounding verses: falsehood, since he is “the Spirit of truth” (John 16:13); unresolved anger, since he is the Spirit of unity (4:3); corrupting speech; bitterness, wrath and slander (v. 31), the opposite of his fruit (Galatians 5:22–23). He is not grieved by weakness, failure or honest struggle; those he meets with intercession (Romans 8:26). He is grieved by wilful, unrepentant persistence in what Christ died to remove.

“Sealed for the day of redemption.” The Spirit himself is the seal (1:13–14), God’s mark of ownership and his guarantee of what is to come. So the appeal is both warning and wonder: do not grieve the very Person who guarantees your future — and he grieves, and stays. His grief is the grief of a love that will not let go (Isaiah 63:10).

A third way to see sin. Most of us file our sins as rule-breaking or self-harm — I broke a commandment, or I hurt myself. Both are true and strangely bearable. This is a third category, and it reaches people the first two never touch: sin grieves a Person who is present, living inside you, nearer than a friend in the next chair. There is a kind of man who will break a rule without a flicker and be undone the moment he realises he has hurt his mother. Paul is speaking to that man, which is all of us. So next time you are on the edge of the thing you keep returning to — the second look, the cutting reply already loaded, someone’s failure you are about to pass on — do not reach first for “this is forbidden”, true as it is. Reach for this: someone who loves me is here, and this will hurt him. That is not a lower motive than fear of judgment but a higher one, and it holds where fear does not. You can grow hardened to a rule, but it is very hard to keep wounding, to his face, a Person who has decided never to leave.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and security until delivery.

parallels.desc: they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamour and slander be put away from you, along with all malice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul lists six things to be “put away” — bitterness, wrath, anger, clamour, slander and malice — like weapons to be surrendered.

The six. Bitterness: the settled sourness of someone who was wounded and chose to nurse the wound — anger kept too long. Wrath (thymos): the sudden hot outburst that leaves wreckage (James 1:19–20). Anger (orgē): its cold twin, the brooding resentment that builds a case and waits (v. 26). Clamour: anger gone public, the raised voice that turns a disagreement into a scene. Slander (blasphēmia): injurious speech about another — the same word as blasphemy against God; in the church it attacks members of Christ’s body. And malice comes last because it is the root: settled ill-will, the soil the others grow in. As in verse 18, the road runs from the heart outward, so the cure must begin in the heart, not only in behaviour.

Bitterness feels like justice. The other five are easy to recognise as wrong. Wrath makes a scene you are ashamed of; slander you know is unkind as you say it. But bitterness grows in soil that has genuinely been wronged — you really were treated badly, the account really is unpaid — so it feels less like a sin than a fact to be honoured. That is why it is the most dangerous, and why Paul lists it first. He does not say the wrong did not happen or that you were oversensitive. He says, set down the thing you are carrying — because he knows where the damage goes. Bitterness does not punish the person who wronged you. It punishes you, daily, on his behalf. He may be asleep and untroubled, having forgotten the whole affair, while you lie awake rehearsing it, giving him free lodging in a mind he does not know he occupies. The old line is exactly right: resentment is drinking poison and waiting for the other person to die.

And Hebrews adds what we never see coming: a “root of bitterness” springs up and causes trouble, “and by it many become defiled” (Hebrews 12:15). Bitterness cannot be kept private. It leaks into your tone, your assumptions, the warnings you pass on about the person, the coldness a whole room can feel without being told why.

Here is a merciful test: is there a name that produces a small tightening when you hear it — a person whose good news you cannot quite be glad about? That is the location. The way out is not to talk yourself into feeling differently, which cannot be done, but to do what verse 32 says: release the debt at the foot of the cross, where a far larger one was released for you. You are not being asked to call the wrong acceptable. You are being asked to stop carrying, at your own cost, an account Christ is entirely able to settle.

verseByVerse.quote: Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In place of what was put away, Paul gives three things — kindness, tenderheartedness and forgiveness — all grounded in one fact: “as God in Christ forgave you.”

The three. Kind (chrēstos): practical, active goodness — the word is used of wine mellowed with age (Luke 5:39), and of Jesus’ “easy” yoke (Matthew 11:30). It looks for ways to be good to the people around you, especially the difficult ones. Tenderhearted: literally “good-hearted” in the gut — genuinely moved by another’s pain, as Jesus “had compassion” on the crowds (Matthew 9:36); the opposite of the hardened heart of verse 18. Forgiving (charizomenoi): from charis, grace. To forgive is to give grace — what the other does not deserve and cannot earn. It is not excusing (pretending the wrong did not happen), and it is not the same as reconciliation (which needs the other’s repentance). It is the wronged person’s decision to release the debt and stop holding the offence as a claim.

Why it is so hard, and how it is possible. It feels like injustice — letting someone off the hook. That is exactly why Paul grounds it in the cross. There the debt was not cancelled by pretending it did not exist; it was absorbed by the One who was wronged. God did not overlook sin; he paid for it himself. Christian forgiveness follows that pattern: you absorb the cost rather than pass it on.

How it hides. Sarah fell out with Mark over a worship-team decision six months ago. He was dismissive, spoke sharply in front of others and never apologised. She serves beside him on Sundays but keeps her distance, answers his messages with bare courtesy, has told two friends what happened — and tells herself she has forgiven him because she no longer thinks about it every day. Paul’s three words show where she really is: kindness gone, tenderheartedness closed, forgiveness incomplete. She has released the sharp pain but kept the verdict. The way forward is a decision made in prayer at the cross — “Lord, I release this. Mark owes me nothing. I received forgiveness I did not deserve; I give the same” — and then behaviour to match: a genuine word toward him, an end to the quiet commentary. It will not feel natural at first, and may need making again tomorrow.

What this does not mean. This verse has been said kindly to people it then badly hurt, so be plain. It does not mean the wrong was small. It does not mean you must feel warmly. It does not mean returning to a place where you are still being harmed, dropping a safeguard, or declining to involve the authorities God appointed to restrain evil (Romans 13:4). Forgiveness can be given alone; reconciliation cannot. But Jesus also said, “if he repents, forgive him” (Luke 17:3), and some Christians therefore hold that forgiveness is completed only when the offender repents. Both are true when forgiveness is seen in two parts. In the heart, before God, the wronged person lets go of bitterness and the wish for revenge whether or not the other repents (v. 31; Mark 11:25). The restored relationship — forgiveness spoken and received — waits for repentance, as God’s reconciliation with us does. So a believer must not nurse a grudge, but neither must he pretend nothing happened.

Where the injury is deep, forgiveness is rarely one act. It is often done again on Tuesday, having been done on Monday, and may go on for years, without meaning the first time was insincere. And if you cannot get there yet, do not pretend. Pray the prayer of someone who wants to want it: “Lord, I am not able to release this; make me willing.” That is not a failure of the command but the beginning of obeying it, prayed at the same cross where your own debt was absorbed.

This is where the chapter has been heading: old clothes off, mind renewed, new clothes on — not so we can admire ourselves, but because Christ is preparing his people to be presented “without spot or wrinkle… holy and without blemish” (5:27). Every truthful word, every anger surrendered before sundown, every hand that gives instead of takes, every debt released, is the bride being made ready.

4.theology:
Ephesians 4 stakes out the great Reformed doctrine of the inseparability of justification and sanctification. The same grace that declares the sinner righteous also begins to make them righteous. Not simultaneously, not automatically — but inevitably. Where the root is real, the fruit will come. Paul’s commands in this chapter are not the conditions of acceptance; they are the evidence of it. The indicative always precedes and grounds the imperative.

The chapter also gives the church its most searching doctrine of common life. The body of Christ is not a collection of private spiritual journeys happening in the same building. It is an organism, with every member genuinely joined to every other — responsible for each other’s growth, dependent on each other’s gifts, harmed by each other’s sin. Falsehood in the body is not a private failure; it is a systemic wound. Unresolved anger is not a personal problem; it is a strategic opening for the enemy. This is the doctrine of the church made viscerally practical.

And at the centre stands the renewal of the mind — the hinge on which all change turns. Not willpower, not behaviour management, but transformation at the level where thinking happens. This is the Spirit’s sovereign work, received through the ordinary means of grace: the word, prayer, honest community, and obedience to what is already known. The Christian does not renew themselves. But they can position themselves daily in the hands of the One who does. cf. Rom. 12:1–2; 2 Cor. 3:18; Phil. 2:12–13.
4.examples:
Then: The Ephesian believers had come out of a culture saturated with the very patterns Paul describes in vv. 17–19 — a world of mystery religions, sexual licence, and moral relativism where the only sin was public embarrassment. To be told to “put off” this was not a minor adjustment; it was a complete reorientation of identity. And the alternative Paul offered — speaking truth, controlling anger, working honestly, forgiving freely — would have looked countercultural to the point of strangeness. The church in Ephesus was being asked to be a visible sign that a different humanity was possible.

Now: The culture has changed; the pressure has not. The same patterns Paul named are alive and well: the mind drifting, the conscience growing quieter, the appetite demanding more. The same temptations assault the same pressure points: to manage rather than truth-tell, to nurse grievance rather than forgive, to speak what entertains rather than what builds. And the same command stands: no longer walk as those who do not know God. Not because you must earn your standing — that is secured in Christ — but because you have been made new, and new creatures do not live in the old way.

You, reading this chapter on a Monday morning, can take one thing to work: the person sitting across from you is either a fellow member of the body or a neighbour made in God’s image. Either way, what you say matters, what you do with your anger matters, how you handle the truth matters. The renewal of the mind is not a mystical event. It is what happens when the Christian opens the Bible instead of the phone, prays instead of broods, speaks the honest word instead of the comfortable one — and does it again tomorrow. This is how the body builds itself up in love.

5.title: Walking in Love and the Mystery of Marriage
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children. <sup>2</sup>And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God. <sup>3</sup>But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints. <sup>4</sup>Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving. <sup>5</sup>For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. <sup>6</sup>Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. <sup>7</sup>Therefore do not become partners with them; <sup>8</sup>for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light <sup>9</sup>(for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), <sup>10</sup>and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord. <sup>11</sup>Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. <sup>12</sup>For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret. <sup>13</sup>But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, <sup>14</sup>for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” <sup>15</sup>Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, <sup>16</sup>making the best use of the time, because the days are evil. <sup>17</sup>Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is. <sup>18</sup>And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit, <sup>19</sup>addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, <sup>20</sup>giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, <sup>21</sup>submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ. <sup>22</sup>Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord. <sup>23</sup>For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. <sup>24</sup>Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands. <sup>25</sup>Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, <sup>26</sup>that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, <sup>27</sup>so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish. <sup>28</sup>In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. <sup>29</sup>For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, <sup>30</sup>because we are members of his body. <sup>31</sup>“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.” <sup>32</sup>This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church. <sup>33</sup>However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children.” The command is breathtaking in its scope, and its motivation is everything. We imitate God not because he is powerful or sovereign or even just — but because we are his beloved children, and children naturally, joyfully imitate those who love them. The motivation for holy living is not duty but delight, not fear but love, not the dread of punishment but the joy of resemblance.

The specific attribute to be imitated is love — but immediately defined by the cross: Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, “a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (v. 2). This phrase reaches deep into the Old Testament sacrificial system. The “fragrant offering” was the language of divine acceptance — from Genesis 8:21 through the Levitical offerings, whenever God declared himself pleased with the sacrifice.

Christ’s self-giving is the final, fully accepted offering that all those animal sacrifices could only foreshadow. The Father smells the fragrance and is satisfied. Wrath propitiated, covenant restored, the guilty declared righteous. This is the love to be imitated: cross-shaped, self-giving, asking not “what do I get?” but “what does this person need and what will it cost me to give it?”

Against this backdrop Paul names what does not belong: sexual immorality, impurity of every kind, and covetousness — the insatiable craving for more, which Paul calls idolatry (v. 5).

The list then moves from deeds to words (v. 4), and the cure Paul prescribes for a corrupted tongue is not silence but thanksgiving.

The warning of verses 5–6 is sobering — those who practice these things without repentance have no inheritance in the kingdom. But a pastoral word is essential: Paul is describing a settled, unrepentant pattern of life, not the experience of the believer who struggles, falls, grieves, and returns. The evidence of genuine faith is not the absence of struggle but the presence of grief over sin and the refusal to make peace with what Christ died to remove.

The dangerous condition is not the fall but the cessation of struggle — listening to the “empty words” of v. 6 and reclassifying sin as not-sin. For the one who is genuinely fighting: “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:1). A bruised reed he will not break (Isa. 42:3).

Verse 7 then draws the practical conclusion: “do not become partners with them.” The line runs between practices, not between people.
verseByVerse.theology:
Cruciform Love as the Pattern of the Christian Life

“A fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (v.2) — Paul's description of Christ's self-giving at the cross is drawn directly from the Old Testament sacrificial language. The burnt offering was described as “a pleasing aroma to the LORD” (Leviticus 1:9; 8:21) — a sacrifice that God receives with satisfaction, that expresses the proper worship of creature before Creator. Paul applies this language to the cross: the death of Christ was the ultimate sacrifice, the perfect offering, the worship that satisfied the holiness of God and secured the salvation of his people.

The implication for ethics is profound: to walk in love in imitation of Christ is to participate in a form of worship. Every act of genuine, self-giving love — every moment of costly service, every forgiveness extended at personal cost, every preference of another's need over one's own comfort — is offered to God as a fragrant offering. The Christian life is not divided into sacred acts (prayer, church attendance) and secular acts (daily life, work, relationships). All of it is worship. The love that looks like Calvary, lived out in the ordinary texture of daily life, is received by God as the aroma of Christ himself.

Covetousness is identified in v.5 as idolatry — a striking identification that requires reflection. Covetousness is not merely wanting what others have; it is the orientation of the heart toward things rather than toward God, treating the creature as the source of satisfaction rather than the Creator. In this sense it is the root of sexual immorality as well: the sexualised culture is a culture of covetousness, of insatiable appetite, of treating persons as objects to be consumed. The gospel addresses this at the root by offering the only love that actually satisfies — the love of God in Christ, which surpasses knowledge and fills us with all the fullness of God (3:19).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Be imitators of God” — in the Greco-Roman world, this language had a specific resonance. The philosophical schools spoke of likeness to God as the goal of the spiritual life. But the path they offered was typically ascetic withdrawal, esoteric knowledge, ritual elevation. Paul offers a radically different path: imitate the God who descended, who gave himself up, who went to the cross for his enemies. The divine pattern to be imitated is not the god on the Olympian heights, remote and powerful, but the God who came down in love and poured himself out in death. The imitation called for is not upward escape but downward love.

Now: Sexual immorality has been rebranded in our age as liberation, as authentic self-expression, as the natural pursuit of desire. Covetousness is marketed as aspiration, ambition, the engine of economic progress. Paul's gospel cuts through all of it — not with a longer list of prohibitions, but with a higher vision. You are a beloved child of the God who gave his Son for you. You have been loved with a love that went to the cross. Now walk in that love: freely, lavishly, cruciformly, without counting the cost. This is not the moralism of a killjoy god; it is the invitation of a Father who wants his children to look like him and to know the joy of doing so.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Be imitators of God, as beloved children.” Not a set of rules to copy, but a Father to watch and resemble — and the ground of it is that we are already his beloved children. We imitate God not to earn his favour but because we already have it.

How children imitate. No father sits a three-year-old down and teaches him how to be like him. The boy simply appears one Saturday with a plastic hammer, having noticed what his father does. He picks up a phrase and uses it slightly wrongly at the table; he stands with his hands in his pockets the way the man stands. It is not effort or obedience; it is what nearness does. That explains something earnest effort never manages: the surest way to become like the Father is not to try harder but to be with him more. When the council saw Peter and John, “they recognized that they had been with Jesus” (Acts 4:13). And it works the other way too: you are being formed right now by whatever you spend your hours with. If most of your week is spent absorbing a screen, you will imitate what it admires, and no amount of Sunday resolve offsets the arithmetic of the hours.

“As beloved children.” Not servants hoping to be noticed or applicants under review. The love is the starting point, not the prize. When you fail badly this week, notice your instinct. If it is to keep away from God until you feel more presentable, you are acting like a hired man rather than a son. A child who has broken something runs to his father, and he can, because nothing he broke put his sonship in question.

The opposite direction. “Likeness to God” was a stock phrase in the Platonist schools for the goal of the spiritual life, and the route was always upward: withdrawal, discipline, secret knowledge, shedding the body until the soul rose toward the divine — every path leading away from ordinary life, so that the higher you got, the fewer people you were any use to. Paul uses the same idea and reverses it. The God we imitate came down, gave himself for his enemies and died between two criminals — so the next verse defines the likeness as walking in love and giving yourself away (v. 2). So do not measure your progress by how high you have climbed or how still your mind has grown. Ask what it has cost you lately to love somebody.

verseByVerse.quote: And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.” The standard and pattern of Christian love is the cross: love that gives itself, at real cost, for the good of others.

Walk. The verb is the spine of the letter (2:2, 10; 4:1, 17; 5:2, 8, 15), and it is the least glamorous picture available. Not soar, burn or feel in love — walk: what you do on an ordinary Tuesday, one foot after another, so many times you stop counting. And it is a present command: keep walking. That is a mercy. Love here is not a temperature to check but a direction to keep. You do not have to feel it to walk it, and if you wait until you feel it you will not move. A man walking north is walking north whether or not he enjoys the weather. But Paul’s definition has a price built in: Christ “gave himself up”. So look back over the last seven days for one time when loving someone cost you something you wanted — an evening, money, a preference, the last word in an argument you could have won. If nothing comes to mind, what you have been calling love has so far been free.

A fragrant offering. This is Old Testament sacrifice language: an offering God accepted and was pleased with. It first appears when Noah steps off the ark onto a planet that is a graveyard and builds an altar, “And when the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma, the LORD said in his heart, ‘I will never again curse the ground because of man’” (Genesis 8:21). Something given rose from the earth; God received it and bound himself to the world in peace. Every animal sacrifice pointed to the cross, the one offering God fully accepted: “by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). And Christ was not seized; he gave himself (John 10:18).

Your kitchen. Paul uses the same phrase in one other place, and not about the cross. The Philippians sent supplies to Paul in prison, and he called their gift “a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God” (Philippians 4:18). Someone packed a bag for a friend in trouble, and the apostle used the language of the altar. So the meal cooked for the family whose week has collapsed, the bill quietly paid, the afternoon given to someone whose company you do not enjoy — these go up. That answers a weariness many carry: loving someone who never notices — the parent of a teenager who registers nothing, the daughter visiting a mother who no longer knows her name, the person holding a marriage together alone for eleven years without thanks. Read the last two words: “to God”. Whether the person noticed, deserved or remembers it is a different question from whether it arrived. It arrived, and it pleased him. And notice whom Christ loved while making his offering: not admirers. “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). That is why this love can be commanded toward people who have not earned it.

A fear, and a guard. “As Christ loved us” is not a standard anyone survives being measured by — and before the cross is a pattern, it is a gift: he gave himself up for us. Your acceptance rests there: “we are the aroma of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:15). You will never smell better to God than you do now, and no bad week can sour it. But this verse has been put to cruel use, quoted to keep people where they are being harmed, as if Christlikeness meant absorbing whatever is done to you. No one took Christ’s life from him; he laid it down of his own accord (John 10:18), chosen and purposeful, aimed at rescue. Someone extracting sacrifice from you by force, fear or manipulation is not making you like Christ. If that is your home, tell someone who can act. The command to walk in love has never contained a command to stand still and be destroyed.
verseByVerse.note: A “fragrant offering” recalls the Old Testament sacrifices that pleased God.

verseByVerse.quote: But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sexual immorality, impurity and covetousness “must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints.” The standard rests on identity: these things do not belong among people who belong to God.

The three. Sexual immorality (porneia) covers every sexual act outside the marriage of a man and a woman, pornography included (the words share a root). Not because the body is evil — it belongs to God (1 Corinthians 6:19–20) — but because sexual union is a covenant act that pictures Christ and the church (vv. 31–32). Impurity reaches the inner life of desire and imagination; Jesus said the lustful look is already adultery in the heart (Matthew 5:28). Covetousness (pleonexia) is literally “wanting more”: the craving for more money, status, comfort or pleasure that is never satisfied. Paul puts it beside sexual sin because the dynamic is the same — wanting what God has not given and enthroning a craving where God belongs; in 1 Thessalonians 4:6 he uses the same word for the man who takes what is not his in sexual matters.

A thought that arrives is not a thought welcomed. That line about the heart has crushed tender consciences, so be careful. Jesus himself “in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15), so being tempted cannot itself be sin. James traces the steps: “each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin” (James 1:14–15). The guilt lies in the welcome — the lingering, turning the thought over for pleasure. As Luther is often quoted, you cannot stop birds flying over your head, but you can stop them building a nest in your hair. The unwanted thought that flashes in and is hated is a call to fight, not a verdict of guilt; the very distress it causes shows the heart has not consented. Turn from it, hand it to Christ, and do not stay to argue with it. If such thoughts are persistent and tormenting, tell a wise pastor or friend; they lose much of their power in the light (v. 13).

In Ephesus. Sexual licence was woven into ordinary life and religion: festivals, temple banquets and drunken revels where licence was expected (the cult of Dionysus was strong there). Prostitution was legal and taxed, and a husband’s use of slaves or prostitutes was not counted adultery; an Athenian orator put the common view bluntly — mistresses for pleasure, concubines for daily care, wives for legitimate children. (The popular claim that the temple of Artemis kept sacred prostitutes is not well supported; she was a virgin goddess, with priestesses bound to chastity.) The temple of Artemis was also the great bank of the province, where wealth was deposited and lent at interest; in Ephesus the goddess and the money were kept in the same building. When the gospel threatened the silver-shrine trade, Demetrius stirred up a riot with profit and piety in one speech (Acts 19:25–27). The Greek philosophers already condemned grasping after more than your share as the root of injustice; what was new was Paul calling it idolatry (v. 5). The church was to be the one community in the city where these things were not normal.

What covetousness is not. Providing for your household is a duty (1 Timothy 5:8); wise saving is commended (Proverbs 6:6–8); enjoying God’s gifts is gratitude, for God “richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17). And ambition is not greed: Paul wrote, “I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named” (Romans 15:20). The difference is direction. Greed measures itself against a neighbour and wants a bigger share; godly ambition measures itself against the task and wants it done well, for others and for God. “Do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not” (Jeremiah 45:5) — the fault was never the “great” but the “for yourself”. The line runs through the heart: is it driven by love and responsibility, or by an appetite that upgrades and immediately eyes the next upgrade? Is it held open-handed, or clutched as security, so that losing it would be devastation? Does it produce generosity or hoarding? At bottom covetousness is a failure of trust: the belief that God cannot be relied on, so security must be seized.

“Must not even be named.” Paul has just named all three, so he does not mean silence. He is not forbidding the sermon that warns, the confession that admits, or the parent who explains to a teenager what pornography does to a soul; exposing is commanded a few verses later (vv. 11–13). He forbids the naming that makes a thing ordinary: the anecdote told with a laugh, the affair discussed as entertainment, the casual reference that assumes everyone finds it normal and mildly amusing. Nothing becomes acceptable by being argued for; things become acceptable by being mentioned often enough in a relaxed tone. If the running joke is how much everyone spends, and the admiring remarks are all about what people have acquired, no Sunday sermon will undo what the tone of the foyer has established. So listen to how these subjects come up in your conversation this week: as things to be grieved, resisted and confessed — or as material?

verseByVerse.quote: Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From deeds Paul moves to words: “Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving.” The Greek and Roman world prized bawdy wit; Paul says it is out of place among people of the cross, and the remedy is not solemn silence but gratitude.

Not a ban on humour. This verse is often misheard. Paul is not describing a people who have decided laughter is worldly and now speak only in careful devotional tones; churches that took it that way produced not holiness but a strained atmosphere where no one says anything real. God invented laughter, and there is wit in Scripture, including on Jesus’ lips: a camel through the eye of a needle (Mark 10:25) and the log in your own eye (Matthew 7:3–5) are meant to be funny. Paul’s target is precise: eutrapelia, the quick verbal turn or ready wit. Aristotle counted it a virtue. Paul names it a vice — not because it is clever, but because of what that particular cleverness is typically used for: making degrading things funny and turning people into material.

So the test is not whether the room laughed but what the laughter was aimed at. Is it something genuinely absurd — and life is full of it — or someone’s body, someone’s marriage, sin dressed up as a story? Two more questions settle most cases: could the subject of the joke stand in the doorway without the tone changing? And what has the joke taught the youngest Christian in the room about how seriously we take this?

The cure: thanksgiving. The obvious answer to a mouth problem would be restraint. Paul prescribes substitution instead, as with the thief told not only to stop stealing but to work and give (4:28). Crude joking treats people and gifts as material for a moment’s effect; thanksgiving treats them as gifts and names the Giver. The two cannot easily share a mouth — which is why the man who begins genuinely thanking God for his wife will find the jokes about her drying up without ever making a rule about it. (The word for thanksgiving, eucharistia, is also the name many churches give the Lord’s Supper: the table where we remember what Christ gave is meant to shape everything we say away from it.)

verseByVerse.quote: For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is blunt: everyone who is sexually immoral, impure or covetous — and the covetous person is “an idolater” — “has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.” These sins are not just moral failures but worship aimed at the wrong object (Colossians 3:5).

Does this mean struggling believers are not saved? Two truths must be held together. First, Paul describes a settled pattern of life, not a moment of failure: the person who is immoral or covetous as an unrepentant way of living, not the believer who falls, grieves, confesses and fights. In a similar list Paul adds, “And such were some of you” — past tense — “But you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11). Second, the struggle itself is evidence of new life. The unregenerate person does not war against his sin; he makes peace with it. “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me?” (Romans 7:24) is not the voice of someone shut out of the kingdom, but of someone who belongs to Christ and knows he is not yet what he will be. The mark of the unbeliever is not that he sins but that he does not fight; the mark of the believer is not that he never falls but that he cannot stay down. If this verse troubles you, that trouble is itself a sign of life.

Greed is idolatry. Not like idolatry; it is idolatry. Most of us can see how someone worships a carved image, and cannot see how someone worships a bank balance. So ask what an idol does for its worshipper. It tells him who he is: his worth is settled by what he has or achieves. It tells him he is safe: the figure in the account stands between him and disaster. It receives his best hours and his idle imagination. It sets the terms of his joy: a good day is a day when it prospers. And it decides what he will sacrifice for it: time, integrity, his marriage, his children’s memory of him. Run those five through a man who has never bowed to a statue but cannot stop wanting more, and every one fits.

That is why it is the hardest idol to see. An affair announces itself. Covetousness looks like diligence, prudence, ambition, providing for the family — genuine virtues, which is the camouflage. It is admired at work and congratulated at church; no one has ever taken a man aside to ask whether he might be worshipping his career. So ask the two questions that find an idol, because you can hide an object of worship but not what happens when it is threatened: what loss would feel like the end of you — not painful, but the end? And what did you last lose a night’s sleep over? Whatever answers those is functioning as your god. An idol holds power only while it goes by another name; once you call it what it is, you can stop asking it for what it was never able to give.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience.” The empty words are the arguments that shrink the stakes: “God is gracious, so this doesn’t really matter”; “everyone struggles with this”; “a loving God would never judge.”

The target is the conscience that wants permission: the smooth voice that talks someone out of repenting and lets him settle into unrepentant sin while keeping a Christian name. The believer who fights, grieves and returns is not the one warned here; over all Paul’s warnings stands “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

Answering the empty words. Each contains a half-truth, and that is its whole power; a plainly false lie persuades no one. “God is gracious, so it doesn’t really matter.” The first half is gloriously true. But grace is not God’s indifference to sin; it is what it cost him to deal with it. Measure sin’s seriousness by the cross. To say grace makes sin unimportant is to say Calvary was an overreaction. “Everyone struggles with this.” Also true, and a good reason to be gentle with others — not a reason to stop fighting. That everyone is ill does not make the illness harmless; it makes it an epidemic. And notice the sleight of hand: Paul has just distinguished the one who struggles from the one who has settled. The phrase is usually used by someone who has stopped struggling and would like to keep the word. “A loving God would never judge.” We do not believe that about anything we care about. A father who watched his child being destroyed and felt nothing would not be loving. Wrath is not the opposite of love; indifference is. God’s anger at what ruins his image-bearers is the form his love takes toward the thing ruining them.

Where do empty words come from? Rarely from the faith’s enemies. More often from a friend who wants us comfortable, a teacher who has learned that the pleasant half of the message fills a room, and most often from ourselves at eleven at night, building a case in our own favour. So when an argument arrives that happens to permit exactly what you already wanted, treat its convenience as evidence. Truth is often unwelcome; an argument that lands exactly where your appetite was already standing has some explaining to do.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not become partners with them;
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore do not become partners with them” — do not share in the practices that bring God’s wrath (vv. 5–6). This is not a call to cut yourself off from unbelievers, but a refusal to take part in what belongs to the old life.

That needs saying strongly, because this verse has done real damage when read as a command to withdraw. Paul had to correct exactly that misunderstanding in Corinth: when he told them not to associate with sexually immoral people, he did not mean “the sexually immoral of this world… since then you would need to go out of the world”, but anyone who bears the name of brother and lives that way (1 Corinthians 5:9–11). The separation runs mainly inside the church, not around it. And Jesus was called “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matthew 11:19), and meant it.

So the line runs between practices, not people. You are not told to avoid the colleague, but not to join in what he is doing. In practice it is drawn at a very ordinary level: not whether you go to the party, but whether you take part in what happens there; not whether you keep the friendship, but whether your presence signals approval of what you both know is wrong. It is the difference between being among and being with. Paul’s word makes the point: “partners” (summetochoi) is the word he used in 3:6, where Gentiles are “partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus”, and it appears nowhere else in the New Testament. You cannot be a partner in Christ and a partner in the works of darkness at once.

So when you are somewhere you would rather not have to describe, do not only ask, “Am I doing anything wrong?” Ask, “If the people I love and the Lord I serve were both watching, what would my presence here be saying?” Complicity is rarely a decision; it is usually a silence — the laugh given so as not to seem difficult, the objection not raised, the thing let pass. Paul is not asking you to leave the world, only to stop lending it your agreement.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“For at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.” The sharpness of this contrast arrests us every time we read it. Not “you were in darkness” — you were darkness itself. Not “you are now in the light” — you are light. The transformation is total, ontological, irreversible. Something has changed at the deepest level of what you are, not merely where you are or what you do. And the imperative that follows — “walk as children of light” — is not a command to achieve something new but to express something already true. Be in your behaviour what you are in your nature. Let the outside match the inside.

Light bears fruit. The fruit of light is “found in all that is good and right and true” (v.9) — three qualities that together describe the character of the God who is light (1 John 1:5). The child of light is not defined primarily by what they avoid but by what they produce: genuine moral goodness, the rightness of life aligned with God's law and character, the transparency of truth-telling in every dimension of life.
