This fruit is not manufactured by effort; it grows naturally from a nature that has been fundamentally changed. Light cannot help but produce light-fruits.

And light exposes what darkness conceals. The children of light do not retreat from the darkness of the culture (withdrawal) or blend into it (accommodation). They expose it — by the simple, consistent, visible presence of a life lived in the open before God. This exposure is not aggressive or confrontational; it does not require denunciation or political engagement (though these may have their place). It requires holiness. “When anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible” (v.13). The most prophetic thing the church can do in a dark age is simply to be genuinely, visibly, persistently light.

Between the fruit and the exposing, Paul slips in the verb that governs the whole of it: “try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord” (v.10). Not what is permitted — what is pleasing; and not a list but a skill, since a rulebook can only ever cover the cases its author foresaw. Walking as a child of light is therefore not compliance but a trained capacity to read a situation and see what would delight him.

And the section closes with what is almost certainly a fragment of an early Christian hymn, sung — many think — at baptisms, as the new believer came up out of the water: “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you” (v.14).
verseByVerse.theology:
Light, Darkness, and the Prophetic Witness of Holiness

The ontological language of this passage — “you were darkness,” “you are light” — reflects the radical nature of regeneration. The new birth is not a moral improvement programme; it is a change of nature. What was dark has become light. What was oriented toward self and sin has been reoriented toward God and holiness. This is the consistent teaching of the Reformed tradition: regeneration is sovereign, total, and irreversible — a work of God in the interior of the person that creates a new appetite, a new orientation, a new capacity for the things of God.

The call to “take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them” (v.11) raises the question of the church's relationship to culture. The Reformed tradition has generally resisted both the temptation to total withdrawal (a pietism that disengages from the world) and the temptation to total accommodation (a liberalism that conforms to it). The middle path — engagement without assimilation, presence without compromise — is what it means to be light in the world. The church that is genuinely, visibly holy is not only doing something good for its own members; it is doing something necessary for the world, exposing by contrast what the world cannot see about itself.

The awakening hymn of v.14 — “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you” — is widely thought to be an early Christian baptismal hymn. It captures the eschatological urgency of the whole passage: the world is asleep, the darkness is presenting itself as normal and comfortable, and the church is called to be the community of the awakened, the risen, the enlightened. Not by shouting but by shining.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The darkness Paul describes in v.12 — “the things they do in secret” — was not merely a moral category. Ephesus had a fully developed underground of occult practice, of ritual darkness, of things done in the night that could not bear the daylight. The mystery religions operated precisely in the realm of secrets, of hidden things, of initiation into darkness. The church's commitment to transparency — to lives that could be lived fully in the open before God — was itself a form of witness against the culture of secrecy. You have nothing to hide because you have nothing to fear. You live in the light because Christ has shone on you.

Now: “Awake, O sleeper” has the ring of an alarm clock going off in a dark room. The world is sleeping — comfortable in its darkness, unaware of its danger, presenting its way of life as simply the normal and natural way to live. The church is called to wake up and to be awake — to see the world as it really is in the light of God's word, to live accordingly, and thereby to be the kind of community whose quality of life is itself an invitation: come and see what happens when Christ shines on you. In a culture that is drowsy with distraction and numbed by comfort, the church's wakefulness is among its most urgent callings.

verseByVerse.quote: for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light
verseByVerse.commentary:
“At one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light.” Not that they were in darkness and are now in light, but that they were darkness and now are light — a change of nature, not just location. And the command follows the fact: you do not walk in the light to become light; you walk as light because you are.

What “darkness” was. Not ignorance that education could fix, but a life turned away from God. Paul has already written its biography: dead in trespasses, following the world, children of wrath (2:1–3); “having no hope and without God in the world” (2:12); darkened, callous, past feeling (4:18–19). That was the address, and it was yours. And notice what he does not say happened to it. God did not find a spark and fan it, or see potential worth developing. Darkness has no raw material. What happened was creation: “God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts” (2 Corinthians 4:6) — Genesis 1:3 spoken over a human being. If you have ever suspected you were a marginal case, that God got less than he bargained for with you: nobody was a promising case. If God had needed a spark to work with, the world would still be dark.

“Light in the Lord.” Paul does not say you are light, full stop, as if a quality had been installed in you. You are light in the Lord — borrowed, held by union, as a branch holds sap. Think of the moon: genuinely light, bright enough for sailors to cross oceans by, yet every particle of that light is borrowed, and turned away from the sun it is a cold rock. So when you read “you are light” and think of what went through your mind on the drive home, and conclude Paul cannot mean you, you are looking in the wrong place. You are searching yourself for your own glow, and the verse never said you had one. The question is not whether you can detect light inside you, but whether you are turned toward him. Do not rummage through your interior for evidence; turn round.

“Children of light” is a Hebrew way of speaking: to be a son of something is to take your nature from it. A Jewish community by the Dead Sea in Paul’s century called themselves the Sons of Light, and Jesus spoke of “the sons of this world” and “the sons of light” (Luke 16:8). It is the same word Paul used in 5:1, “beloved children”: in both places the family you belong to is the reason for the behaviour, never the price of admission to it.

The order. “You are light” comes first, as fact; “walk” second, as command. Scripture never reverses them. Most of us try to walk well enough to establish the identity — to get enough good weeks behind us that the word “light” would not feel like a lie. Paul gives the identity and then asks for the walk. And the fact that he has to ask shows the gap is real: you can be light and walk badly. That is not a paradox but every Christian’s ordinary experience, and the reason this letter has three chapters of instructions.

So think of the last time you sinned badly enough to be ashamed. What did you conclude afterwards? Did some part of you say, “That is not who I am”? Or did it feel like just another instalment of yourself, in character? In a child of light, sin is a contradiction, and it feels like one: it sits wrong, will not settle, wants confessing. In a child of darkness it is self-expression and feels like nothing much. A stain shows on white cloth and disappears on black; the fact that yours showed tells you what colour the cloth is.

verseByVerse.quote: (for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Light produces fruit — “all that is good and right and true” — and the life of light involves learning to “discern what is pleasing to the Lord.” The fruit is goodness, right dealing with others, and truthfulness: not rules performed but the natural produce of a changed life.

Discern. Paul usually gives direct commands, but here he says “discern” (dokimazein) — test, examine, approve after careful evaluation, the word for assaying metal. Why? Because the Christian life cannot be reduced to a rulebook. Rules cover the cases the lawmaker foresaw; life keeps producing situations no rulebook addressed. Paul wants something deeper than compliance: the ability to read a situation in the light of knowing Christ and see what would please him. That needs a renewed mind (4:23) — “that by testing you may discern what is the will of God” (Romans 12:2).

Pleasing, not permitted. Paul does not say discern what is allowed. Most of us facing a decision ask a boundary question: is this a sin? Where exactly is the line? That question has a peculiar property: it is asked by someone who wants to know how close he may go. A husband who asks what he can do and still be technically faithful has already told you the state of his marriage; a husband who asks what would please his wife is in a different marriage, and he is not consulting a rulebook. Take an ordinary case. You are offered a promotion: more money and standing, and sixty hours a week for three years, with two children at home. The boundary question returns nothing useful: ambition is not sin, providing is a duty, no commandment broken. Paul’s question brings in everything relevant: what happens to those children in years you cannot get back; whether this is stewardship of a gift or the covetousness of verse 5 in respectable clothes; what your motive really is; what your wife would say if she believed you truly wanted to know; what this does to the church you would largely stop seeing. None of that can be looked up. It is what someone sees who knows the Lord well enough to know what pleases him — which is why the answer may differ for two men in two situations, and why Paul gives a verb, not a list.

A skill learned by practice. No one develops taste by reading about it. The mature are those “who have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil” (Hebrews 5:14). A Christian of thirty years often sees at once what a younger believer agonises over, not because he is cleverer, but because he has asked the question ten thousand times, in Scripture, prayer and ordinary decisions, and his palate has changed. So you are not asked to arrive, only to start practising. Take one decision this week, a small one, and ask the second question instead of the first: not “am I allowed?” but “what would please him?” You will not always get it right. But someone who has asked it a thousand times will one day find he can see what is right without having to work it out.

verseByVerse.quote: Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret.” Darkness bears no fruit that lasts; believers are not only to abstain from it but to bring it into the light.

What “expose” does not mean. It is not a licence to become an investigator, hunting for what people hide — the shameful things are done in secret and Paul leaves them there; a Christian with an appetite for uncovering others’ sin has badly misread him. It is not exposing persons; Paul says expose the works. And it is not a mandate for loud denunciation of a world behaving exactly as one would expect; judging outsiders, Paul says, is not his business (1 Corinthians 5:12–13).

What it does mean takes three ordinary forms. Living so that the contrast is visible: someone who simply does not join in has, without a word, made something visible (Matthew 5:16). Refusing to let something pass as normal — not a sermon, but the quiet sentence that declines to laugh, or says, “I don’t think that’s right,” and lets the silence sit. It costs surprisingly much and does surprisingly much. And the harder one, where the command mostly lands: going privately to a brother about something you can see and he cannot (Matthew 18:15; Galatians 6:1) — gently, with no interest in being right.

Verse 12 governs the manner. You can bring something into the light without describing it in detail; the difference is whether the telling serves repentance or curiosity. A sermon, conversation or confession so vivid that the hearers are entertained rather than sobered has stopped exposing darkness and started retailing it. So before you speak, ask what outcome you want. If it is that this person be restored and this thing end, you are exposing. If part of you wants to be proved right, or seen as the one who noticed, that is not light; it is the pleasure of holding a torch.

In Ephesus. Ephesus was the magic capital of the ancient world; its written spells were famous as the “Ephesian Letters”, and its mystery cults were built on secrecy — knowledge given only to initiates, rites at night. Secrecy was the product being sold. That is why Luke records that when the gospel took hold there, magicians “brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all”, worth fifty thousand pieces of silver (Acts 19:19) — publicly, at ruinous cost, when they could have sold them on. Some of those reading this letter had probably stood in that crowd. Paul is reminding them of the smell of smoke.

And this command runs between two ditches. One is withdrawal: treating darkness as contamination and retreating until a church knows no one outside itself and has no light to shed because it shines into a mirror. The other is accommodation: staying in the world and becoming indistinguishable from it, until there is nothing left to expose because the contrast is gone. Paul asks for presence without participation — harder than either ditch, because each offers relief and this offers none. But it is the only one that leaves anyone with something to see.

verseByVerse.quote: But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, 'Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When light exposes something, it becomes visible — and what is brought into the light begins to be changed by it. “Therefore it says, ‘Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.’”

Light changes what it touches. Think of a believer who has carried a hidden sin for years, never told to anyone; the weight has grown, not lifted. When it is finally brought into the light — confessed to God and to a trusted friend or pastor — its grip weakens. Not because confession is magic, but because secrecy is the one condition sin really needs. Shame’s whole power is one sentence: “If they knew what you are, they would be finished with you.” As long as no one knows, that sentence is never tested and so is believed. Confession tests it. You say the thing aloud to a Christian friend, and he does not recoil; he prays with you, and next week asks how you are getting on. The lie you lived under for fifteen years is disproved in front of you by someone who knows the worst and is still sitting there. That is why James says, “confess your sins to one another… that you may be healed” (James 5:16). The healing comes through the “one another”.

The quotation. “Therefore it says” is how Paul usually introduces Scripture, yet these words are not in the Old Testament. Most likely they come from an early Christian hymn — many think it was sung at baptisms — gathering up Old Testament language: “Your dead shall live… awake and sing” (Isaiah 26:19); “Arise, shine, for your light has come” (Isaiah 60:1).

Who is the sleeper? It is a call to the unconverted to rise into Christ’s light, in the resurrection language of the whole letter (2:1–6). But Paul is writing to saints, already raised with Christ, so it is just as naturally a call to drowsy believers — and the church has heard it both ways. Scripture keeps addressing the sleeping Christian: “the hour has come for you to wake from sleep” (Romans 13:11); “Wake up, and strengthen what remains” (Revelation 3:2), said to a church with a reputation for being alive. The sleeping Christian has renounced nothing. He is at church most Sundays and would answer any doctrinal question correctly. But nothing costs him anything, no sin has been fought in years, prayer has become words rather than talking to a Person, and he cannot remember when he last expected God to do anything. He is not in rebellion; he is asleep — everything looks normal and nothing is happening.

And the defining feature of sleep is that the sleeper does not know it. The rebel knows what he is doing; the drowsy person is the last to notice, because the dullness dulls his noticing too. So the call has to come from outside — a hymn, a sermon, a friend, a verse that will not leave him alone. Ask yourself the questions a sleeper cannot ask himself: When did something in Scripture last genuinely arrest you? When did you last pray expecting an answer? When did obedience last cost you something you noticed? If those are hard to answer, this verse is addressed to you.

And see the promise: “Christ will shine on you.” Not “wake up and get your discipline in order, and God may eventually take an interest.” The light is already shining; the only thing between the sleeper and the sunrise is a pair of closed eyes.
verseByVerse.note: These lines are not found in the Old Testament; they may come from an early Christian hymn, echoing Isaiah.

arise, shine, for your light has come

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil.” The third walk imperative carries a quality of urgency that is eschatological in character. The Christian does not live in a neutral moment; they live in a moment freighted with significance, in days that are evil (and therefore time-limited in their evil), in a window of opportunity that will not remain open forever. Wisdom means seeing this clearly and acting accordingly — not frantic and anxious, but alert and intentional, making the most of every opportunity because the Kingdom has come and its King is returning.

And that wisdom is immediately given a definition, which the section would be poorer without: “do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is” (v.17). To understand the will of the Lord is to grasp what he has already made plain about the kind of person he is making, and then to live from that grasp. The wise life is not the one that guessed correctly. It is the one that is doing what it already knows.

The contrast Paul draws between drunkenness and fullness of the Spirit is one of the most theologically provocative contrasts in the letter. He is not simply contrasting vice and virtue, or bad behaviour and good. He is contrasting two kinds of fullness — two ways of trying to transcend the ordinary, to escape the limitations of sober consciousness, to find ecstasy. Wine offers dissolution — the loss of self, the blurring of edges, the temporary escape from sobriety into sensation. The Spirit offers something entirely different: not the loss of self but the fullness of self as God intended it, overflowing with a joy that is oriented outward, that expresses itself in song and gratitude and the mutual submission that makes genuine community possible.

The Spirit-filled life Paul describes is intensely communal in its expression. It erupts in singing — “psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (v.19) — a rich triad suggesting the full range of musical and devotional expression available to the church. It issues in “giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” — a gratitude so comprehensive that nothing is excluded from its scope. And it produces “submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ” — the mutual humility that Paul will apply to marriage, family, and household in the verses that follow. The Spirit-filled community looks and sounds different from the world around it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fullness of the Spirit and the Worshipping Community

“Be filled with the Spirit” (v.18) is a present passive imperative — go on being filled, continuously, repeatedly. The fullness of the Spirit is not a one-time crisis experience; it is the ongoing reality of a life open to and dependent on God's Spirit. The passive voice is significant: we do not fill ourselves; we are filled. We create the conditions — prayer, the word, corporate worship, obedience — and God does the filling. The Spirit is given to those who ask (Luke 11:13), and the asking is to be persistent, humble, and expectant.

The triad of “psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (v.19) has been the subject of considerable historical discussion about the nature of Christian worship. What matters more than the categorisation is the character: the worship is corporate, directed toward God, spirit-animated, joyful, and overflowing into the rest of life. Worship is not an event on Sunday that is unrelated to life on Monday; it is the expression of a fullness that shapes everything the Spirit-filled person does.

The closing imperative — “submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ” (v.21) — is the theological hinge on which everything that follows turns. Paul will apply mutual submission to wives and husbands, children and fathers, servants and masters. But the foundation is the mutual submission of the Spirit-filled community: a posture of other-centredness, of preferring one another, of deferring in love to the needs and preferences of those around us. This is the overflow of a life that has been filled with the Spirit of the One who “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself” (Philippians 2:6–7).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Several of the cults of Ephesus, above all that of Dionysus, were soaked in wine, in ecstatic states, in the pursuit of transcendence through altered consciousness. The Dionysian festivals were characterized by drunkenness and sexual abandon as means of communing with the divine. Against this entire religious culture, Paul offers the Spirit-filled community as the true alternative: not the dissipation of Dionysus but the fullness of the Holy Spirit, not the frantic ecstasy of the cult but the joyful, ordered, outward-facing overflow of a community that has been possessed not by wine but by God. The church was, in Ephesus, a genuinely countercultural gathering — a community whose worship looked and sounded like nothing else in the city.

Now: We live in an age of spiritual hunger and an age of extraordinary means for filling the void — entertainment, substance, distraction, the endless dopamine of the digital feed. None of it satisfies. The hunger returns, more insistent than before. Paul's word to a hungry generation is unchanged: be filled with the Spirit. The fullness he gives is not the temporary satiation of appetite but the genuine, overflowing, outward-directed joy of a life in which God himself has taken up residence. The church that is genuinely, visibly, joyfully full of the Spirit — that sings with gratitude, that submits in love, that gives thanks for everything — is offering the watching world a glimpse of what it was made for.

verseByVerse.quote: Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil.” Live deliberately, with attention, because the age runs against you.

A surgeon does not walk into an operating theatre the way she walks into a supermarket: not anxious, but trained, focused, aware of what each moment needs. Paul asks for that attention across the whole of life — not anxiety, but wakefulness; not frantic busyness, but refusal to drift. And because the days are evil, the current runs against you; a boat on a river does not stay still by doing nothing. This is a warning against the life that just happens, where years pass and chances to pray, speak a word for Christ, serve or invest in someone’s faith slip by unconsidered. No one decides to waste his life; the unwise simply never decide not to. “Teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom” (Psalm 90:12).

Buying up the time. “Making the best use” (exagorazomenoi) is a merchant’s word — to buy up, purchase out of the market, the root behind “redemption”. Every purchase costs something. Time cannot be saved, only spent, and you cannot make more. So you are buying continuously, whether or not you are choosing, with the only non-renewable thing you own. The man who says he has no time to pray has not run out of time; he has bought something else with it.

Opportunities close. The word for time here is kairos, the right moment, not clock time — and opportunities have expiry dates. The conversation with an ageing parent while he can still follow it; the neighbour who moves next year; the friend in crisis who is soft and asking questions now and in eighteen months will have rebuilt his defences; the child at the age when he still wants your company. None of these announces its closing time. That is why Paul says buy it up, as you buy something you have noticed is about to leave the market.

Not hurry. This verse is often drafted into service for something Paul is not saying. Redeeming the time is not maximising output. Jesus was never in a hurry: with the weight of the world on him, he stopped for a blind man on the road (Mark 10:46–52) and slept in a boat in a storm (Mark 4:38). A frantic life and a wasted life can be equally unredeemed; the busiest person you know may be spending his whole allowance on nothing. The question is not how much you got through today, but what you bought.

So name one person God has put within reach whose window is closing — parent, neighbour, friend, child, the colleague who has started asking. Then name what has actually been buying up your evenings this month. Set the two side by side, and the price becomes visible.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.” The wise life is steered not by what is convenient or what everyone else does, but by the question: what does the Lord want here? That understanding comes through Scripture, the Spirit and the counsel of God’s people.

Two senses of “God’s will”. Christians agonise over this phrase more than almost any other, and most of the anguish comes from confusing two senses Scripture uses. There is God’s hidden will: his sovereign plan for what will actually happen. It governs everything and is not published. You do not know whether you will get the job, marry that person, or be alive next year. “The secret things belong to the LORD our God” (Deuteronomy 29:29). And there is God’s revealed will: what he has plainly told us he wants, which fills the Bible and is not in the least mysterious.

Notice where we spend our energy. Most of what people mean by “finding God’s will” concerns the hidden will — which house, which career, which person — and the fear of missing the one right path and living outside it ever after. But that will was never given to you to read. Meanwhile the revealed will lies open on the desk and is often the thing least attended to. Scripture is direct about it: “this is the will of God, your sanctification” (1 Thessalonians 4:3); “give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you” (1 Thessalonians 5:18); “this is the will of God, that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people” (1 Peter 2:15).

That changes the whole exercise, mercifully. God’s will is not a hidden dot you must find and are ruined for missing. It is a direction he has already described in detail, and a person he is making you into. The one who is pursuing holiness, giving thanks, telling the truth, loving his wife and doing good work is in God’s will, whichever of two reasonable job offers he takes. And Scripture never tells an anxious believer how to divine the hidden will; it tells him to obey the revealed one, and discernment for the genuinely open questions grows out of that obedience (v. 10).

So if you are stuck, change the question. Not “What is the one thing God wants me to do?” but “What has God already made clear, and am I doing it?” Most people who cannot hear God on the big decision have a small one outstanding that they can hear perfectly well.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit.” Instead of being controlled by wine, be continually filled with God’s Spirit. In Ephesus wine was central to ecstatic cults that sought spiritual experience through intoxication; Paul rejects the counterfeit. “Debauchery” (asōtia) is the reckless life without restraint, the word used of the prodigal son’s “reckless living” (Luke 15:13).

Does this forbid all alcohol? No. Paul forbids drunkenness, being controlled by wine, not wine itself. Scripture calls wine a gift, “wine to gladden the heart of man” (Psalm 104:15); Jesus made wine at Cana and drank it (John 2:1–11; Luke 7:34); and Paul told Timothy to “use a little wine” for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23). But freedom has limits. A Christian should not drink in a way that harms himself or causes a brother to stumble (Romans 14:21), and some, because of their own weakness, their family or their witness, will wisely choose not to drink at all.

“Be filled.” The command is present and passive: keep on being filled. Yesterday’s filling does not cover today; it is more like breathing than a reservoir topped up once. To be filled is to be controlled and energised by the Spirit as a sail is filled by wind. It is not a second blessing received once or an ecstatic experience detached from ordinary life. It is the Spirit who already lives in every believer (Romans 8:9) given full control, rather than being grieved (4:30) or quenched (1 Thessalonians 5:19).

If it is passive, why a list of things to do? The sail answers it. A sail cannot make wind, and no effort in a flat calm will move the boat an inch. But a sail can be raised or left furled, and that is the sailor’s business. So: stop grieving the Spirit through unconfessed sin (1 John 1:9); stop quenching his promptings; stop numbing the inner life with substitutes — entertainment, busyness, any socially acceptable intoxication that fills the space he means to fill. And raise the canvas: ask — “how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” (Luke 11:13); immerse yourself in Scripture; worship; obey the prompting you already have; stay among God’s people.

Word and Spirit. Compare the twin letter. Here: be filled with the Spirit — speaking in psalms, hymns and songs, singing, giving thanks, submitting (vv. 18–21). In Colossians: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly” — teaching in psalms, hymns and songs, singing, giving thanks, then wives and husbands (Colossians 3:16–18). Same results, same order, almost the same words; only the cause is named differently. These are not two separate attainments, one ordinary and one rare. They describe one reality, because the Spirit wrote the word and works through it. So someone who wants to be filled with the Spirit and does not know where to begin is not left waiting for a mood: get the word of Christ into you richly.

How would I know? Paul does not send you inward to check your feelings. He gives the evidence in the next three verses, all external: song, thanksgiving “always and for everything”, and submitting to others — the least likely product of any counterfeit. That is why the comparison with drunkenness fits: no one needs to be told when a man is drunk; it shows in how he speaks and treats people. The Spirit’s filling should be every bit as visible. If you want to know which is filling you, do not consult your feelings. Ask the people who live with you.

verseByVerse.quote: addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Spirit-filled church sings — “addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart” — and gives thanks “always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Worship runs two ways: to the Lord, and to one another.

The three kinds of song, and two disputes. The Reformed tradition has treated the Psalms as the church’s God-given hymnbook, and some hold they are the only proper sung praise, reading “hymns and spiritual songs” as further names for the Psalms — a serious position; all three words appear in the Greek Old Testament’s psalm titles, so the tidy three-category scheme cannot be pressed hard. But Paul names three kinds of song here and in Colossians 3:16, and the New Testament itself contains Christian songs about Christ (v. 14; Philippians 2:6–11; 1 Timothy 3:16). The more likely reading is that the church may sing the Psalms and also new songs faithful to Scripture, so long as the word of Christ dwells richly in them. And instruments? Some Reformed churches sing unaccompanied, holding that the New Testament gives no warrant for them. But “with your heart” does not forbid instruments; it locates where the music must begin. The Psalms call God’s people to praise him “with lute and harp” (Psalm 150:3), and nothing in the New Testament withdraws that. Instruments help singing; they do not replace it. Notice that Paul himself does nothing with the categories — no definitions, no repertoire rules. What interests him is the direction the singing travels.

To one another. Sunday singing is not a room of individuals each having a private moment with God. Paul says you sing to each other, “teaching and admonishing one another” (Colossians 3:16). That is why the congregation matters to the man in the third row who could not have said one true thing about God that morning. His marriage is coming apart, or he buried someone on Tuesday, and the words will not come. He does not have to produce them; they are being sung over him by people who can manage it this week. And think of the worst week of your life and what came to you at three in the morning. For most people it is not a paragraph from a sermon but a line from something they have sung a hundred times, arriving with its tune, carrying doctrine into a mind too tired to reason. What you sing is what you will believe when you cannot think.

To the Lord, with your heart. The verb for “making melody” originally meant to pluck a string, and the instrument Paul names is you. If you have a poor voice, or were told long ago that you cannot sing, the Lord is listening to the instrument, and yours is in tune; no one is disqualified by his larynx. But equally, “with your heart” is no licence to stand silent and call it inward worship, because the other half of the verse requires that someone can hear you.

“Always and for everything.” Any reader who has buried a child, sat with a scan result or watched a marriage end may stop here and ask whether this can mean what it says. It does not mean calling evil good; Scripture never asks you to call a tumour a blessing or a betrayal a gift, and God himself calls evil evil. Nor does it mean grief is a failure of faith; roughly a third of the Psalms are laments, and God put “How long, O LORD?” in the church’s hymnbook permanently. What makes the command possible is the next phrase: thanks is given “to God the Father” — not to fate or the universe, but to a Father who chose you (1:4) and adopted you (1:5). You are not asked to believe that everything that happens is good, but that nothing reaches you except through his hands, and that he can take what was meant to destroy you and make it serve you. “We know that for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28) — we know, which you can still say with your face wet. So take a smaller step if you must. You may not be able to say “thank you for this”. You may be able to say “thank you that you are still my Father in this” — the same thanksgiving offered from further back. And this verse describes what a filled life eventually overflows into; it was never meant to be handed to a grieving person as an instruction. Job, having lost everything, said, “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21). He did not bless the loss; he blessed the Name. That is the distinction: not gratitude for the wreckage, but gratitude, in the wreckage, to a Father who has not moved.

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” is not a password added to make prayers valid. A name stands for the whole person. To give thanks in Jesus’ name is to come through him as the one Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5), on his authority as children admitted by his invitation (John 16:24), and in line with his character and purposes (John 14:13–14). Even “thank you, Father, for this meal” rests on the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.” This is the fourth mark of the Spirit-filled life (vv. 18–21) and the hinge into the household instructions that follow (5:22–6:9).

The grammar. “Submitting” is a participle, the last of a chain hanging from the single command of verse 18: be filled with the Spirit — speaking, singing, giving thanks, submitting. Two of the four are what we would expect (song and thanks); the other two concern how you treat the person next to you. And verse 22 has no verb in Greek; it borrows “submit” from verse 21. So the marriage passage is grammatically welded to the filling of the Spirit, and detaching it is misusing it. No one here is told to be filled with the Spirit so that he may govern his household; a household ordered like this is what the filling looks like when it reaches the kitchen.

The word. Hypotassō was originally military: to arrange under, to take one’s ordered place. Two things must be said. It says nothing about worth: the Son submits to the Father and will hand over the kingdom to him (1 Corinthians 15:28), and no Christian has concluded that the Son is a lesser God. Equal in being, ordered in relation — drawn from the life of God himself. And it is voluntary: submission is given; no one can submit someone else. A man who sets out to make another person submit has made it impossible, and shown that what he wants is control.

How mutual? Egalitarian readers argue that “one another” means every Christian submits to every other, so husbands submit to wives as wives to husbands, and that verse 22, borrowing its verb from verse 21, cannot then mean something different. But in the instructions that follow, submission always runs one way: wives to husbands, children to parents, slaves to masters (5:22–6:9); husbands are never told to submit to their wives but to love them, and Paul grounds the husband’s headship not in culture but in Christ and the church (vv. 23–25). The better reading is that “one another” means each to those God has placed over him, all with the humility of Christ. The distinctions are real, and mutual humility governs how each is lived.

What every first reader would have felt. Ancient household codes addressed the head of the house about how to manage his wife, children and slaves. Paul addresses the wife, the child and the slave first and directly, as responsible people who answer to Christ themselves. And when he turns to the one with power, he asks more of him, not less: the husband gets three times as many lines as the wife, and is commanded to love as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. Whatever else is true of the structure, the weight of cost runs downhill toward the strong.

“Out of reverence for Christ” is both the limit and the engine. The limit: submission here is never mere convention, never fear of the other person, and never the self-erasure that lets evil continue; because it is reverence for Christ, it cannot require what Christ forbids. The engine: you yield not because the other person has earned it, but before the face of the Lord who yielded everything — which is why the real test is not what you do when submission is deserved, but what you do when it is not.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From the Spirit-filled community of mutual submission (v. 21), Paul descends into the most intimate community of all — marriage — and what he finds there is not merely a domestic arrangement to be governed by wise principles but a living, breathing proclamation of the gospel itself. His disclosure in v. 32 — “this mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church” — reveals that marriage was never merely about human beings. It was always a sign pointing beyond itself to the most magnificent love story in the universe. Every faithful Christian marriage is a living icon of the gospel.

The wife is called to submit to her own husband, as to the Lord (vv. 22–24) — a role, not a rank, freely given and bounded by Christ. The husband is called to love his wife as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (v. 25) — headship defined by the cross, aimed at her holiness and flourishing (vv. 26–27), and lived out as care for his own flesh (vv. 28–31). The section closes with the double summary of v. 33: the husband loves, the wife respects — each addressed at the point of their deepest calling.

The household code tradition (Haustafeln): Paul engages a well-established literary genre — Aristotle, the Stoics, Hellenistic Jewish writers all taught household management through three pairs: husband/wife, parent/child, master/slave. Paul uses the same structure but transforms it radically: he addresses the subordinate party first (giving them full moral standing as agents accountable to Christ); grounds every command in Christ rather than nature or social utility; gives the longer and more demanding command to the dominant party; and embeds the entire code in mutual submission (v. 21). The form is conventional; the content is a quiet revolution.
verseByVerse.theology:
Marriage, Headship, and the Gospel Mystery

Ephesians 5:22–33 is the most theologically freighted passage on marriage in all of Scripture. Its central claim — that marriage is a living image of the relationship between Christ and the church — elevates the institution beyond any merely human social arrangement. Marriage is a sign. Its structure (the husband's headship, the wife's willing embrace of it) is not arbitrary or culturally conditioned; it images something real and eternal: the self-giving authority of Christ over his church, and the church's joyful, trusting response to her Lord.

The husband's headship is defined entirely by the cross: “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (v.25). Any interpretation of headship that does not immediately move to sacrifice and self-giving has misread the passage. The head of the church is the one who died for it, who washed it, who nourishes and cherishes it (v.29). The husband who exercises headship in this mode is not dominating but descending — following the pattern of the One who “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28).

The wife's calling — to “submit to your own husband, as to the Lord” (v.22) — is the free, willing, graced response of a woman who is secure in Christ. It is not coerced compliance; it is the image of the church's joyful response to her loving Lord. This mutual imaging of the gospel — husband as Christ, wife as church — requires both partners to draw from wells deeper than themselves. No man can love his wife as Christ loved the church from his own resources; no woman can embody the church's response to Christ on her own. Both require the same Spirit who filled the community in v.18. Marriage is a Spirit-dependent vocation for both.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In the Greco-Roman world, the husband's authority over his wife was nearly absolute and assumed to be primarily for his benefit. The paterfamilias was the household's lord in every sense. Paul's command for husbands to love their wives sacrificially — to give themselves up for them, to nourish and cherish them as their own bodies — was not a reinforcement of existing cultural norms. It was their radical subversion. The Roman husband used his authority to be served. The Christian husband was to use his authority to serve. This was not a minor adjustment to the household code; it was a revolution grounded in the cross.

Now: Christian marriage swims against two powerful currents simultaneously. The first is the culture's dismissal of permanent covenant — the reduction of marriage to an expressive partnership that may be dissolved when it no longer meets individual needs. The second is the sometimes shallow version of complementarianism that invokes headship without the cross, demanding submission without offering service. Against both, Ephesians 5 offers the third way: covenant love, shaped by the cross, sustained by the Spirit, oriented toward the other's flourishing, and pointing always beyond itself to the love that holds the universe together. A marriage like this is a miracle — and miracles point to a Miracle Worker.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord.” The verb is carried over from verse 21: wives are called to the same posture Paul urges on all believers, now applied in marriage — and “as to the Lord”, because it is finally obedience to Christ, who ordered marriage this way. The husband’s authority is borrowed and bounded.

What it is. A wife willingly honours her husband’s God-given leadership — supporting him and deferring to him in the ordering of the household — not grudgingly but as a gift; trust, not passivity. She is no silent, opinionless presence. She brings her full wisdom, gifts and voice, and a good husband depends on them. But where agreement cannot be reached, she trusts the structure God has given rather than insisting on her own way. It speaks of role, never worth: in Christ “there is no male and female” as to standing before God (Galatians 3:28), just as the Son submits to the Father without being lesser (1 Corinthians 11:3).

What it is not. Not inferiority. Not blind obedience to sin: “as to the Lord” means that if a husband asks her to sin, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Not enduring abuse: nothing here requires a wife to remain in danger; a husband who abuses his wife is not exercising headship but violating it catastrophically, and the church’s duty is to protect her, not bind her. Not voicelessness (Proverbs 31 pictures a woman of great competence and influence). And not a burden uniquely hers: it follows the call to all believers to submit (v. 21) and precedes the far heavier charge to the husband to love as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (v. 25). If the wife is called to submit, the husband is called to die.

“Your own husbands.” Paul does not say women are to submit to men. A wife submits to her own husband — one man, the one she made promises to. The verse has been stretched far past that boundary, to imply that women owe deference to men in general at work, in the street or in the church foyer. Nothing of the kind is here.

In practice it is mostly the texture of ordinary life: not undermining him in front of the children, speaking well of him, choosing to trust after her voice has been fully heard. Suppose a husband is offered a significant post in another city. His wife is deeply reluctant — her friendships, her work, her ageing parents are all here. They talk it through honestly, and he still believes they should go. Submission is not being overruled without a voice; it is choosing to trust his judgment after her concerns have been genuinely weighed, and not letting the decision harden into a permanent grievance — while he carries the weight of it and owes her every sacrifice to make it work.

The harder case. That example assumes a husband who listens and carries the cost. Many women are not in that marriage. Their husband is not abusive — that guard stands absolutely — but he is spiritually passive, self-absorbed, or simply not leading anything: he will not pray with her, lets every hard decision drift until it decides itself, and is present in the house but absent from the marriage. Scripture does not pretend she does not exist. Peter writes to her: “even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives, when they see your respectful and pure conduct” (1 Peter 3:1–2). He treats the situation as common enough to address, and tells her that her steady life has power in it, and that God can use it to reach a man sermons have not reached. That is not a consolation prize; it is a real assignment, harder than the one given to wives of good men.

The counterfeit. Submission is easy to counterfeit: compliance with the heart withheld — doing what was decided while making sure he knows what it cost you; going along with it and then being conspicuously unhelpful about the consequences; a silence that is not peace but accounting. So the question is not whether you did what was agreed, but whether you did it in a way that left him freer or heavier. And it can be done even when he has not earned it because of the phrase the verse hangs on: “as to the Lord”. You are not finally handing yourself over to his judgment, but trusting the Lord who ordered this, who sees what it costs, and who has never asked a wife to submit without himself standing behind her.

verseByVerse.quote: For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul grounds the husband’s headship in Christ’s headship of the church — and the comparison both establishes that authority and radically reshapes it. Christ is head as the church’s Saviour, who gave himself for her and nourishes and cherishes her (v. 29). Headship is servant leadership, cross-shaped from the start. And “in everything” does not mean obedience without limit: the church submits to Christ, not to anyone who contradicts him, and no husband may command what the Lord forbids.

What headship means. Taking ultimate responsibility: when things go wrong, the head does not look for someone to blame but asks what he failed to do. Adam’s sin was that he stood by, silent and passive, when he should have led (Genesis 3:6), and God came looking for him first (Genesis 3:9). Initiating love rather than waiting for it, as Christ loved us while we were enemies (Romans 5:8). Leading the spiritual life of the home in prayer and the word, rather than delegating it to his wife as “her department”. And making decisions shaped by service: not “I lead, therefore I decide”, but “I lead, therefore I bear the cost of this for her sake”, having genuinely listened and weighed her good as heavily as his own.

What it does not mean. Not autocracy: a wise husband draws on his wife’s wisdom and makes many decisions together. Not spiritual superiority: she may be the more mature and discerning; headship is a role, not a certificate. Not an authority that overrides Scripture: it is entirely borrowed from Christ and answerable to him. Not silencing her: a husband who hears her honest disagreement as a threat is protecting his ego, not exercising headship; Christ is not threatened by the church’s questions. And not comfort but cost: if he is resting while she is exhausted, pursuing his interests while hers go unmet, he is not leading but being served.

In real life. Picture a decent, hard-working husband who provides well and is rarely harsh, but is largely absent from the spiritual life of the home. He does not pray with his wife or lead the children, and when she speaks of her loneliness he listens for a few minutes and moves on. He holds the position without bearing the cost. Headship would look different: he starts the hard conversation before she has to; he owns his absence as his failure; he begins, awkwardly, to pray with her; he makes choices that replenish her rather than assuming she will manage. It needs no new personality — only the decision to lead as Christ leads, turning toward rather than away.

“And is himself its Savior.” Here Paul marks the limit of his analogy. The husband is head as Christ is head; he is not Saviour. He cannot atone, forgive sin or be the ground of her standing before God. That diagnoses two mirror-image failures. There is the wife who has made her husband her saviour — needing him to finally make her feel secure, valuable and at peace — and so finds him failing at a job he was never given. No man can carry another soul’s ultimate hope; he will collapse under it or resent her for it. And there is the husband who has taken that role on, believing he must fix and complete her, and ends up exhausted or controlling, because a man who thinks he is responsible for someone’s salvation will eventually think he is entitled to manage her life. The clause frees them both.

“As the church submits to Christ.” The church does not submit to Christ to secure his love, or to a Lord whose intentions are unproven. She responds to one who has already given himself for her entirely. A husband who wants the response while withholding its ground has inverted the analogy he quotes. A man who has to remind his wife that he is the head is like a man who has to remind people he is funny. Christ never told the church to submit to him; he washed feet (John 13:5) and went to a cross, and the church has followed him ever since.

A note on “head”. Scholars debate whether kephalē in Paul means authority or source (as a river has a head); both senses appear in Greek of the period. Here the more likely sense is authority, exercised in love: the head is the one to whom the wife submits as the church does to Christ (v. 24), as God made Christ “head over all things” (1:22); and in 1 Corinthians 11:3 “the head of Christ is God” cannot mean that the Father is the Son’s source of being. But Paul does not leave the word to a dictionary. He defines it himself, in the next verses, with a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.” The husband receives the longer and harder instruction, and his love is measured by the cross. The verb is agapaō, self-giving covenant love, not sentiment. And Paul does not say “lead your wives” first, but “love” them; the leadership exists to serve her flourishing.

How strange this was. Ancient household codes told the head of the house how to rule his wife, children and slaves. None told a husband to love his wife as a Saviour gave himself up. Marriage was understood as being for property, heirs, alliances and an orderly household; a wife’s affection was a pleasant extra. So the men in Ephesus braced for the usual instruction on managing their households and heard instead a command none of them had heard before: love her the way God loved people who wanted him dead.

What was the church like? Paul has told us: dead in trespasses, following the world and the prince of the power of the air, children of wrath (2:1–3). That is the bride. He did not find her radiant and decide she was worth it; he gave himself up for her in that condition, and the radiance came afterwards (vv. 26–27). The love does not respond to loveliness; it produces it. So “when she is easier to live with”, “when she stops doing that” and “when she deserves it” are, in this passage, arguments for withholding the very thing that would change the situation. Christ did not wait for a bride worth dying for. He died, and so got one.

In an ordinary week. This towering standard is for Tuesdays. It looks like noticing what she carries and moving to relieve it without being asked — she has had a hard week with the children, and he takes over the evening without comment. It looks like giving up his preferences cheerfully, without the pointed silence that makes her feel guilty for asking. It looks like taking her walk with God seriously: praying for her, asking how she is doing with the Lord (v. 26). It looks like choosing her above career and comfort when they truly conflict. And it looks like asking forgiveness promptly and specifically: “I was unkind this morning, and I am sorry. Will you forgive me?” — with no “but you also…”. Repeated over years, that builds a marriage in which she knows she is safe with him.

The test. The standard is not “provide” but “gave himself up”. Providing can be done without surrendering anything a man wanted; a lot of hard work is quietly self-serving, and long hours can be escape dressed as devotion. So the question is not what you supply but what you have given up. Name something — an ambition, a promotion, a friendship, a hobby, a Saturday, a picture of the life you expected — that you surrendered in the last year for her flourishing rather than your own. If nothing comes to mind, this verb is not yet operating in your marriage, however well the household is run.

Where the power comes from. If you have been measuring yourself against Calvary, the reasonable conclusion is despair — and it is half right. You cannot love like this, and the standard is not lowered. But this command does not stand alone. The whole household code grows out of one imperative: “be filled with the Spirit” (v. 18). This is the filled life reaching the home: fruit, not an entrance requirement. So the question for a husband who keeps failing is not chiefly “how do I try harder?” — he has tried in bursts for years, and the bursts are the problem — but whether the man who comes through the door at six is being filled. A marriage is largely lived on the overflow, and nothing pours out of a life that was never filled. A husband whose praying has dried up and whose Bible has been shut for months will find that the tenderness he intends is simply not available at seven on a Thursday when he is tired and she says the wrong thing. That locates the failure without excusing it. And there is comfort here. If this love were a matter of temperament, naturally warm men would have an advantage no one else could make up. It is fruit, and fruit grows on a branch because the branch is attached (John 15:4–5). The husband who grew up where no one said anything kind, with no model for this at all, is not disqualified. He is asked to stay attached, which he can do. The command was never addressed to your willpower, but to a man who is being filled — and that filling is asked for, not achieved (Luke 11:13).

verseByVerse.quote: that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ gave himself for the church “that he might sanctify her… so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle” — holy and without blemish. The purpose of his self-giving is her holiness now and her perfection at the last.

“The washing of water with the word.” This phrase is a chief text for baptismal regeneration — the teaching that the water of baptism itself washes away sin and gives new birth. But look at what Paul joins to the water: the word. The cleansing agent is the gospel received by faith; baptism is its outward sign and seal, not its cause. “Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John 15:3); God cleansed the Gentiles’ hearts “by faith” (Acts 15:9); we are born again “through the living and abiding word of God” (1 Peter 1:23). That is why Simon the magician could be baptised (Acts 8:13) and still be “in the gall of bitterness” (Acts 8:23), while the thief on the cross, never baptised, went that day to paradise (Luke 23:43). The water shows outwardly what the word does within. To merge the two is to trust the picture instead of the gospel it pictures.

Spot and wrinkle. They are not the same defect twice. A spot is a stain — something that landed on her from outside. A wrinkle is not contamination but wear — what comes with time, of things having gone on too long. Christ removes both: the sin and the weariness, the guilt and the exhaustion. That is worth hearing if what you feel about yourself is less like dirtiness and more like fatigue. He is not only washing his bride; he is making her new (Revelation 21:5).

“To himself.” In an ordinary wedding of that world the bride was prepared by others and presented to the groom. Here the groom does both. He prepares her himself and receives her himself, which tells you what all this costly labour is for: not repairing a damaged asset out of duty, but getting her ready because he wants her. It was “for the joy that was set before him” that he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2). You are looking at the joy.

What this means for husbands — and a warning. A husband who loves like Christ sets before himself not a programme of control but a vision of his wife’s holiness and flourishing. Think of a wife who grew up under a critical father, whose self-image was worn down early, who dismisses her own gifts and struggles to believe God loves her. Her husband makes it his slow mission to speak truth into exactly those places: when she waves off a gift, he names specifically what he sees in her; when she doubts God’s love after a hard season, he opens Scripture with her, not to win an argument but to wash her with the word; he prays over her by name, against the particular lies she has confessed to him. He is not her therapist or pastor, but her husband. But this passage is easily misused. A husband reads that Christ sanctifies his bride and appoints himself his wife’s spiritual improver — noticing faults, correcting theology, holding up the standard until she rises to it. The passage will not carry it. Christ sanctifies his bride because “he gave himself up for her”; the cross is the method. He does not cleanse her by cataloguing her blemishes but at his own expense. So ask: when you think about your wife’s growth, which list comes more readily — the things that need to change in her, or the things it will cost you to help her flourish? A wife is rarely made radiant by being told what is wrong with her. She is often made radiant by being loved at cost by a man who has stopped keeping score.
verseByVerse.note: Before a wedding the bride was washed and adorned.

parallels.desc: I bathed you with water

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself.” In marriage the two become one flesh (v. 31), so to love your wife is, in a real sense, to love yourself, and to neglect or wound her is to injure yourself.

The argument. Paul nowhere commands a man to love himself; he assumes it and builds on it. That is safe, because self-love is the one form of love that needs no instruction. No one has ever needed reminding to notice his own hunger. So the command is not “rise to a standard beyond you”, but “you already have exactly the competence required, and you use it a hundred times a day in one direction — transfer it.” A man does not ignore a pain in his shoulder because he is busy, dismiss his own hunger because it is inconvenient, or tell his body it is being oversensitive. He attends to it, because it is his.

In real life. James has been so absorbed in a demanding season at work that he has not noticed Sarah pulling back for three weeks: quieter at dinner, slower to reach for him, carrying something he has not asked about. He tells himself she is fine and he will check in when things ease. He would never reason that way about a pain in his own chest. One flesh means her withdrawal is his signal and her heaviness his concern. The husband who understands this stops asking “are you okay?” as a formality and starts asking it as a real question — and waits for the real answer. So the test is exact: if her needs got the same automatic, unprompted, unresented attention your own hunger, tiredness and pain receive, would she be better cared for than she is now? Most of us know the answer within a second, and the second is uncomfortable.

Two standards that are one. In verse 25 the measure is Christ’s love for the church, impossibly high; here it is a man’s love for his own body, close at hand. They turn out to be the same: the church is Christ’s body (1:23; 5:30). When Christ loved the church he was loving his own body; when a husband loves his wife as his own body, he is doing what Christ did.

For the man this does not fit. Some people do not love themselves at all — they neglect their bodies and speak of themselves with contempt — and “as his own body” measures little for them. Do not conclude that your wife should expect the same neglect you give yourself. Paul has given the deeper standard, which does not depend on your self-regard: love her as Christ loved the church. The self-love argument is his shortcut for the ordinary case; the cross is the measure when the shortcut fails.

verseByVerse.quote: For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, because we are members of his body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one hates his own flesh; he “nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, because we are members of his body.” A husband is to feed and warm his wife as he naturally cares for himself — and as Christ cares for his people.

Two ordinary verbs. Ektrephō, nourish, means to feed something up to maturity; Paul uses it again for fathers who “bring them up” (6:4). It is the word for twenty years of meals, none of which looks like love. Thalpō, cherish, means literally to warm, as a mother bird keeps her young alive with the heat of her body, or as Paul was among the Thessalonians “like a nursing mother taking care of her own children” (1 Thessalonians 2:7). So the charge, stripped of decoration, is: feed her and keep her warm. Not rescue, correct or impress her — feed and warm.

How marriages actually fail. Paul does not say “do not hate her”; he treats that as too obvious to argue. He is writing to men who are simply not feeding their wives, and that is how most marriages fail: not in an atrocity, but in a slow drop in temperature no one could date. Ask her what is wrong and she cannot name one thing. He has never raised his hand or his voice, never been unfaithful; he works hard and the bills are paid. She would sound ridiculous complaining about him. And she has been cold for four years. Nothing was done to her; something was never done for her. So two tests. First: is she growing — not coping, growing? Name one way she is more alive, more herself, more at home with God than when you married, and your part in it. If she has been quietly shrinking — smaller opinions, fewer friends, shorter hopes, less laughter — you have not been nourishing her. Second, faster and impossible to cheat: what happens to her face in the two seconds after you come through the door? Not what she says — she has had years of practice at that — but her face, before she decides. Warmth is measured at the door.

“Just as Christ does the church.” Present tense. His giving himself up is finished (v. 25); his feeding and warming has not stopped for a day. He is not a husband who did something magnificent once and has coasted since. That matters if you have half suspected that Christ did something enormous for you long ago and has been broadly indifferent since. The cross is past tense; the nursing is present tense. And it answers the ache verse 27 can open: the church presented “without spot or wrinkle” — and then you look at your church and yourself and see spots and creases everywhere. Verse 27 is the presentation, still future; verse 29 is what he is doing meanwhile. He is not standing at the far end of the aisle with arms folded, waiting for you to make yourself presentable. He is at the near end, feeding you.

“Members of his body.” Not subjects or admirers, but limbs — parts of him. Saul of Tarsus never touched Jesus, yet when he persecuted Christians the risen Christ asked, “why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). Touch the hand, and the head says “me”. That makes this one of the safest truths in the letter. A body does not amputate a part for being weak; it reorganises around it, and a broken arm gets more attention than a sound one (1 Corinthians 12:22–26). For Christ to neglect you, he would have to neglect himself.

For the wife reading this as a list of what she lacks. You are not being greedy; God commands warmth, so wanting it is not weakness. Say so, plainly, to someone — a coldness this verse calls failure is not something you must absorb in silence — and if there is more than coldness in your home, tell someone who can act. But you have not gone without nourishing altogether. Christ has been feeding you all along, in ways you may have filed under something else: the friend who rang on the wrong day for the right reason, the verse that went in like warmth, the strength that came in the morning for a day you dreaded. You may be underfed at home. You have never been unfed. And the husband is left with less excuse and more resource: he is not asked to manufacture a tenderness he has never seen, only to pass on the warmth he is already being kept in.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 — “a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh” — the creation charter of marriage, spoken by God before sin entered the world.

“Therefore.” Paul has just said we are members of Christ’s body (v. 30), and to support it he quotes a verse about a wedding. That only works if Genesis 2:24 was about Christ and the church all along, which he says outright in the next verse. So marriage is not a human arrangement to which the church later attached a religious illustration. It was designed, in the week the world was made, with the gospel already in view. And notice who first heard the sentence: Adam had no father or mother to leave. It is legislation for everyone after him, given before there was a child or a sin to correct. Marriage is not a repair issued after things went wrong; it is original equipment.

One flesh. More than sexual union, though it includes it: a total, exclusive, covenant union. Physical — sexual union is the sign and seal of the covenant, which is why even union with a prostitute makes “one flesh” (1 Corinthians 6:16): the act signs a covenant that is not there. Relational — two lives intertwined, so that his failure touches her and her suffering is his; the husband who says “that’s her problem” has not understood what he became. Covenantal — witnessed by God and binding (Malachi 2:14), not dissolved by distance or fading feeling. Exclusive — one man, one woman. But it does not erase identity; each keeps his or her own personality, gifts and walk with God. It does not mean unbroken harmony; two sinners face conflict together. And it is not achieved instantly: the covenant is made at the wedding, but the deep knowing and trust are built over years of choosing each other.

Leave. The instruction most quietly ignored in Christian marriages, and it is not mainly about geography. A man can live four hundred miles from his mother and still be run by her, and his wife always knows. It looks like a decision made together on Tuesday and reopened on the phone on Wednesday; eleven years of Christmases arranged by someone else; a man who defends his wife to no one and explains her to everyone. Parents can refuse to release as firmly as sons refuse to go. So: when you and your wife decide something that disappoints your parents, whose disappointment do you feel more? And when something happens to you on a Thursday afternoon, whom do you tell first? Every wife knows the answer to that about her own marriage.

Hold fast. Proskollaō means to be glued. Glue two boards properly and try to separate them next day: they do not part at the join, which is now the strongest part; the wood tears, and each board comes away carrying fibres of the other. That explains why ending a marriage does not feel like ending an agreement. To the reader who has been divorced or left: this verse is not a fresh sentence on you but an explanation of the wound. You were not weak when it went on hurting long after others assumed you should have recovered. Something God joins had been pulled apart, and it tore and took part of you with it. Where the fault was yours, there is complete forgiveness in Christ; where it was done to you, God counts such tearing as violence (Malachi 2:16). Neither his love for you nor his use of you is reduced.

May a marriage ever end? God designed it for life: “What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate” (Matthew 19:6). But Jesus allows divorce for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9), and Paul allows it when an unbelieving spouse deserts (1 Corinthians 7:15). Some Christians hold that remarriage is never permitted while a former spouse lives; others allow it more widely. The more likely reading is that in cases of adultery or desertion the innocent party is free to remarry, though reconciliation is better wherever possible.

And every clause was fulfilled before it was obeyed. The Son left his Father’s glory — “I came from the Father and have come into the world” (John 16:28). He holds fast to a bride who has let go of him a thousand times. And he took flesh to become one with her. Christian marriage is a picture, and the original holds even in the weeks when the copy does not.

parallels.desc: a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife

verseByVerse.quote: This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.” The one-flesh union of Genesis 2 was always a picture of Christ and his people. That does not make marriage less real; it makes it more glorious.

The whole Bible. God called himself Israel’s husband — “your Maker is your husband” (Isaiah 54:5) — wooed her back through Hosea (Hosea 2:19–20), and grieved her unfaithfulness as a wounded spouse. Scripture opens with a wedding in a garden and closes with “the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9). Everything between is, in one sense, the story of a Bridegroom coming for his Bride.

“Mystery” in Paul is not an unsolved puzzle but a secret God has chosen to tell: “hidden for ages and generations but now revealed” (Colossians 1:26; see 3:3–5). In a city where mystery cults sold their secrets to initiates, Paul’s mystery is read aloud to ordinary people, and its point is that outsiders have been let in.

Is marriage a sacrament? The Latin Bible translated mystērion as sacramentum, and in time marriage was counted among the sacraments of the Roman Catholic Church. The instinct — that marriage is holy — is right. But the Greek word does not carry that meaning, and Paul is not making marriage a means of grace; he is telling us what an Old Testament verse was about. The Reformed reading honours marriage as a sign of great dignity without making the sign a channel of salvation. Marriage points to the gospel; it does not dispense it.

And the unmarried? Twelve verses on marriage climbing to this — what of the single man of forty who assumed he would be married by now, the widow, the woman whose husband left? Start with a striking fact: the Lord Jesus never married, and Paul, writing this, was unmarried (1 Corinthians 7:7–8). The two who understood this mystery most deeply had no experience of marriage and did not consider themselves impoverished. The most complete human life ever lived was a single one. More than that: if marriage is the sign, the union of Christ and the church is the reality, and every single Christian already has it in full — the same Bridegroom, on the same terms. No one gets a reduced share of Christ for want of a wedding. And “in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30), not because something good is withdrawn, but because signs come down when you arrive. Every earthly marriage ends, by its own vows, at a graveside; the marriage it pointed to never does. God said this first to the people the ancient world pitied most. To the eunuch, who could never marry or have children, he promised “a monument and a name better than sons and daughters… an everlasting name that shall not be cut off” (Isaiah 56:5). Better than sons and daughters: a promise of more, made to the person with least.

A guard. If every faithful marriage pictures the gospel, what does a bad marriage say about the gospel, and about me? Nothing about the gospel. A road sign knocked into a ditch does not move the city it points to. Your marriage is a picture of the gospel, not the gospel, and pictures can be poor without the original being any less. So ask the honest question without dread: if someone watched your marriage for a month, knowing nothing else about Christianity, what would they conclude about how Christ treats his people and how his people answer him? Ask it as a Christian, not as a defendant; the verdict on you was settled at the cross. God built into the world an institution most people would enter and all would witness, so that no generation would grow up without a living model of covenant love — and then he came and did in earnest what it had been rehearsing since the garden. Some are given the picture for a while. All of us are given the reality for ever.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

parallels.desc: your Maker is your husband

verseByVerse.quote: However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
