The soaring theology lands in two plain commands: “let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.” “However” brings Paul straight down from the mystery to a husband and wife who have to get through Tuesday. The glory is the reason for the practicalities, not an escape from them.

For the husband. He does not neglect his own hunger or tiredness. He is to give her the same attention — which for a man of few emotional words means learning to ask and stay: not “are you okay?” but “tell me how you’re actually doing”, then sitting with the answer rather than fixing it; showing affection before she has to signal for it; naming what he notices: “You seem heavy today. What’s going on?”

For the wife. Paul’s verb is the ordinary word for fear (phobeomai), here meaning reverence and honour. A man respected at home is freed to lead; a man regularly diminished retreats. In practice: holding back the correction in front of the children and saving it for a private moment; letting him make a low-stakes decision she thinks slightly wrong and not revisiting it; saying something admiring of him where he can hear it; telling him when he has led well — “That was a good call.” Respect is less a feeling than a practice, and a man, like anyone, tends to become more of what he is told he is.

“Each one.” Paul addresses two individuals separately, and attaches no conditions. He does not say “love your wife once she respects you”, or “respect your husband as soon as he loves you like Christ” — which is exactly what we would have written. That is the standard deadlock of struggling marriages. She is waiting for him to love her as verse 25 describes, and she is right to want it. He is waiting for her to respect him as verse 33 describes, and he is right to want it. Both are willing to move; both are waiting for evidence of movement first; and they can hold that position for eleven years, each sincerely reasonable. Paul cuts through it with two words. You cannot obey your half jointly; you can only obey it first. And there is a permanent temptation to become the household expert on your spouse’s half. A husband who can quote “let the wife see that she respects her husband” but cannot say, without looking, what he was told in the same breath is not studying Scripture; he is arming himself. Of the two halves of this verse, which have you thought about more this year? The half you were given is the only half you were given.

A caution about the pairing. It is broadly true and useful that many men are starved of respect and many women of tenderness. But that is an observation, not a law of nature. Do not deduce your spouse’s need from a diagram: ask which of the two she is actually short of, and believe the answer. And respect needs guarding just as headship did. It is not pretending, agreeing with everything, staying silent while something wrong goes unaddressed, or absorbing harm; the limits of verse 22 stand. What it governs is manner. The hardest sentence in a marriage can be said with honour or with contempt; the words may be nearly identical, and only one is obedience. A wife whose husband has given her little to admire is not asked to manufacture admiration she does not feel. She is asked to refuse contempt — which is possible on a bad day, and is often the last thing standing between a marriage and its end.

So the chapter that reached to the union of Christ and the church ends with two people who each have one thing to do tomorrow. The mystery gets enacted by a man who asks a second question at dinner and stays for the answer, and a woman who declines to say the sharp thing in front of the children. Neither will feel cosmic at the time. Both are.

6.title: Household Duties and the Armour of God
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. <sup>2</sup>“Honor your father and mother” (this is the first commandment with a promise), <sup>3</sup>“that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land.” <sup>4</sup>Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. <sup>5</sup>Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ, <sup>6</sup>not by the way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, <sup>7</sup>rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man, <sup>8</sup>knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a bondservant or is free. <sup>9</sup>Masters, do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him. <sup>10</sup>Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might. <sup>11</sup>Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil. <sup>12</sup>For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. <sup>13</sup>Therefore take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm. <sup>14</sup>Stand therefore, having fastened on the belt of truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, <sup>15</sup>and, as shoes for your feet, having put on the readiness given by the gospel of peace. <sup>16</sup>In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; <sup>17</sup>and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, <sup>18</sup>praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints, <sup>19</sup>and also for me, that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel, <sup>20</sup>for which I am an ambassador in chains, that I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak. <sup>21</sup>So that you also may know how I am and what I am doing, Tychicus the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord will tell you everything. <sup>22</sup>I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are, and that he may encourage your hearts. <sup>23</sup>Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>24</sup>Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Spirit-filled community of 5:18–21, expressed in the marriage covenant of 5:22–33, now extends into the full household: children and parents, servants and masters. These are not grand or glamorous relationships — they are the daily, ordinary, sometimes tedious texture of domestic life. And yet Paul charges every one of them with gospel significance. The Spirit who fills the worshipping community also fills the kitchen, the nursery, the workshop, the field. There is no space in the Christian household that is exempt from the Lordship of Christ, no relationship that lies outside the sanctifying reach of the gospel.

The commands are given with careful balance. Children are told to obey — but fathers are immediately told not to provoke. Servants are told to serve faithfully — but masters are immediately told to treat their servants with justice and fairness. In every pair, both parties receive commands; in every pair, both parties are accountable to Christ. This symmetry is itself a theological statement: in the household of the Spirit-filled community, no one is merely the recipient of others' service and no one is merely the dispenser of commands. All are servants of Christ, all are accountable to the same Lord, all are engaged in the same vocation of making their ordinary relationships a theatre of God's glory.

To the children Paul quotes the fifth commandment, the first with a promise attached (vv. 2–3; Exod. 20:12) — and honour, unlike obedience, does not end with childhood.

The motivating principle that runs through the entire passage is Paul's repeated phrase “as to the Lord” or “as bondservants of Christ.” The child who obeys parents is obeying “in the Lord” (v.1). The servant who works faithfully does so “as to the Lord and not to man” (v.7). The master treats servants justly “knowing that he also has a Master in heaven” (v.9). Every human authority is relativised by a higher authority; every human service is dignified by being rendered to Christ. The gospel transforms every relationship in the household not by changing its external form but by changing the motivation, the orientation, and the significance of everything done within it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Authority, Service, and the Lordship of Christ

The household codes of Ephesians 5:22–6:9 have sometimes been misread as Paul's accommodation to Roman social structures — a domestication of the gospel that reinforces existing hierarchies. The opposite is true. Paul takes every relationship in the household and transforms it from within by the same double principle: both parties have obligations, and both parties are accountable to Christ. This is not the endorsement of hierarchy for its own sake; it is the sanctification of ordered relationships by the presence of a Lord who stands above every human ordering.

The instruction to servants (vv.5–8) is particularly searching. “Obey... as you would Christ,” “doing the will of God from the heart,” “rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man, knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord.” Paul is not telling slaves that their situation is just; he is telling them that no situation, however unjust, is outside the reach of Christ's transforming presence. The servant who works faithfully for an unworthy master, doing it as for the Lord, is engaged in genuine worship — and will receive the Lord's commendation at the last day, whatever commendation or condemnation the human master gave or withheld.

The warning to masters — “do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him” (v.9) — is one of the most socially radical statements in the New Testament. The master has a Master. The one with authority is under authority. Before the throne of the impartial God, all distinctions of status dissolve. This truth, fully believed and consistently applied, has done more to dismantle unjust social structures than any legal or political programme. It was ultimately the logic of this verse, applied over centuries, that made slavery in the Christian world an untenable contradiction.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Roman paterfamilias held virtually absolute authority over his household — his wife, his children, and his slaves were all, in various degrees, subject to his legal control. Children had no independent legal standing; slaves were property. Paul's household code addresses children and slaves first, and addresses them as moral agents capable of genuine obedience to God — not as objects to be managed. This is itself a dignity-claim that the Roman household code did not make. And the commands to fathers (don't exasperate) and masters (treat them justly) placed obligations on the powerful toward the powerless that Roman law did not require. The Christian household was different — visibly, consistently, counter-culturally different.

Now: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord” and “Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger” — both imperatives are needed in every age, and our age tends to violate both simultaneously. We live in a culture that simultaneously refuses to discipline children (producing entitled, poorly-bounded young people) and fails to give them the patient, encouraging, Christ-centred nurture that Ephesians 6:4 envisions. The Christian home where authority is exercised in love, where children are both appropriately disciplined and genuinely encouraged in the Lord, where the name of Christ is spoken and the word of God is read — this home is a counterculture, a community of formation in a world that has largely forgotten what formation is for.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“In the Lord” qualifies and deepens the obedience: children obey not merely because parents have authority but because Christ is Lord of the household and has ordered it this way. “This is right” — not merely commanded but fitting, consistent with the created order and the moral structure of the family. Paul addresses children directly — they are full members of the congregation, present when the letter is read aloud, accountable to Christ for their own response to his word. The qualifier “in the Lord” also provides the limit: obedience is within the scope of the Lord’s own commands, not extending to what Christ himself forbids. (cf. Col. 3:20; Prov. 1:8)

Stop for a moment on the fact that he says it at all, because it is easy to miss how odd this was. Picture the letter arriving. A household in Ephesus, the room full, somebody reading aloud — and the children are there, as children always are, on the floor at the edge of the room, half listening. Then the reader says: Children. Heads come up. In a world where a child had no independent legal standing, was legally closer to property than to person, and would certainly never be addressed by a public document, an apostle stops the letter and speaks to them directly.

He does not say “fathers, make your children obey”, which is what every household code of the period would have said. He speaks to the child, gives the child a reason, and waits for the child to answer for himself. Paul is treating a six-year-old as a member of the church who can hear Christ and respond to him.

And notice that he does not reuse the word from the marriage passage. Wives were told hypotassō, to order themselves under — a voluntary arranging of oneself. Children are told hypakouō, which is built from the verb to hear: to listen underneath, and then to act. The distinction matters and the church has often blurred it. A wife is not a child, and a husband who reads his wife’s role out of this verse rather than out of chapter 5 has taken the wrong word from the wrong paragraph. What is asked of a child is straightforward obedience, and it is asked because a child genuinely does not yet know enough to run his own life — which is a temporary condition and is treated as one.

Then watch Paul stack up his reasons, because he gives three in three verses and they are each of a different kind. It is right — dikaion, fitting, built into the moral shape of things, so that even someone who had never seen the commandment would sense it (v. 1). It is commanded — written into the law at Sinai (v. 2). And it is blessed — it carries a promise (v. 3). Conscience, Scripture, and consequence, in that order. Paul is not relying on the parent’s volume.

Now the guard, and it must be said plainly, because this is one of the verses most easily turned into an instrument. “In the Lord” is not decoration. It is the boundary drawn around the whole command, and it means a parent’s authority is borrowed, never absolute. No parent has been given the right to require a child to sin, and none has been given the right to injure a child.

If you are a young person reading this in a house where you are being hurt, frightened, or asked to keep a secret about what an adult does to you, this verse is not telling you to submit to it. Tell someone — a teacher, a pastor, another adult you trust — and keep telling until somebody acts. That is not disobedience and it is not dishonour; it is obedience to the Lord in whose name the whole command was given. And any adult who quotes this verse to keep a child quiet has taken Christ’s words and used them against the very person Christ stopped a letter to address.

For the great majority of readers, of course, the childhood in question is long over, and it is worth asking what a verse like this does for a woman of fifty. Two things at least. It explains something about how you were formed: the first authority any of us meets is a human one, in a kitchen, and how that went shapes how we later hear the idea of an authority we cannot see. If you grew up under someone arbitrary, or absent, or impossible to please, you may find that submitting to God feels like bracing for something — and it is worth knowing that this is a learned reflex rather than a true reading of him.

And it sends you to verse 4, because the moment you understand what obedience cost you as a child, you have been handed the reason Paul immediately turns round and speaks to the fathers.

But the last word belongs somewhere else, and it is the sentence that keeps this verse from being merely domestic management. There has been exactly one child in the history of the world who had every right to disregard his parents. He had made them. He knew more at twelve than either of them would learn in a lifetime — the one recorded incident of his boyhood has him astonishing the teachers in the temple (Luke 2:46–47).

And Luke, having told that story, finishes it like this: he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them (Luke 2:51). Then nothing for eighteen years. The Son of God spent the better part of two decades doing what he was told in a small town by a carpenter and his wife, and Scripture says he “learned obedience” (Heb. 5:8). So a child who obeys is not doing something beneath the dignity of heaven. He is doing the thing the Lord of heaven did first, for longer, and with far less reason to.

verseByVerse.quote: Honor your father and mother (this is the first commandment with a promise), that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul reaches to the fifth commandment (Exod. 20:12) and notes its distinction: it is the first that carries a promise. And “honour” is broader than childhood obedience — it is the ongoing respect, care, and esteem owed to parents right through adult life. The promise of well-being reflects a wisdom God built into human community: the generation that honours its parents sustains the social fabric across time. So the command outlasts the household, shaping the grown child’s posture toward ageing parents long after direct obedience has ceased to be the mode of the relationship.

In practice, honour means speaking of them with respect (not retelling their failures as entertainment, even when every word is true); treating them with consistent courtesy as they grow slower and more repetitive; and giving practical care in old age — Paul says the one who will not provide for his household “has denied the faith” (1 Tim. 5:8). It means listening to their wisdom (Prov. 23:22) and keeping them warmly included in family life rather than quietly sidelined.

But honour does not mean blind obedience in adulthood — marriage creates a new primary loyalty (5:31), and the adult who cannot decide anything without a parent’s approval has not yet left. Nor does it mean placing parents above a spouse.

Think of the difference between a woman who calls her forgetful mother every week and answers the same question without sarcasm, teaching her own children how they will one day treat her — and a man who retells his father’s failures at every gathering, calls him “the old man” with veiled contempt, and is always unavailable when help is needed. (cf. 1 Tim. 5:4; Col. 3:20)

Two things in this quotation deserve more than they usually get, and the first is a puzzle that a careful reader will spot and most commentaries hurry past. Paul calls it “the first commandment with a promise” — but the second commandment already has one attached, about God showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love him and keep his commandments (Exod. 20:6). So in what sense is this the first?

The likeliest answer is that the clause in the second commandment is a statement about God’s character appended to a prohibition, and applies to the whole law rather than to one command; whereas this is the first time a specific command is given a specific outcome attached to it — do this, and this will follow. Others take “first” to mean first in the second table of the law, the one governing our dealings with people, which makes honour of parents the foundation of every other human obligation. Either reading leaves Paul’s point intact: God has singled this one out and hung a promise on it.

The second thing is what Paul does to the promise itself. In Exodus the wording is “that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you” — a promise about Canaan, made to Israel, about a specific piece of ground. Paul quotes it and quietly drops the last clause. What was a promise about one territory becomes a promise about life anywhere, offered to Greek children in a city in Asia Minor who had no stake in Canaan whatever. That is not carelessness; it is the same move he has been making throughout the letter. The blessings of the covenant have been opened to the nations.

But the promise itself needs handling honestly, because read as a personal guarantee it is not true, and pretending otherwise damages people. Godly children die young. Honouring your parents does not immunise you against a drunk driver or a diagnosis. Scripture knows this perfectly well — it is the whole argument of the book of Job and a recurring complaint in the Psalms.

What is being given here is a proverb in the biblical sense: a statement of how life generally goes, built into the way God has ordered the world, not a contract enforceable in every individual case. And it is observably true at the level it is pitched. A person who grows up learning to honour legitimate authority, who can receive correction, who does not treat every constraint as an insult, will as a rule live a longer and considerably less damaged life than one who cannot. And a society in which the generations honour one another holds together across time; one in which they do not comes apart, and you can watch it happening.

Now the part of this command that actually keeps people awake, and it must not be dodged. Paul attaches no clause about sufficiently good parents. He does not write “honour your father and mother if they deserved it”. And a great many readers have a father who was frightening, or a mother who was cruel, or a parent who simply left — and they read this verse with a kind of dread, hearing it demand that they pretend the childhood was something it was not.

It demands nothing of the kind. Honour is not the same as approval, and it is not the same as pretending. You can honour a person and tell the truth about them; the Bible does it constantly, recording the failures of its own heroes in detail without ceasing to treat them with dignity. Honour is compatible with a boundary — the adult child who limits contact with a destructive parent, calmly and without contempt, for the sake of his own household, has not broken this commandment. It is compatible with grief, and with the long, unfinished work of forgiving. What it rules out is contempt: the sneer, the public mockery, the settled determination to make them pay.

And notice how small the actual duty is at its core, and how it survives almost any history. It is to refuse to treat the people who gave you life as though they were nothing.

Here is the test, and it is a strange one until you try it. Think of how you speak about your parents when they are not there — to your spouse, to a friend, to your own children. Not what you feel; what you say, and the tone you say it in. Most of us discover that our real assessment lives in the anecdotes we choose to repeat, and that we have been quietly training the next generation in exactly how they will one day speak about us.

And there is one more thing, for the reader whose parents are old and difficult and whose duty here has become heavy. Watch what Jesus did with this commandment. He used it to attack the religious experts of his day, who had invented a device called Corban by which a man could declare his assets dedicated to God and so escape the obligation of supporting his parents. Jesus called that “making void the word of God by your tradition” (Mark 7:9–13) — and note what he thought the fifth commandment actually required: money, provision, the unglamorous cost of looking after people who can no longer look after themselves.

Then watch him keep it himself. He is on the cross, in the middle of bearing the sin of the world, and he sees his mother standing there. And with what breath he has, he arranges her care: “Woman, behold, your son!” and to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” — and from that hour the disciple took her to his own home (John 19:26–27). He was in the act of redeeming the world and he stopped to make sure his mother would have somewhere to live.

parallels.desc: honour your father and your mother
that it may go well with you

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prohibition is precise: do not provoke your children to anger — do not exasperate or embitter them. The positive command is threefold: bring them up, discipline them, instruct them — and all of it “of the Lord.” The father is not forming the child in his own image but in the Lord’s.

Nurturing looks different at every age but runs in one direction. With young children it is presence and affection, calm and consistent boundaries, and God woven into ordinary talk — “God made that butterfly,” “let’s thank God for our food” (Deut. 6:7) — and prayer for them, by name, aloud. With older children it is genuine interest in their world (the father who does not know his child’s best friend has not yet earned the right to be heard), correction that is private and tied to character rather than mere behaviour, and Scripture opened with real curiosity rather than performed duty.

With teenagers it is moving from authority to influence — “what do you think?” and actually listening — engaging the hard questions honestly rather than avoiding them, and above all letting them see a real father’s own walk with God: praying, struggling honestly with the word, confessing sin, returning to Christ after failure. More is caught than taught.

The goal through every age is not a child who performs Christianity in front of his father, but one who has tasted the goodness of God in his own heart because his father kept pointing him there. The father does not save his children — only God does. But he is the primary human instrument God most often uses. The responsibility is enormous; the grace available for it is more enormous still (cf. Deut. 6:4–9; Ps. 78:4–7; Prov. 22:6).

Notice first who is addressed, because it is not who we would expect. Paul has just spoken to children; the natural counterpart would be “parents”. He says fathers. The word can mean parents in some settings, and mothers are certainly not exempt from what follows — but the address is deliberate, and it is aimed at the one who in that household held the power. In the Roman world the father’s authority over his children was close to absolute; a paterfamilias could in principle disown, sell, or expose a child. Paul takes the man with all the power in the room and gives him a prohibition and a job.

And the prohibition comes first, which is worth registering. Before the father is told what to do, he is told what he must not do — because in a relationship of that much asymmetry, the damage a man can do without ever intending to is the first problem to be dealt with.

The word is parorgizete, and the tense means a settled pattern rather than a bad afternoon. Every father loses his temper. What Paul forbids is the atmosphere: the steady drip that teaches a child something permanent about himself. And the companion verse in Colossians names the outcome exactly — do not provoke your children, “lest they become discouraged” (Col. 3:21). The word there means to lose heart, to have the wind go out of you. That is the injury: not a child who is angry, but a child who has quietly stopped trying, because he has worked out that nothing he does will be enough.

Which is why the provocations are worth reading slowly rather than nodding at. Almost none of them is a sin a man would confess. Criticism that only ever notices what is missing. Expectations that move. Comparison with a sibling. Promises casually broken because a child’s disappointment is easy to absorb. Sarcasm, which a child cannot answer and does not forget. Absence — the father in the house and behind a screen. And the commonest of all: a man who is warm when things are going well and cold when they are not, so that a child grows up managing his father’s mood and learns, without ever being told, that love is a thing you earn by performance.

Set that beside the God this letter has been describing for five chapters, and the reason Paul cares becomes plain. A child’s first picture of authority is a human one, in a kitchen; his first working model of a father is the man at the table. Nobody thinks their way out of that model easily. The man who is arbitrary teaches his children that God is arbitrary; the man who is never satisfied teaches them that God is never satisfied — and they will spend thirty years trying to unlearn it, and some of them never will.

Then the positive command, and its three words are worth separating. Ektrephete — nourish, feed up to full growth; the same verb used of a husband nourishing his own body (5:29). Paideia — the whole business of training, including correction and discipline, the shaping of a person over years. Nouthesia — instruction by word, the placing of things in the mind: explaining, warning, reasoning with a child rather than merely issuing rulings.

So this is not permissiveness. Paul commands discipline in the same breath in which he forbids provocation, and a father who never corrects anything is failing this verse just as surely as the man who crushes. The two errors look opposite and share a root: both are easier than the patient, costly work of shaping a person who will one day not be under your authority at all.

Does discipline include physical discipline? Proverbs says Whoever spares the rod hates his son (Prov 13:24), and many Christians understand that to allow measured physical correction of young children, given calmly, never in anger, never to injure, and always with love and explanation. Others take the rod as a figure for discipline in general, and some believe physical discipline is unwise in every case. Whatever a parent decides, this verse rules out anything that provokes, humiliates or harms a child. Discipline that crushes a child’s spirit (Col 3:21) is not the Lord’s discipline, and abuse must never hide behind Scripture.

And the governing phrase is the last one: “of the Lord”. The father is not forming the child in his own image, or in the image of the career he wishes he had had, or into a credit to the family. He is bringing up someone else’s child — a person who belongs to God and will answer to him — and his own preferences are not the standard.

Here is the test, and it is the one most fathers will not run, which is a good reason to run it. Do not ask yourself whether you provoke your children. Ask one of them. A teenager, or a grown son or daughter, and the question is: “Is there something I do that makes you feel you can never quite get it right?” Then say nothing at all until they have finished, and do not explain. Most fathers have no idea, and the reason they have no idea is that nobody has ever been able to tell them.

Which brings the last word to the reader this verse is most likely to wound: the father whose children are grown, who has read that list and recognised himself in it, and for whom it is far too late to do the thing differently. That grief is real and should not be talked away. But two things are true and both matter.

The first is that it is not too late to say so. An apology from a father to an adult child — specific, without excuses, without a single “but you also” — is one of the most powerful things in the world, and it does not diminish a man’s authority; it is very nearly the only thing that can restore it. The second is that God is not limited to what you gave them. He has been a Father to your children in ways you never managed, and he is entirely capable of repairing what you broke, which is a thing he has been doing with families since Genesis.

And there is a picture to leave with, because Paul is asking fathers to imitate a Father. At the Jordan, before Jesus had preached a sermon, healed anybody, or done one recorded thing in public ministry, a voice came out of heaven and said, in the hearing of a crowd: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). The approval came first, and it came out loud, and it was not earned by a track record because there was not yet a track record to earn it with. That is the Father this verse is asking you to reproduce in a kitchen.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul addresses the slave first — itself a gesture of moral dignity in a world where slaves were often treated as property without standing. The command is for whole-hearted service: “fear and trembling” is not terror but the solemn awareness of standing before the living God. “With a sincere heart” — singleness of heart, without duplicity. “As you would Christ” — the real master is not the human employer but the Lord who observes all and to whom account is given. This fundamentally relativizes every human authority without removing the obligation of faithful service.

But a modern reader recoils at the command itself, and rightly wants an answer: how can a Christian letter tell a slave to obey a slaveholder at all? Does Paul endorse slavery? Two things must be said plainly. First, this is not the slavery a modern reader pictures. Greco-Roman slavery was a great evil, and Paul’s world was full of its cruelty — but it was not the race-based, kidnap-fed chattel slavery of the transatlantic trade.

Slaves were not a despised ethnic underclass; they were a large share of the empire’s population, drawn from every people, often through debt or capture in war, sometimes selling themselves to clear a debt. Many were educated — doctors, teachers, estate managers — and manumission was common enough that many slaves could hope to be freed, and some went on to become Roman citizens.

It was still bondage, still an assault on human dignity, and the New Testament never once calls it good. But the man-stealing that fed the later trade is condemned outright in the same New Testament — Paul lists “enslavers” (andrapodistai, kidnappers who sell people) among the worst of sinners (1 Tim. 1:10), which by itself would have outlawed the Atlantic slave trade at the root.

Second, why does Paul address a slave’s conduct rather than call for revolt? Because a slave revolt in the first century would have been drowned in blood — the thousands crucified after Spartacus had never been forgotten — and it would have branded the young church as sedition and buried the gospel with it. Paul takes a longer and surer road.

He does not leave the institution as he found it; he plants under it a charge that must eventually blow it apart: the slave is addressed as a full moral agent, a “bondservant of Christ” (v. 6); master and slave stand on identical ground before an impartial Judge (vv. 8–9); and in the letter to Philemon, Paul sends a runaway slave back to be received “no longer as a bondservant but… as a beloved brother” (Philem. 16). Once two men share one table and one Lord, one of them cannot go on owning the other. It was Christians formed by exactly these texts — Wilberforce and the abolitionists — who finally struck the institution down. Paul regulates what he found and sows what would undo it; he does not bless it.

Take the three phrases Paul attaches to the command, because each of them moves the ground under a slave’s feet.

“With fear and trembling” sounds at first like an instruction to be frightened of the master, and it is not. Paul uses the same phrase of himself arriving at Corinth — “I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (1 Cor. 2:3) — and, most tellingly, of the Christian life as a whole: work out your own salvation “with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you” (Phil. 2:12–13). It is the language of a man who knows that what he is handling is serious and that God is watching. So the trembling is not aimed at the man holding the whip. It has been redirected upward, over his head.

“With a sincere heart” is haplotēs, singleness — the opposite of a divided interior. It describes a person who is one thing all the way through, with no second self kept back for private use. For a slave, whose entire existence invited duplicity, that is a startling thing to ask and a considerable gift to be given: you may be owned, and you need not be divided.

And “as you would Christ” is the sentence that changes the architecture of the whole relationship. The slave is not told that his master deserves this. He is told to look past him. There is another figure standing behind the man who owns him, and the work is actually being handed to that one.

Which is why the first thing Paul does here — addressing the slave at all — was the radical act. Every household code of the period spoke to the owner about the management of his property. Paul speaks to the property, and speaks to him as a person with a conscience, a Lord, and choices to make about how he does his work. A man with no legal standing is told that his ordinary labour is being offered to Jesus Christ and will be assessed by him. Nobody in that world talked to slaves like that.

And notice what he is not told. He is not told that his situation is just; Paul never says that anywhere. He is not told that God ordained his slavery or that he should be content to remain in it as a matter of principle — indeed, writing to Corinth, Paul says plainly that if a slave can gain his freedom he should take the opportunity (1 Cor. 7:21). What he is told is that his circumstances, unjust as they are, cannot prevent him from serving Christ, and cannot reduce the value of what he does.

That is worth transferring carefully, because the modern equivalent is not employment as such — an employee is not owned, and the New Testament is emphatic about the wickedness of withholding wages and exploiting the weak. But the principle reaches every reader who has to work under conditions they did not choose and cannot change: the manager who will never be fair, the industry that rewards the wrong things, the job taken because the mortgage exists. Paul’s answer to a man in a far worse version of that is not resignation and not resentment. It is a change of employer at the level that matters.

Here is the test, and it takes one honest minute. Think of the part of your work that nobody senior will ever inspect. Now ask what governs the quality of it. If the honest answer is “whether it is likely to be noticed”, then whatever you believe about God, your functional employer is the person who signs the form. If the answer is “because it is the work I have been given”, something has already changed hands.

And there is one more thing here, which the ancient reader would have felt immediately and we tend to miss because the English hides it. The word for slave in this verse is doulos. It is the same word Paul reaches for when he describes what the Son of God did: though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, “taking the form of a servant” — morphēn doulou — and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2:6–8).

So when a slave in Ephesus heard this letter read aloud and was told to serve as to Christ, he was being addressed by a Lord who had taken his job title. Not as a gesture, and not briefly. The one who owns everything took the position of the one who owns nothing, obeyed to the end, and was raised and seated in the heavenly places — which is precisely where chapter two says the man listening has been seated too (2:6).
verseByVerse.note: Slavery was part of everyday life in the Roman world; many early believers were slaves or owned slaves.

verseByVerse.quote: not by the way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Eye-service” is working only when watched, performing only for the observing eye, the default mode of coerced labour. His alternative is not better performance management but a different master. When the ultimate audience is Christ — who sees all, records all, and will reward all — the human supervisor’s presence or absence becomes irrelevant. Labour offered to the Lord is worship; labour performed for human approval is mere performance.

The slave-master world has no direct equivalent, but the principle maps precisely onto the modern workplace. Think of an employee whose manager is demanding and not always fair, whose credit has been taken by others, who was passed over for a deserved promotion. The temptation is exactly eye-service: do the minimum when unwatched, invest effort only in what will be seen.

Paul’s answer is not a better argument for harder work; it is a different audience. She is not, in the deepest sense, working for her manager but for Christ — who was in the meeting where her credit was taken, who saw the extra hour no one noticed, and who will miss nothing at the final accounting (v.8). That changes not her circumstances but her interior: the quality of her work is no longer hostage to the fairness of her employer.

In practice it means the same quality of work whether or not the manager is in the building; integrity in the small things no one will ever check — the expense report filled in accurately, the corner not cut; a genuine goodwill toward a difficult manager rather than performed collegiality over quiet resentment; and releasing the question of fairness to God, since “whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord” (v.8).

The one who has been overlooked is not owed nothing; he is owed everything, by a Master who keeps perfect accounts. The result, lived out, is a worker who stands out — not because he is performing Christian witness as a strategy, but because he does not change when the boss leaves the room, and that consistency is itself a testimony (cf. Col. 3:23–24; 1 Pet. 2:18–19).

The first of the key words in this sentence appears nowhere before Paul, and a man does not invent vocabulary unless he cannot find anything that will do. Ophthalmodoulia — eye-service, eye-slavery: work that exists only while it is being looked at. Beside it stands anthrōpareskoi — people-pleasers, whose whole orientation is the management of what others think of them.

And what he is describing is not laziness. Eye-service can be extremely energetic. It is a matter of where the effort is aimed: the report polished because it will be read by the right person, the visible task done first, the hours arranged so as to be seen. It produces a person who is never quite the same twice, because he is always calibrating to an audience — which is exhausting in a way that hard work never is.

Then comes the phrase that ought to stop any Christian who has ever suspected his job is spiritually irrelevant: “doing the will of God from the heart”. Look at who that is said to and what he does all day. This is a slave. His work is cleaning, carrying, cooking, accounting, minding somebody else’s children. There is nothing religious about any of it. And Paul says that when he does it well, he is doing the will of God — the same phrase used elsewhere for sanctification and for the great purposes of the Almighty.

Which quietly demolishes the division most of us carry about without examining: that there are sacred activities — prayer, church, evangelism, the Bible — and then there is everything else, which is at best neutral and has to be redeemed by having a Christian motive bolted onto it. Paul will not have it. The letter has already said that we are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works which he prepared beforehand (2:10), and here is what a good work looks like on a Tuesday: it looks like a floor properly swept by a man nobody is watching.

It is worth being concrete, because this is one of the places where a doctrine changes a life. The nurse on the night shift, the accountant reconciling figures nobody will check, the mother whose entire day’s output will be undone by bedtime, the man who drives a van — none of these is doing something less spiritual than the person leading the service on Sunday. Different callings, identical dignity, and the same Lord receiving both. There is no promotion in the Christian life from ordinary work to real ministry, because the ordinary work was never the waiting room.

“Rendering service with a good will” presses further still. The words mean something like serving with genuine goodwill, a positive readiness — not merely complying, but wanting the person you serve to do well. That is a considerable thing to ask of a slave about the man who owns him, and it is a considerable thing to ask of an employee about a manager who took credit for her work.

And notice that Paul does not ask for a feeling he has not supplied a reason for. The reason is in the next clause and in the next verse: “as to the Lord and not to man”, and “knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord”. Goodwill toward an undeserving employer is not manufactured by trying to like him. It becomes possible when the transaction has been re-routed — when what you do is no longer being paid for by him at all.

Now a guard, because this passage has been used to keep people in situations they should have left. Nothing here requires a Christian to stay in an exploitative job, to accept illegal treatment, to decline a better position, or to refuse to raise a grievance. Paul told slaves to take freedom if they could get it (1 Cor. 7:21); James thunders against employers who withhold wages (Jas. 5:4); and the same Paul used his Roman citizenship without embarrassment when it protected him. Working heartily for the Lord and advocating for yourself are not in competition. What is forbidden is not self-protection; it is the divided heart that gives a man his hours and withholds his integrity.

So the test is the one the passage itself supplies, and it is unusually easy to run. Notice what changes in your work when the person who assesses you leaves the building — the pace, the care, the attention to the part nobody sees. The gap between those two versions of you is the exact measure of how much of your working life is currently being done for God and how much is being done for an audience.

And it is worth ending where Paul does, with the strange dignity of the arrangement. A slave in a house in Ephesus, whose name appears in no record, whose work was credited to another man, is told that he is a bondservant of Christ doing the will of God from the heart. He had no career, no recognition, and no prospect of either. He had a Master who was watching, and work that was going somewhere.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a bondservant or is free.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great equalizer: divine justice makes no distinction of social status. “Whether he is a bondservant or is free” — the slave and the freeman stand before the same judge and receive the same reward for faithful labor. No deed done for the Lord is wasted, overlooked, or unrewarded, whether it was performed in a position of prestige or in a slave quarter. God shows no partiality; the service of the humblest slave, done in faith, is as acceptable to him as the offering of kings. This is a profound subversion of every social hierarchy: the eternal calculus does not follow the ledgers of Rome.

This verse explains why a Christian can work well for an employer who does not deserve it, but it deserves opening on its own account, because it is making a claim about the universe and not merely about morale, and every word of it is load-bearing.

Start with the first one: knowing. Paul does not say hoping, or trusting that somehow it will all come right in the end. The whole weight of the sentence rests on a thing that is known — a fact about how God has arranged reality, which you can be as certain of on the worst Thursday of your working life as on the best. Feelings are not asked to carry this and could not. You are being handed something to know, and then told to go back to work on the strength of it.

Then the scope, which is wider than we let it be: whatever good anyone does. Not whatever great good. Not whatever public or spiritual or impressive good. There is no threshold named, and no category of work excluded — which in the original setting meant a man sweeping a floor that his owner would never inspect, and in yours means the meal cooked for a family who did not think to say thank you, the shift quietly covered, the expense claim filled in honestly when nobody was ever going to check it, the patience held with the same difficult relative for the ninth year running.

Jesus set the bar at exactly this height and used almost comically small currency to do it: a cup of cold water given to a disciple, and the giver “will by no means lose his reward” (Matt. 10:42; Mark 9:41).

And the letter to the Hebrews puts it the other way round, as a statement about God’s character: “God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name” (Heb. 6:10). Note what that makes forgetting. If God let one of these things drop, he would not be merely forgetful. He would be unjust.

Then the verb, which is the best thing in the verse. Komizō does not simply mean to be given something; it means to receive back what is yours, to collect what was deposited. Which reframes every unnoticed thing you have ever done. It is not lost, and it was not wasted, and it has not evaporated because nobody saw it. It has been deposited. Paul uses the same verb of the judgment seat, where each one may receive back what is due for what he has done (2 Cor. 5:10). The good you did in the dark is on account, and the account is held by someone who does not lose things.

Feel the force of that for the person it was first written to. A slave’s work did not bear his name. Whatever he built, grew, mended or managed was credited to the man who owned him; there was no prospect whatever of recognition, no promotion, no record, and at the end of a life of competent labour there would be nothing anywhere with his name on it. Paul tells that man that a complete and accurate record exists, kept by the only one who was actually watching, and that it will be read back to him in person. That is not a consolation for the powerless. It is a statement that the visible accounting of this world is the inaccurate one.

Which is why this verse belongs to a great many readers who have never been near a slave quarter. The woman who has cared for a parent with dementia for six years, and whose work is invisible precisely because it is done well. The father whose whole ordinary life is a series of things nobody will ever thank him for. The believer who has served one small congregation for thirty years and whose name will not appear in any history of anything. You have done things nobody ever knew about, and some of them cost you a great deal. This verse says they were not thrown away. They were banked.

One necessary guard, because the sentence sits four chapters after “by grace you have been saved through faith… not a result of works” (2:8–9), and the two must not be set fighting. What Paul promises here is not wages earned but reward given; not the ground of your acceptance but the Father’s pleasure in what his own Spirit produced in you. Nothing on that record was generated by you unaided — the willing and the working were both his gift — which is why Augustine could say that when God crowns our merits he is crowning his own gifts. Salvation is not what is being handed back on that day. Salvation is the reason you are standing there at all.

And be honest about the timing, because Paul is. He does not say you will receive it back next quarter, or that the credit stolen from you will be publicly restored in this life, or that the family will eventually notice. Most of it will not be settled here, and a Christianity that promises otherwise is setting people up. What he says is that there is a day, and a Lord who keeps the books, and that nothing is pending indefinitely. The wait is real. The loss is not.

So the ledgers of Rome recorded a household’s output under the owner’s name, and that was the only record anyone could see. It has long since rotted. The other record has not, and on it, in full, is every good thing done by every person nobody was keeping track of — each one entered under the name of the one who actually did it.

verseByVerse.quote: Masters, do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the master is brought under the very same rule as the slave: he too has a Master, his authority is delegated and conditional, and he is to treat those under him with the same integrity of heart he expects from them — “do the same to them.” The specific prohibition, “stop your threatening,” targets the master’s most characteristic abuse of power, and the ground is theological: “he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him.” This was no anti-slavery manifesto in the modern sense — it was something more radical in the long run, placing master and slave under one moral governance and one eternal accountability, a logic finally incompatible with the institution itself.

The power differential between employer and employee — manager and team, owner and contractor — maps closely enough that the logic lands with full force. “Do the same” means the same standard applies to the one who holds the power. It means treating people as persons rather than resources — knowing the names and situations of those who report to you, noticing when someone is carrying more than the metrics show.

It means giving credit where it is due rather than absorbing it upward. It means paying fairly and promptly — the Old Testament is sharp here (“the wages of a hired worker shall not remain with you all night,” Lev. 19:13; “the wages… which you kept back by fraud are crying out,” James 5:4). And it means creating conditions in which people can actually do good work, rather than setting them up to fail and then penalising them.

“Stop threatening” prohibits the most familiar abuse of managerial power: ruling by fear, using reviews as a weapon, making public examples to keep others compliant, reminding people how easily they could be replaced. Paul forbids it — not because it is commercially unwise (though it often is), but because it treats persons as means, and does to them precisely what the master’s own Master never does to him. For before the throne of God the chief executive stands on exactly the same ground as the intern; title and salary buy not a single degree of advantage in that courtroom.

Picture a leader facing redundancies under real financial pressure, who chooses transparency over a minimal-notice announcement, writes personal references for everyone let go, and insists the process be handled with dignity rather than mere efficiency. It costs more and is harder — but he has a Master who saw every person on that list before they were born and knows their name (cf. Col. 4:1; Luke 16:10).

Two words carry this verse and the first is the most startling thing in the household code: “do the same”. Paul has just spent four verses telling slaves how to work — with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as to Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, with genuine goodwill. And he turns to the men who own them and says: the same. Not a parallel standard adapted for masters. The same.

Nothing in the ancient world talked like that. The codes of the moralists explained to a master how to get the best from his household; they did not place him under the identical obligation as his property. Paul has taken the instruction given to the person with no rights and handed it, unaltered, to the person with all of them.

Then the prohibition, and it is precisely targeted: “stop your threatening”. Not stop punishing — stop threatening. The characteristic instrument of a master was not the whip so much as the constant possibility of it, and that is a cheaper and more effective tool: a household can be run for years on fear without a blow ever landing. Paul forbids the atmosphere. And the form of the verb suggests something already going on that must now cease.

Which transfers with unpleasant accuracy. The modern equivalent is rarely a threat spoken outright; it is the reminder of how competitive the market is at the moment, the review used as leverage, the public dressing-down that is really addressed to everyone else in the room, the manager whose displeasure is never stated and always available. It costs nothing to deploy and it reliably produces compliance. Paul forbids it — and note the ground he forbids it on. Not that it is ineffective, because it works. That it does to a person what God does not do to you.

Because that is the argument of the whole verse, and it is compressed into a phrase that would have been offensive to a first-century master: “he who is both their Master and yours”. One word, kyrios, used once, governing both men. Not their master and your Lord, as though there were two categories with two arrangements. The same Master, over both, at the same time. The slave and the slaveholder are, before that throne, colleagues.

And Paul finishes the thought with the clause that gives the whole passage its edge: “and that there is no partiality with him”. The word is prosōpolēmpsia, built from the Hebrew idiom of “lifting the face” — the courtroom picture of a judge who raises a man’s face to see who he is before deciding the case. God does not lift the face. He does not check first whether he is dealing with a magistrate or a labourer.

It is one of the steadiest claims in Scripture. “The LORD your God… is not partial and takes no bribe” (Deut. 10:17). Peter, standing in a Gentile house against every instinct of his upbringing: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality” (Acts 10:34). And James, to a congregation that had seated a rich visitor well and a poor one badly, treats it as a denial of the faith itself (Jas. 2:1–9).

So a master who has spent his life in a world where status determines outcome is told that in the only court that finally sits, his advantages do not exist. Everything that would ordinarily protect him — property, standing, the ability to make trouble for people — is simply not admitted. He will be assessed on the same basis as the man who cleans his house, by a Judge who cannot be impressed.

Which is why this verse has had consequences out of all proportion to its length. It does not abolish slavery in a sentence, and Paul does not pretend it does. What it does is place master and slave under one Lord and one impartial judgment — and once two men genuinely believe that, and sit at one table, and call each other brother, the institution has lost its foundation and is living on borrowed time. It took far too long, and Christians defended the indefensible for generations. But when it finally came down, it came down to arguments built out of verses like this one.

Now the test, and it is not for chief executives only. Almost everyone has power over somebody: a parent over a child, an elder over a congregation, a customer over the person serving him, a manager over one junior colleague, a healthy adult over an ageing relative who now depends on them. So ask the question that finds it. How do you speak to someone who cannot answer back, and who has no way of making it cost you anything? That is the measure, because it is the one situation in which nothing but character is operating.

And then let the verse do the thing it was written to do. The Master in heaven who will assess your treatment of the people under you did not come into the world as a master. He came as a doulos — the very word used of the men addressed four verses earlier — and he washed the feet of people who worked for him (John 13:5), and he was still praying for those with power over him while they nailed him down (Luke 23:34). The one before whom you will stand without advantage is the one who laid all of his aside.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The letter’s last great word is a call to battle: “Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might” (v. 10). Everything Paul has taught — what God has done in Christ (chapters 1–3) and how his people now live (chapters 4–6) — is opposed by a real enemy. Not people, but “the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places” (v. 12). Paul’s answer is not a technique but a set of armour. God supplies it; the believer puts it on and stands.

Paul was writing in chains (v. 20), and he takes the kit of a Roman soldier and fills each piece with something God has given. Most of the pieces come from Isaiah, where God himself goes to war: “He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head” (Isa. 59:17). This is God’s own armour, handed to his people.

The armour at a glance

The belt — truth (v. 14). A soldier’s belt went on first and held his clothing and sword together. Truth comes first because the devil’s weapon is the lie — about God, about you, about what will satisfy you. God’s truth lets you recognise the lie, and an honest life gives the liar nothing to use.

The breastplate — righteousness (v. 14). It guarded the heart, where one blow kills. The devil’s deadliest blow is accusation, and often the charge is true. Christ’s righteousness, counted to you, answers it: God accepts you on Christ’s record, not on yours.

The shoes — the gospel of peace (v. 15). Studded sandals kept a soldier from being knocked off his feet. The gospel’s news that your war with God is over (Rom. 5:1) is ground that does not move when your feelings do, and it makes you ready to carry that news to others.

The shield — faith (v. 16). A large shield caught fire arrows before they could start a fire. Sudden doubts, fears and ugly thoughts work like fire arrows; faith puts them out by answering them with what God has promised.

The helmet — salvation (v. 17). A blow to the head stuns a man so that he drops everything. The enemy aims at the mind with despair; the helmet is the sure hope that God will finish what he began (1 Thess. 5:8).

The sword — the word of God (v. 17). The short sword was the one weapon for attack, at close quarters. Scripture, believed and spoken, is how you answer the lie at the moment it comes, as Jesus did in the wilderness: “It is written.”

Prayer (v. 18). Not a seventh piece but how the whole is worn. Every piece comes from God, and prayer is how you keep drawing on him: “praying at all times in the Spirit.”

The command that runs through it all is stand (vv. 11, 13, 14). Christ has already won. The Christian is not told to win the war but to hold the ground that grace has given him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Spiritual Warfare and the Victory of Christ

The passage grounds the doctrine of spiritual warfare in the victory already achieved by Christ. The Reformers consistently insisted that the Christian fights from victory, not toward it. At the cross and resurrection, Christ decisively defeated the powers: “He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15). The “rulers and authorities” of Ephesians 6:12 are already defeated enemies — real, malevolent, and active, but operating under the authority of One who has conquered them. The Christian's warfare is not the decisive battle; it is the mopping-up operation conducted in light of a victory already won.

This context — victory already achieved — is what makes “standing” the characteristic posture of the Christian warrior rather than “advancing.” Paul does not say “take more territory.” He says “stand.” Hold what Christ has secured. Don't give ground to a defeated enemy. Don't abandon the position that grace has placed you in. This is not a passive posture; it requires every piece of armour, every act of faith, every prayer offered in the Spirit. But it is a posture of confidence, not of uncertainty — the confidence of those who know how the battle ends and who are fighting in the strength of its Victor.

Prayer (vv.18–20) is the atmosphere in which the armoured Christian stands. It is “at all times in the Spirit” — not occasional, not formal, but the constant, Spirit-sustained reaching toward the Commander. Paul's request for prayer for himself (vv.19–20) is among the most searching things in the letter. The apostle who has written the most magnificent theological letter in the New Testament asks his readers to pray that he would have the boldness to speak the gospel clearly. He is acutely aware that the proclamation of the gospel is itself a spiritual warfare activity, requiring not merely intellectual preparation but Spirit-given courage and divine enablement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus was a city saturated with occult practice. The book of Acts records that when the gospel came to Ephesus, it confronted demonic powers directly — the sons of Sceva, the burning of the magic books, the riot engineered by Demetrius the silversmith whose trade in Artemis-shrines was threatened (Acts 19). The Ephesian Christians knew, from personal experience, that spiritual warfare was real. When Paul tells them to stand against “the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places,” he is not speaking metaphorically to a congregation that has only ever faced theoretical opposition. He is arming people who have already been in the fight.

Now: The tendency in contemporary Christianity is to spiritualise spiritual warfare into invisibility (it's just a metaphor for human sin and social structures) or to sensationalise it into obsession (seeing demonic activity behind every difficulty). Paul's teaching steers between both errors. The powers are real — personal, intelligent, malevolent.

But they are defeated — operating under the authority of the risen Christ who has already triumphed over them. The Christian response is neither to ignore them nor to be paralyzed by them, but to stand — in the truth, in righteousness, in the gospel, in faith, in salvation, in the word of God, and in unceasing prayer. This is neither the naivety of the denier nor the anxiety of the obsessed. It is the steady, armoured confidence of those who know their Commander.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Paul means. “Finally” turns to the last thing Paul has to say, and it is a command you cannot carry out by trying harder. “Be strong” is passive in Greek: be strengthened, go on being made strong. Paul is not telling weak people to summon courage — nobody says “be strong” to someone who already is. He is telling them where strength comes from: “in the Lord,” the risen Christ who already reigns over every power (1:20–22). And he measures that strength. “The strength of his might” uses the same words as his prayer in chapter one for “the working of his great might that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead” (1:19–20). The strength on offer is resurrection power, and chapter one says it is directed “toward us who believe.”

Notice where this comes. Paul has just been talking about telling the truth, anger, honest work, marriage, children and employers (4:25–6:9). Then: “Finally, be strong in the Lord.” The battle is not a separate religious arena. It is fought over whether you tell the truth at work and speak kindly at home on an ordinary Thursday evening.

In real life. Watch where your mind goes in the first moments when something hard arrives — a conversation you dread, a temptation that has beaten you before, bad news. Most of us turn first to our own competence and pray afterwards, once our own resources have run out. Paul reverses the order: go to the Lord first, because that is where the strength is. If you read this verse and feel you have nothing of what it asks for, you have understood it. The strength is given, not mustered — and the proof that God can supply it was given once, on the third day, at an empty tomb.

verseByVerse.quote: Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil. For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Paul means. “Put on the whole armor of God”: the full kit, nothing left out, and God’s, not yours. Its purpose is to “stand” — to hold ground Christ has already won, not to conquer new ground. Then Paul names the enemy. “We do not wrestle against flesh and blood”: your real opponent is never the difficult colleague, the hostile neighbour or the government. It is “the rulers… the authorities… the cosmic powers over this present darkness… the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places” — what the rest of the Bible calls the devil and his angels: personal, intelligent, invisible, organised, and set against God and his people. They are not a figure of speech for social pressures, though they work through people and systems.

They work by “schemes” — planned methods — and you can learn to recognise them. Accusation: Satan is called “the accuser of our brothers” (Rev. 12:10), and he keeps a believer going over sins the cross has already settled. (Conviction from God leads to repentance and freedom; condemnation goes round in circles.) Deception, beginning as it did in Eden with a question: “Did God actually say…?” (Gen. 3:1). Division in the church, through the anger and slander Paul has just warned against (4:26–27, 31). Discouragement, which persuades a soldier to lay down his arms. And plain distraction: a life so full that no room is left for prayer and Scripture.

The Ephesians needed no persuading. They had seen the seven sons of Sceva overpowered when they used Jesus’ name as a formula, watched converts burn their magic books, and lived through the riot over Artemis (Acts 19).

Two errors, and two disputed questions. One error empties the passage: the powers are only a way of talking about psychology and society, so the armour is a metaphor for trying harder. The other sees a demon behind every difficulty, and treats depression, illness or plain sin as needing deliverance rather than a doctor, repentance or a hard conversation. Paul avoids both. He never tells believers to hunt, name or bind these powers; he tells them to put on the armour and stand. Some teach that a Christian can be inhabited by a demon. But a believer is sealed by the Holy Spirit as God’s own (1:13–14), and God “has delivered us from the domain of darkness” (Col. 1:13): a Christian can be tempted, deceived and attacked, but not owned. Others teach that territorial spirits over cities must be mapped and bound, pointing to “the prince of the kingdom of Persia” (Dan. 10:13). Daniel shows that such powers are real, but he never addressed them; he prayed, and God sent help. Our part is the armour and prayer.

In real life. The attack rarely looks dramatic. A new believer, ashamed of a returning sin, stops telling anyone, stops reading his Bible because he feels too unclean, and drifts from his Christian friends — accused into silence. Two church leaders let a disagreement go cold, and within two years there are two camps and no outreach. A busy professional misses church one month, then most months, and three years later prays only in emergencies. In each case the answer is the same: name the real enemy, stop treating people as the enemy, and stand in the whole armour — truth, Christ’s righteousness, peace with God, faith, the hope of salvation, God’s word and prayer.
verseByVerse.note: Paul may have written with a Roman soldier guarding him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Paul means. “Therefore”: given an enemy like that, putting on the armour is not optional for the especially keen; it is the only sensible response. Paul changes the verb. In verse 11, “put on” is the word for getting dressed; here, “take up” is the word for a soldier picking up his equipment when the alarm sounds. Both are needed: armour you live in every day, and armour you seize in the moment of attack.

The armour is for “the evil day.” Paul may mean the whole present age (“the days are evil,” 5:16) or particular days of fierce attack; both are true. Either way the armour has to be on before the attack, because nobody puts on armour in the middle of an assault. And the goal is modest: “having done all, to stand firm.” Not to win, advance or see results, but to be still on your feet at the end. The war itself was won at the cross, where Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame” (Col. 2:15). The believer’s task is not to win that war again but to refuse to give up the ground.

In real life. Learn to recognise an evil day. Sometimes it is a phone call, a scan result or a sentence from your spouse that changes everything. Just as often it is quieter: the afternoon a temptation suddenly feels overwhelming, the week God seems silent, the evening you are drafting a reply meant to wound and enjoying it. What holds you then is what you did on ordinary days — the reading, the habit of prayer, short accounts with God, friends allowed to ask you hard questions. So test yourself. Think of the last really hard thing that happened to you, and what you actually reached for on the first day. If it was distraction, or someone to agree with you, that is not a verdict on your faith; it is a report on your ordinary weeks, and this week can be different. And if this year feels like failure — the marriage still hard, the depression not lifted, the prayer unanswered — but you are still believing and still coming back to God, Paul calls that standing. It is not a consolation prize. It is the goal.

verseByVerse.quote: Stand therefore, having fastened on the belt of truth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
What it was. The Roman soldier’s belt was the first thing he put on and the thing everything else hung from. It gathered his tunic so it would not tangle his legs, and it carried his sword. A soldier with his belt on was ready for duty; without it he was ready for nothing.

What Paul means. Truth comes first because the enemy’s chief weapon is the lie. Jesus called the devil “a liar and the father of lies” (John 8:44), and nearly every attack in this chapter is a lie in some form: accusation lies about your standing with God, temptation lies about what will satisfy you, discouragement lies about what God is doing. In Ephesians truth has two sides, and Paul means both. It is the truth God has spoken — “the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation” (1:13). And it is truthfulness in the believer — “having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbor” (4:25). The first tells you what is real; the second keeps you living in it. A man who believes the gospel but lives a double life has his belt hanging loose, and he will trip over his own clothes when the pressure comes. The image is Isaiah’s, where the coming King wears righteousness and faithfulness as “the belt of his waist” (Isa. 11:5). Christ wore this belt first.

Notice how the sentence is built. “Stand” is the main verb, and the pieces hang from it: “having fastened… having put on…” Paul is not adding six new tasks to the command to stand. He is describing what standing looks like.

In real life. Most of us do not tell outright lies; we shade. The figure rounded in our favour, the wrong impression we let stand, the story in which we come out a little better than we did. The belt loosens one notch at a time, and every notch is easy to deny. So for one week, notice them — count them instead of defending them — and put each one right. Two habits keep the belt tight. Fill your mind with what God says, because a lie is hard to spot in a mind that has nothing true to measure it against. And give one trusted friend permission to tell you what they see, because self-deception is the one lie that arrives already believed. Integrity is a command, but it is also a relief: a man with one story has nothing to keep track of. David, who hid his sin for months, said “my bones wasted away” (Ps. 32:3). The man with nothing to hide can sleep.
verseByVerse.note: The soldier’s belt held his tunic and sword in place.

parallels.desc: righteousness shall be the belt of his waist

verseByVerse.quote: and having put on the breastplate of righteousness,
verseByVerse.commentary:
What it was. The breastplate covered the chest — the heart and lungs. A soldier could fight on with a cut arm or a bruised leg; a blade through the chest ended the fight. This piece guarded the place where a blow was fatal.

What Paul means. Righteousness guards the heart against the enemy’s deadliest attack, which is accusation (Rev. 12:10 calls him “the accuser of our brothers”). The image again comes from Isaiah, where the LORD himself “put on righteousness as a breastplate” (Isa. 59:17): it is God’s righteousness before it is ever ours. Two things are meant, and both matter. First and chiefly, the righteousness of Christ counted to the believer: you stand before God not in your own record but in his. Second, the practical righteousness of an obedient life, which Paul has been describing since chapter 4.

The first answers the accusation that actually undoes Christians. It is usually not a lie but a true fact, brought up at the worst moment: you did that. A defence that depends on denying the charge collapses the day the charge is true. Paul does not deny the record; he points to the Judge. “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died” (Rom. 8:33–34). The second matters too. Deliberate, unconfessed sin cannot cancel Christ’s righteousness, but it leaves a buckle undone: it drains your confidence and gives “opportunity to the devil” (4:27).

In real life.
