When you fall into the old sin again and the voice says, “a real Christian wouldn’t do this — don’t bother going back to God,” do not answer with your good points: “but I also served, gave, tried.” That is cardboard, and it will not hold. Answer with Christ: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:1). Confess the sin, get up and go on. If you have confessed many times and still feel filthy, remember that armour is not a feeling. You know it was there because, after the blow, you are still standing and still coming back to God. And remember where this breastplate came from. Christ went into his own decisive battle with nothing over his heart, and “one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear” (John 19:34). He left his heart uncovered so that yours could be covered.

parallels.desc: he put on righteousness as a breastplate

verseByVerse.ref: v. 15 — The Shoes of the Gospel of Peace
verseByVerse.quote: and, as shoes for your feet, having put on the readiness given by the gospel of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What it was. Roman soldiers wore heavy sandal-boots with studded soles, strapped tight to the foot. In close fighting the enemy tried first to knock a man off his feet, because a man who slips is easily finished, and one man down opens a gap in the line. Good footing decided battles.

What Paul means. The footing God gives is “the readiness given by the gospel of peace.” Paul has already explained this peace: Christ “himself is our peace” (2:14), and he has ended the hostility between God and us. That is solid ground: God is no longer against me. The picture comes from Isaiah: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace” (Isa. 52:7) — the runner bringing news of a victory already won. So the shoes do two things. They let you stand firm, because your war with God is over. And they make you ready to move, carrying that news to others. (The word for “readiness” can mean either being prepared or having a firm footing; both fit.)

Do not confuse peace with God and the peace of God. “We have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 5:1) is a fact, like a signed treaty, and it does not change with your mood. “The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4:7) is something you feel, and it comes and goes with sleep, health and circumstances. You can lie awake anxious at three in the morning and still be standing on ground that has not moved an inch.

In real life. Test your footing like this: does God seem warmer to you after a good week and colder after a bad one? If so, you are standing on your record, not on the treaty, and your record will give way just when you need it. Go back to Romans 5:1 and stand there. Then the readiness. Peter describes it as “always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you” (1 Pet. 3:15). You are not told to hunt for conversations, but to be ready when someone asks. Could you say in three plain sentences, without church words, what the good news is and what it has done for you? If not, that is this week’s lace to tie. And hold on to the promise at the end of Romans: “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Rom. 16:20) — the very feet he is trying to knock from under you.
verseByVerse.note: Roman soldiers wore sturdy studded sandals for a firm footing.

parallels.desc: the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace

verseByVerse.quote: In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What it was. The Roman shield was not a small round buckler but a large curved board about four feet tall, made of wood and covered with leather, big enough to hide most of a man. Soldiers could lock them together into a wall. Armies shot fire arrows to set men and gear alight; the shield caught them before they did their damage.

What Paul means. The shield is faith: trusting that what God has said is true and that what Christ has done is enough. The “flaming darts of the evil one” are his sudden attacks — a doubt that lands out of nowhere, a fierce temptation, a wave of fear, an ugly or despairing thought. A fire arrow does not need to kill you; it only needs to lodge somewhere and start a fire. That is how such thoughts work: one suggestion catches another, until an hour later you believe something you would never have accepted as a single sentence. Faith puts the fire out by answering the lie with what God has said. Notice that Paul changes the verb here. The belt, breastplate and shoes are put on and worn; the shield must be “taken up” — grabbed in the moment of attack.

Two comforts. First, the arrival of the thought is not your sin. You did not fire it. It becomes yours only when you welcome it and give it room to burn; the horror you feel at it is the shield doing its work. Second, the shield’s strength does not depend on the strength of your grip. Faith saves because of what it holds, not because of how firmly it holds. Weak faith in a strong Christ is safe. The father who cried, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24) was not sent away; his son was healed.

In real life. Most Christians are hit by the same two or three darts for years: you’re a fraud; God is tired of you; you will never change. Name yours. Write down the sentence in the exact words it uses on you, because unnamed it feels like the truth and written down it looks like what it is. Then find the promise that answers it — against condemnation, Romans 8:1; against “God has left you”, Romans 8:38–39 — and learn it now, because nobody builds an argument well at two in the morning. And do not fight alone. Roman shields worked as a wall. In a hard season you may be covered by the faith of others when you can barely lift your own, so stay where other believers are holding theirs (cf. 1 Pet. 5:9).
verseByVerse.note: The Roman shield was large, about four feet tall, wood covered with leather; soldiers could lock shields into a wall.

parallels.desc: he is a shield for all those who take refuge in him

verseByVerse.quote: and take the helmet of salvation,
verseByVerse.commentary:
What it was. The helmet protected the head. A blow there might not kill, but it could stun and confuse, and a dazed soldier soon dropped everything else. No soldier went into battle bareheaded.

What Paul means. The helmet is salvation — God’s rescue in all its tenses. You have been saved (2:8), you are being kept, and you will be fully saved on “the day of redemption” (4:30). Paul makes the point plainly elsewhere: “for a helmet the hope of salvation” (1 Thess. 5:8). The helmet guards the mind with certainty about how your story ends. The enemy’s aim here is despair: not chiefly to make you sin, but to persuade you that standing is pointless, so that you put the shield down yourself. Once more the piece is God’s own. Isaiah saw the LORD put on “a helmet of salvation on his head” (Isa. 59:17) when no one else could save. You are not asked to make this helmet, only to take it.

That matters, because assurance is what anxious Christians most often try to manufacture. God wants you to have it: John wrote “that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13). It rests first on God’s promise, which stands outside you — “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). Then on the Spirit’s witness that you are God’s child (Rom. 8:16). And only third on the evidence of a changed life. Troubled believers usually reverse that order and spend the night examining themselves. Look at Christ first.

In real life. Finish this sentence honestly: “When ______ happens, I’ll be all right.” When the scan is clear, when the money comes in, when this season ends. Whatever you wrote is what you are actually wearing on your head, and any of it can be knocked off by one phone call. The hope of salvation cannot. If your assurance has gone, ask why. If there is a specific sin, confess it; the relief often comes quickly. If there is only fog, remember that you have a body. Grief, exhaustion and depression speak in your own voice about God, so be slow to trust your verdict on your soul after weeks without sleep. When Elijah wanted to die, God first let him sleep and fed him (1 Kgs. 19:5–8).

parallels.desc: a helmet of salvation on his head

verseByVerse.ref: v. 17b — The Sword of the Spirit
verseByVerse.quote: and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
What it was. The Roman soldier’s sword was short, a stabbing blade for close combat, and legionaries were trained to close in and fight at arm’s length. It is the one piece in Paul’s list made for attacking rather than protecting.

What Paul means. This is the only piece Paul explains, so that no one can mistake it: “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” It is the Spirit’s sword because he gave the word and he makes it cut: “the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword” (Heb. 4:12). Jesus showed how it is used. Tempted in the wilderness, he answered the devil three times with “It is written” (Matt. 4:4, 7, 10). All three answers come from Deuteronomy 6–8, Moses’ sermon on Israel’s forty years in the wilderness — where Israel failed at exactly the points where Jesus was now being tempted. He did not pick verses at random. He knew which battle he was in and answered from the place in Scripture that spoke to it. And when the devil quoted Scripture at him (Psalm 91), Jesus did not drop the Bible. He said, “Again it is written”: Scripture rightly read answers Scripture twisted.

So the sword is not cleverness, and it is not Bible verses swung as a club to win arguments. It is God’s word, believed and spoken at close quarters: against the lie in your own head, in the conversation you are actually in, at the moment of temptation.

In real life. You do not need to master all sixty-six books before the sword is of any use. Jesus won with a few chapters of one book that he had made his own. Take the dart you named at verse 16, find the verse that answers it, and carry it with you until you know it by heart. Jesus promised that the Spirit “will… bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you” (John 14:26). He reminds, so he can only bring back what has gone in; the ordinary mornings of reading are sword practice. And when the lie comes, say the verse out loud, as Jesus did. A silent thought arguing with another thought in a tired head is an even fight; a word of God spoken aloud is something from outside you. It feels strange for a few seconds, and then it does not.
verseByVerse.note: The Roman sword was a short blade for close combat.

parallels.desc: he made my mouth like a sharp sword

verseByVerse.quote: praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Paul means. Prayer is not a seventh piece of armour; it is how the whole armour is worn. Every piece comes from God, and prayer is how the soldier keeps drawing on him. Paul says “all” four times: at all times, with all prayer, with all perseverance, for all the saints — no moment, no kind of prayer and no believer is left out. “In the Spirit” is not a special technique; this letter has already explained it: “through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (2:18). You pray to the Father, through the Son, helped by the Spirit, who “helps us in our weakness” when we do not know what to pray (Rom. 8:26). So halting prayer is not second-rate prayer. (Some take the phrase to mean praying in tongues, cf. 1 Cor. 14:15; Paul’s own use in this letter points to the access the Spirit gives.)

“Keep alert” is a sentry’s word: stay awake and watch. The disciples slept in Gethsemane when Jesus asked them to watch and pray (Matt. 26:40–41). And Paul pairs “prayer” with “supplication” — particular requests for particular needs.

In real life. Pray specifically: name the person, the job interview, the scan, the son. Prayer that risks nothing specific can never be seen to be answered. Keep watch over the people God has put near you — the friend who has gone quiet, the marriage that has changed its tone, the man who has stopped coming — and turn what you notice into prayer; your prayer may be the shield they do not know they are standing behind. When you are weary of praying for the same person after years, remember that Jesus told a parable “to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1). If a persistent widow could move an unjust judge, how much more will your Father, who is not unwilling, hear his children. Perseverance is not pressure on God; it is refusing to conclude that he is not listening. And pray for “all the saints” — including three Christians you find difficult. It is very hard to go on resenting someone you are asking God to bless.

verseByVerse.quote: and also for me, that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains, that I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Paul means. Having armed the church, Paul asks it to pray for him — not for release from prison, but for boldness to speak. “That words may be given to me”: even the apostle depends on God for what to say. He calls himself “an ambassador in chains,” and the phrase is meant to shock. In the ancient world an ambassador’s person was protected; to chain one was an insult to the king who sent him. Rome has chained the envoy of the King of kings, yet the chain has not cancelled his commission. It even became his pulpit: soldiers took turns guarding him, and he could write that the gospel had become known “throughout the whole imperial guard” (Phil. 1:13).

What he wants boldness to say is “the mystery of the gospel,” which this letter has defined: the Gentiles are “fellow heirs, members of the same body” (3:6). That message is the reason he is in chains — the riot in Jerusalem began with the charge that he had brought Greeks into the temple (Acts 21:28). He asks them to pray that he will keep saying the very thing that cost him his freedom.

Courage was not Paul’s natural temperament. He told the Corinthians, “I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (1 Cor. 2:3), and the Lord once had to say to him in the night, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent” (Acts 18:9). His boldness was given to him again and again, in answer to prayer.

In real life. If your mouth goes dry when a conversation turns to faith, nothing is wrong with you; the apostle needed help with the same thing. Ask for the words, as Jesus promised: “what you are to say will be given to you in that hour” (Matt. 10:19) — and still prepare, as Paul did. Then look at your own prayer requests from the last year. Most of us ask only for things to change: the illness healed, the job found. Paul, facing a capital charge, asked for help to be faithful inside the situation that was not changing. Asking for relief is not wrong; Paul asked three times for his thorn to be taken away (2 Cor. 12:8–9). But it is poor to ask for nothing else. And pray for your church’s preachers and missionaries as Paul asked to be prayed for: not chiefly for their comfort, but for their mouths.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The letter that began before the foundation of the world ends with the most human of moments — a friend carrying a message, a shepherd anxious for his flock, a blessing spoken over people he loves and misses. Tychicus, “the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord” (v.21), will carry the letter from Rome to Ephesus. He will not only deliver the words; he will bring the news of Paul himself, so that the Ephesians may know how their apostle is faring, and so that their hearts may be comforted. The cosmic letter is delivered by a trusted friend. The theological monument is wrapped in pastoral care.

Paul's parting benediction is one of the most theologically compressed sentences in the letter — four words, each one a world: peace, love, faith, grace. These are not conventional closing pleasantries; they are a final summation, a last gathering-up of the letter's great themes into the shortest possible form.

Peace — the peace that Christ made between God and man and between Jew and Gentile, the peace that passes understanding, the peace the Spirit-filled community is called to live in and preserve. Love — the love of the Father, the love of Christ who gave himself up, the love that is the first fruit of the Spirit and the walk this letter commands (5:2). Faith — the gift through which grace is received, the shield that quenches every fiery dart, the channel of union with Christ. Grace — the beginning and the end, the undeserved and inexhaustible kindness that is the source of every blessing the letter has described.

The closing phrase — “Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible” — is quietly magnificent. The grace of God is offered not to those who have performed well or achieved much or maintained perfect doctrine, but to those who love the Lord Jesus with genuine, undying love. This love is not a prerequisite for grace — grace produces it. But it is the mark of those on whom the final blessing rests. The letter that began with the love of God from before the foundation of the world ends with the love of the people of God for their Lord — the response of the beloved to the One who loved them first.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace as the Alpha and Omega of the Christian Life

Ephesians begins with grace (1:2: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ”) and ends with grace (6:24: “Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ”). The entire letter is enclosed within this grace — and this is not merely a rhetorical device. It is a theological statement: the Christian life from first to last, from election before time began to the consummation of all things, is entirely an affair of grace. There is no moment in the Christian's experience that is not sustained by grace, no achievement that is not the fruit of grace, no prayer that is answered by anything other than grace.

The Reformed tradition has consistently defined grace as God's undeserved favour — not merely his assistance added to human effort, but his sovereign initiative in the face of human helplessness. Ephesians 2:8–9 defines salvation by grace through faith, with the explicit denial that this is our own doing. But grace is not only the initial gift; it is the sustaining reality of the entire Christian life. “I am what I am by the grace of God,” Paul writes to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 15:10). The letter to the Ephesians is the fullest exposition of what that grace is, what it has done, and what it looks like in the life of those who have received it.

Tychicus — the letter-carrier, the beloved brother, the faithful minister — is himself a theological figure in the ending of the letter. He represents the ordinary, faithful, unglamorous work of ministry that keeps the church alive between the apostolic moments: the friend who carries the letter, who brings the news, who comforts the worried flock. Every church is sustained by Tychicuses — people whose names are not famous, whose ministry is not spectacular, who are simply faithful. The letter that contains the most magnificent theology in the New Testament is delivered by one such person. Grace works through the ordinary.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul is in a Roman prison when he writes these final words. He may never see the Ephesians again. His benediction — “peace... love... faith... grace be with you” — is spoken over people he cannot reach with his hands or his presence, people he is releasing into the care of the God about whom he has been writing for six chapters.

This is what pastoral love looks like at its most costly and most beautiful: the shepherd who cannot be with his flock entrusting them to the Chief Shepherd, speaking blessing over them, sending them a trusted friend, and then releasing them in faith. Paul's imprisonment did not imprison his hope. The chains on his wrists did not chain the word of God (2 Timothy 2:9). The letter reached Ephesus. The grace it describes reached its readers. It reaches us still.

Now: “Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible.” The word translated “incorruptible” (aphtharsia) is the same word used for the resurrection body — imperishable, undying, not subject to decay. The love of the true believer for Christ is not a passing emotion or a seasonal feeling; it is something that has been planted by God in a soul that has been made alive in Christ, and it partakes of the imperishable quality of its Object.

This love will outlast every earthly thing. It will survive death, outlast time, and find its perfect and eternal fulfilment at the Marriage Supper of the Lamb. The letter ends with this love — and this love, in its countless expressions across the centuries, has carried the gospel from Rome to Ephesus to the ends of the earth, and to us. Grace to you. And peace. And love incorruptible.

verseByVerse.quote: So that you also may know how I am and what I am doing, Tychicus the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord will tell you everything. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are, and that he may encourage your hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tychicus appears as Paul’s personal courier and pastoral representative (cf. Acts 20:4; Col. 4:7). He will not only deliver the letter but report on Paul’s circumstances and encourage the community. The personal dimensions of Paul’s ministry are always present even in his most doctrinal letters. Theology is never abstract; it is always carried by people who love one another.

Begin with the man, because he is easy to walk past and the New Testament will not let us. Tychicus is named five times in the New Testament, four of them in Paul’s letters, and the pattern is always the same: he is going somewhere for somebody else. He is from Asia and travels with Paul toward Jerusalem (Acts 20:4). He carries Colossians, with the same commission almost word for word (Col. 4:7–8). He is sent to Ephesus again years later (2 Tim. 4:12), and Paul considers sending him to Crete to relieve Titus (Titus 3:12).

Not one sermon of his survives. Not one sentence he wrote. We do not know whether he was married, how old he was, or where he died. What we know is that when something needed carrying several hundred miles to people who were anxious, Paul thought of Tychicus.

And consider what he was actually holding on that road. Somewhere in his luggage, between Rome and the coast of Asia, was the only copy in existence of the letter you have just finished reading — chosen before the foundation of the world, raised and seated with Christ, the mystery of the Gentiles, the husband and the wife, the whole armour of God. There was no second copy in a drawer in Rome. If Tychicus had lost the bag, or turned back, or decided the journey was more than he could face, we would not have Ephesians. The most magnificent theology in the New Testament travelled to us in the hands of a man about whom we know almost nothing, and it arrived because he was reliable.

Which is why the two words Paul gives him are worth weighing rather than skimming. Beloved brother — the language of family and affection, not of employment; and faithful minister, where the word is diakonos, a servant, and the adjective is the one that matters. Not gifted. Not impressive. Not eloquent. Faithful — the quality of a man who does what he said he would do, on the day he said he would do it, whether or not anybody is watching. It is the least glamorous virtue in the Christian vocabulary and it is the one Scripture reaches for most often when it wants to say that a life counted for something.

So a word to a particular reader, who is more common in every congregation than anyone admits. You have been a Christian for years. You are not the preacher, you do not lead anything much, nobody would put you on a platform, and you have quietly concluded that your part in all this is decorative — that the real work is done by other people and you make up the numbers.

Look at the last four verses of this letter. When Paul has finished writing about the eternal purpose of God, he hands the whole thing to an ordinary man and sends him on a journey. Every church is held up by Tychicuses: the woman who has opened the building on Sunday mornings for nineteen years, the man who drives two elderly members to church and back and has never once mentioned it, the person who noticed a family had stopped coming and went round. None of them will be named in a history. All of them are doing the thing this verse honours, and the letter you love is in your hands because somebody like them carried it.

Then verse 22, which tells us why Paul is really sending him, and it is not the letter. “I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are, and that he may encourage your hearts.” Read that as the Ephesians would have.

Their apostle, the man who had spent three years among them and wept with them at Miletus (Acts 20:31, 36–38), was in custody in Rome awaiting the judgment of Nero, and they had no way of finding out whether he was alive. There was no post, no messenger service, no way to ask. There was only rumour, and the distance, and the silence — and anyone who has ever waited for news about someone they love knows exactly what that silence does to a person at two in the morning.

So Paul, who is the one in chains, spends his letter-carrier on their peace of mind. He does not merely mention his circumstances in a closing line; he sends a man on a journey of many weeks so that they will not have to keep imagining. And notice the verb, because Paul chooses it deliberately: parakaleō, to encourage, to comfort, to come alongside — the verb from which the Spirit’s own title, the Helper, is drawn (John 14:16). Tychicus is not being sent to inform them. He is being sent to steady them.

There is a lesson here that costs nothing and is almost never taken. Most of the anxiety people carry about those they love is not caused by bad news; it is caused by no news. Paul, with a capital charge hanging over him, understood that the kindest thing he could do for a church hundreds of miles away was to let them know how he was. Which is worth turning into something you actually do this week, since the whole letter has been pressing toward a life lived for other people: somebody is quietly wondering about you and will not ask. Tell them how you are. And somebody else has gone silent, and you have assumed the silence means nothing much. Go and find out.

The letter that began before the foundation of the world ends with a friend on a road, carrying news so that some worried people in Asia can sleep. God’s eternal purpose is enormous, and it moves at the speed of an ordinary man keeping his word.
verseByVerse.note: Tychicus came from the province of Asia and carried this letter and Colossians.

verseByVerse.quote: Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The final blessing moves through four gifts: peace, love, faith, grace. Each is sourced in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ — the same divine source that opened the letter in 1:2. The letter is a theological arch: the grace and peace invoked at the beginning is the grace and peace pronounced at the close. What God began in eternity he brings to completion in time.

“All who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible” — a love that cannot rot or die. The love of the believer for Christ is not a fragile human affection; it is a love that participates in the imperishable life of the age to come. It is the love of those who have been sealed by the Spirit for the day of redemption. It cannot finally perish, because the one who is loved cannot perish, and the love itself is his gift.

That is the note the whole letter ends on: the love of Christ for his people is incorruptible — and so, by his gift, is theirs for him. This is not sentiment; it is certainty. The believer who feels weak at the finish is still utterly safe, because this love began before the foundation of the world (1:4) and ends in the same love on the last day.

Those four words are not a pleasant way of signing off, and it is worth refusing to let them blur, because every one of them has an address in this letter. Peace is not calm feelings: it is the war ended at 2:14–17, where Christ “himself is our peace”, the dividing wall pulled down and peace preached to the far off and the near — and it is what the soldier was standing on eight verses ago.

Love is the letter’s first movement and its last: in love he predestined us (1:4–5), “the great love with which he loved us” while we were dead (2:4), the love that surpasses knowledge (3:19), the love the church is to walk in (5:2) and a husband to spend himself on (5:25).

Faith is the empty hand of 2:8 and the shield of 6:16. And grace is the word this letter cannot stop saying — the grace he lavished (1:7–8), by which you have been saved (2:5, 8), given even to the least of all the saints (3:8), and measured out to every believer (4:7). Paul is not wishing them well. He is handing back, in four words, everything he has spent six chapters unfolding.

And notice the odd pairing in the middle: “love with faith”. It reads strangely until you remember how the letter opened. Paul began by telling them what he had heard about them — “your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints” (1:15) — and prayed in the middle of it that Christ would dwell in their hearts through faith, so that they would be rooted and grounded in love (3:17). The same two, at the beginning, the centre and the end — only now love comes first. He is not adding a new thought at the door. He is asking God to keep giving them the thing he thanked God for on the first page.

Then something easy to miss, and it changes who is standing in the room. Throughout six chapters Paul has said you — you were dead, you were sealed, you are light, put on the whole armour. Here, in the last two sentences of the letter, he stops addressing them directly: peace be to the brothers, grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ.

He turns and speaks about them rather than to them. The most likely reason is the one noted at 1:1 — that this letter was written to be carried from congregation to congregation and read aloud in each. So Paul deliberately leaves the last blessing unaddressed. It is not pronounced over the Ephesians as against anybody else; it is pronounced over whoever is in the room when the letter is read out. Which is to say it was left open on purpose, and you are in the room.

Look, then, at how he describes the people the final grace is for, because he could have said many things and says only one. Not “all who have understood this letter” — and after three chapters on election, the mystery, and the heavenly places, that would have been a fair anxiety. Not those who have got their doctrine straight, or their household in order, or their armour properly buckled. All who love our Lord Jesus Christ. It is at once the lowest bar in the letter and the most searching, because a man can pass a doctrine examination he does not mean, and can behave well for a season out of fear or habit, but nobody sustains love for a person he does not actually love.

Which raises the question the anxious reader will ask, and it must not be left hanging: how do I know whether I love him? One guard first. This is a description of the people grace rests on, not a condition they met to obtain it — the whole letter forbids that reading, since love for Christ is not the price of grace but its product; we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). The last sentence is not the one place where Ephesians changes its mind and puts something back on your account.

And then the answer itself, which Scripture gives in a scene rather than a definition. On a beach in Galilee, a man who had denied three times that he knew Jesus is asked three times whether he loves him. Peter does not appeal to his feelings, and he certainly does not appeal to his record — he has just wrecked it.

He appeals over his own head to the one asking: “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you” (John 21:17). That is what love for Christ looks like on a bad day, and it is available to you.

So do not run the test as do I feel warmly toward him?, which will tell you mostly about your sleep and your circumstances. Run it as direction: in the worst week you have had this year, did some part of you still want him — even while you were avoiding him? Does it still gladden you, somewhere under the numbness, to hear him spoken well of? Would you rather be near him than not, if you could? A man who can answer yes to that, however faintly, is described by this verse, and the blessing at the end of Ephesians has his name in it.

Finally, the word Paul chooses for that love, because he could have said “sincere” or “faithful” and instead reached for something startling. Aphtharsia is a resurrection word. It is what Paul says happens to a body: sown perishable, raised imperishable (1 Cor. 15:42, 53–54); it is what Christ brought to light through the gospel (2 Tim. 1:10).

So the love a Christian has for Christ — which today may feel thin, distracted, and considerably less than he wishes it were — is made of the same material as the resurrection body. It does not decay. It will not be left behind in the grave with everything else that perishes; it goes through and comes out the other side, and what happens to it there is that it finally becomes what it has always been trying to be.

Which is how the letter ends. The last word Paul writes to these churches, in the Greek, is that one: imperishable. A letter that opened before the foundation of the world closes beyond the reach of decay — and everything in between, the choosing, the raising, the wall pulled down, the household, the armour, is held between those two points. Nothing in it started with you, and nothing in it can rot.
